provenance.rightsNote: Lectio Edition (SDIT): clear modern English of Dante, synthesized from the public-domain translation tradition (Longfellow 1867; Cary 1814; Norton's prose 1892) and checked against the Italian; modern verse translations consulted, not quoted. Verse lines kept. In progress, canto by canto.
sourcesCited: Charles Eliot Norton, prose (1892, public domain)
modern verse translations (Ciardi, Mandelbaum, Hollander, consulted, not quoted)

character: Plain modern English — the sense of the original, made to read with ease today.
overview: The Lectio Edition renders Dante in clear modern English that keeps the forward pull of the journey and the sharpness of his images, without the inversions and archaism of the older verse. Kept line by line, canticle by canticle.
introduction: Longfellow's 1867 Dante is faithful and grave, but its nineteenth-century inversions slow a modern reader. The Lectio Edition keeps Dante's line-by-line structure and his concrete, startling imagery — the dark wood, the gates of Hell, the souls like autumn leaves — in English that moves the way Dante moves. The older verse translations and the Italian are a tap away.

divergences.phrase: selva oscura
divergences.older: a forest dark (Longfellow); a gloomy wood (Cary)
divergences.lectio: a dark wood
divergences.note: Longfellow's inverted 'a forest dark' is the kind of nineteenth-century word-order that trips a modern reader; the Italian is plainly noun-then-adjective, 'dark wood.' We keep it concrete and unadorned — it is the canto's master image.

divergences.phrase: là dove 'l sol tace
divergences.older: where the sun is silent (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the place where the sun is silent
divergences.note: Dante writes that the sun is silent, not merely dark — a deliberate crossing of senses (a place where light has gone so dead it has no voice). We keep the strangeness rather than tidy it into 'where the sun never shines.'

divergences.phrase: tra feltro e feltro
divergences.older: 'Twixt Feltro and Feltro (Longfellow); 'Twixt either Feltro (Cary)
divergences.lectio: between felt and felt
divergences.note: The veltro's (Greyhound's) birthplace is one of the most debated lines in the poem — whether 'feltro' means the towns Feltre and Montefeltro, humble felt cloth, or something else. The line is meant to be a riddle, so we keep it as a riddle rather than resolve it for the reader.

divergences.phrase: Beatrice am I, who do bid thee go
divergences.older: I am Beatrice, who do bid thee go; / I come from there, where I would fain return; / Love moved me, which compelleth me to speak.
divergences.lectio: I am Beatrice, who send you on this. / I come from the place I long to return to. / Love moved me, and makes me speak.
divergences.note: Italian 'Amor mi mosse, che mi fa parlare' — the engine of the whole rescue is love, stated plainly. We keep the simple subject 'Love' so it lands as a force, not a flourish, and drop 'fain'/'compelleth.'

divergences.phrase: I not Aeneas am, I am not Paul
divergences.older: I not Aeneas am, I am not Paul, / Nor I, nor others, think me worthy of it.
divergences.lectio: I am not Aeneas, I am not Paul. / Neither I nor anyone thinks me worthy of it.
divergences.note: Dante's 'Io non Enea, io non Paulo sono' is two stark, parallel denials — the hinge of the canto's self-doubt. We straighten Longfellow's inverted word order so the repetition hits like the original's, with nothing between the reader and the names.

divergences.phrase: the smallest of the heavens
divergences.older: all contained / Within the heaven that has the lesser circles
divergences.lectio: all that the smallest of the heavens holds
divergences.note: 'Il ciel c'ha minor li cerchi sui' is the sphere of the Moon, whose orbit is smallest — i.e., everything beneath the heavens, the whole sublunary world. We name the cosmology plainly rather than reproduce Longfellow's 'lesser circles,' which leaves a modern reader guessing.

divergences.phrase: Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate
divergences.older: All hope abandon, ye who enter in! (Longfellow); All hope abandon, ye who enter here (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Abandon every hope, you who enter here.
divergences.note: The most famous line carved over Hell's gate. Longfellow's inverted 'All hope abandon, ye who enter in' is exactly the archaic word-order The Vernacular removes. The Italian is a plain, terrible imperative — verb, object, then the address — so we keep it that way: 'Abandon every hope.' We say 'every' (ogne) rather than 'all,' since Dante stresses each separate hope being given up, and 'here' for the gate the reader is standing at.

divergences.phrase: che fece per viltade il gran rifiuto
divergences.older: Who made through cowardice the great refusal (Longfellow); who in his cowardice / Made the great refusal (Cary)
divergences.lectio: who out of cowardice made the great refusal
divergences.note: Dante deliberately leaves this shade unnamed — most readers take it for Pope Celestine V, who abdicated the papacy, but the poem will not say so. We keep the figure anonymous and keep the resonant phrase 'the great refusal' intact rather than explaining it, because the withholding is the point.

divergences.phrase: Come d'autunno si levan le foglie
divergences.older: As in the autumn-time the leaves fall off (Longfellow); As fall off the light autumnal leaves (Cary)
divergences.lectio: The way the leaves let go in autumn
divergences.note: The canto's central image — the dead dropping one by one into Charon's boat like falling leaves. Dante's verb is 'si levan' (lift away / let go), gentler and stranger than 'fall off.' We keep that releasing motion ('let go') so the simile carries the eerie willingness Dante gives it, matching the falling-leaves image already named in this edition's overview.

divergences.phrase: cignesi con la coda tante volte / quantunque gradi vuol che giù sia messa
divergences.older: Girds himself with his tail as many times / As grades he wishes it should be thrust down (Longfellow); Girds him with his tail. As many times / As he would have it thrust into the abyss (Cary)
divergences.lectio: coils his tail around himself as many times / as the number of circles it must be flung down
divergences.note: Minos, the infernal judge, assigns each soul its circle by the grotesque mechanism of winding his tail: the number of coils is the number of the circle. Longfellow's 'girds himself' and 'grades' obscure the physical image. We keep the concrete, animal motion — a tail coiling — and name 'circles' plainly, since that is what the count means for a reader following the descent.

divergences.phrase: Amor, ch'al cor gentil ratto s'apprende ... Amor, ch'a nullo amato amar perdona ... Amor condusse noi ad una morte
divergences.older: Love, that on gentle heart doth swiftly seize ... Love, that exempts no one beloved from loving ... Love has conducted us unto one death (Longfellow); Love, that in gentle heart is quickly learnt ... Love, that denial takes from none beloved ... Love brought us to one death (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Love, which is quick to seize the gentle heart ... Love, which absolves no loved one from loving ... Love led the two of us to a single death.
divergences.note: Francesca's three tercets each open with 'Amor' — an anaphora that is the rhetorical heart of the canto and a deliberate echo of the courtly-love doctrine (Guinizzelli's 'al cor gentil') Dante is at once moved by and judging. We preserve all three 'Love' openings so the drumbeat survives in English, and keep the famous middle line's terrible symmetry — to be loved is to be condemned to love back ('absolves no loved one from loving') — without untangling it into prose. Longfellow's 'exempts' is legalistic but cold; 'absolves' keeps the religious weight Dante sets against this love.

divergences.phrase: Galeotto fu 'l libro e chi lo scrisse
divergences.older: Galeotto was the book and he who wrote it (Longfellow); The book and writer both / Were love's purveyors (Cary)
divergences.lectio: A Galeotto was that book, and the one who wrote it.
divergences.note: In the Lancelot romance Paolo and Francesca were reading, Galehaut (Italian Galeotto) is the go-between who brings Lancelot and Guinevere together — so 'Galeotto' had become an Italian word for a pander, a love's-procurer. Dante's line says the book itself, and its author, played that role for them. We keep the proper noun 'Galeotto' (the architecture of the allusion) but cast it as 'a Galeotto,' so the reader feels it working as the title it has become: the book was their go-between. Cary's 'love's purveyors' explains the pun but loses the name; Longfellow keeps the name but leaves a modern reader stranded. Our phrasing keeps both.

divergences.phrase: 'l maestro di color che sanno
divergences.older: The Master of those who know (Longfellow); the master of the sapient throng (Cary)
divergences.lectio: the master of those who know
divergences.note: Dante's famous title for Aristotle — never named, only honored as the one who masters all knowing. The Italian is plain and absolute: 'the master of those who know.' We keep it exactly, without naming Aristotle for the reader, because the withholding of the name is part of the reverence — to a medieval mind he simply was 'the Philosopher.'

divergences.phrase: un possente, con segno di vittoria coronato
divergences.older: a Mighty One, / With sign of victory incoronate (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: a Mighty One ... crowned with the sign of victory
divergences.note: This is the Harrowing of Hell — Christ descending to free the patriarchs — but Dante, in Virgil's pagan mouth, will not say the name. He gives only 'un possente,' a powerful one, crowned with victory. We keep that veiling ('a Mighty One') and drop Longfellow's Latinate 'incoronate,' since the point is a power Virgil witnessed but could not name.

divergences.phrase: sanza speme vivemo in disio
divergences.older: without hope we live on in desire (Longfellow); we without hope live on in longing (Cary)
divergences.lectio: with no hope, we go on living in longing
divergences.note: The whole sentence of Limbo in five words: not fire, not torment, but desire that can never be answered. We keep the bare antithesis Dante builds — hope set against longing — rather than soften it, because that ache is the precise punishment of the virtuous unbaptized, and the canto turns on it.

divergences.phrase: la parte selvaggia ... colui che testé piaggia
divergences.older: the rustic party / Will drive the other out (Longfellow); the savage part / Shall scatter forth the other (Cary)
divergences.lectio: the party from the woods will drive the other out ... by the power of one who now plays both shores
divergences.note: Ciacco's prophecy is deliberately veiled, and Dante's first readers had to decode it: 'la parte selvaggia' is the White Guelphs (Dante's own side, cast as the 'rustic' or 'woodland' party because its leaders came from the contado), and 'colui che testé piaggia' — literally 'the one who now hugs the coast,' i.e. temporizes, plays both sides — is Pope Boniface VIII, whose backing would restore the Blacks. We keep the veil rather than naming Boniface, because the riddling indirection is the canto's politics; but we render 'piaggia' with its concrete nautical image, 'plays both shores,' instead of Longfellow's flat 'is on the coast.'

divergences.phrase: Giusti son due, e non vi sono intesi; / superbia, invidia e avarizia sono / le tre faville c'hanno i cuori accesi
divergences.older: The just are two, and are not understood there; / Envy and Arrogance and Avarice / Are the three sparks (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: The just are two, and no one there will hear them. / Pride, envy, and greed are the three sparks / that have set every heart on fire.
divergences.note: Dante names the three sins in a fixed order — superbia, invidia, avarizia (pride, envy, avarice) — that he returns to across the poem; Longfellow reshuffles them to 'Envy and Arrogance and Avarice,' losing both the order and the plain word 'pride.' We restore Dante's sequence. And 'non vi sono intesi' is not 'not understood' but 'not heeded, not listened to' — the just men are there but no one in Florence pays them any mind — so we render it 'no one there will hear them.'

divergences.phrase: Ritorna a tua scïenza ... quanto la cosa è più perfetta, / più senta il bene, e così la doglienza
divergences.older: Return unto thy science, / Which wills, that as the thing more perfect is, / The more it feels of pleasure and of pain (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Go back to your science, which holds that the more perfect a thing is, / the more it feels of pleasure and of pain.
divergences.note: Virgil sends Dante back to 'tua scïenza' — Aristotle, the philosophy Dante studied — for the canto's hard doctrine: after the Last Judgment the damned will be reunited with their bodies and so made more complete, and a more perfect being feels everything more keenly, suffering included. The thought is genuinely difficult and we keep it difficult; we only strip Longfellow's archaic 'which wills, that as the thing more perfect is' down to a clause a modern reader can follow, without softening the chilling conclusion that being made whole makes the pain worse.

divergences.phrase: Pape Satàn, pape Satàn aleppe
divergences.older: Pape Satan, Pape Satan, Aleppe! (Longfellow); Ah me! O Satan! Satan! (Cary, who attempts a paraphrase)
divergences.lectio: Pape Satàn, pape Satàn aleppe!
divergences.note: Plutus's opening cry is one of the famous puzzles of the poem — a line of garbled, half-infernal language that no one has ever convincingly translated, and that Dante surely meant to be unintelligible (a few lines later he calls it the 'voce chioccia,' the clucking, strangled voice). Cary tried to make sense of it; Longfellow wisely left it alone. We keep it untouched in the Italian, accents and all, so the reader meets exactly what Dante meant them to meet: noise that means menace without meaning words.

divergences.phrase: Taci, maladetto lupo
divergences.older: Be silent, thou accursed wolf (Longfellow); Peace, cursed wolf (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Be quiet, you cursed wolf.
divergences.note: Virgil silences Plutus by calling him a wolf — the same animal as the she-wolf of greed from Canto I, the beast of insatiable appetite — which fixes this whole circle as the place of avarice before a single hoarder is named. We keep the plain, hard noun 'wolf' rather than softening it, and let 'cursed' carry its full force, because the insult is doing the work of an exorcism.

divergences.phrase: là dove Michele / fé la vendetta del superbo strupo
divergences.older: where Michael wrought / Vengeance upon the proud adultery (Longfellow); where Michael wreak'd / Vengeance upon the proud adultery (Cary)
divergences.lectio: there where Michael / took his vengeance on the proud rebellion.
divergences.note: Dante's 'superbo strupo' refers to the war in Heaven, where the archangel Michael cast down the rebel angels. 'Strupo' is an old, violent word (a doublet of stupro, ravishment / violation), and the older translators render it 'adultery,' which lands strangely on a modern ear and obscures the event. The sin being punished is pride — angels who 'violated' the order of Heaven by revolting. We render it 'the proud rebellion' so a reader instantly knows what Michael's vengeance was for, while keeping 'proud' (superbo), which names the sin.

divergences.phrase: Perché tieni? / Perché burli?
divergences.older: "Why keepest?" and, "Why squanderest thou?" (Longfellow); "Why holdest thou?" "Why throwest away?" (Cary)
divergences.lectio: "Why hoard?" and "Why throw it away?"
divergences.note: The two crowds rolling weights against each other are the hoarders and the spendthrifts, and the entire logic of their punishment is in these two shouted accusations they hurl as they collide — each crowd condemning the other's vice. We keep the curt, taunting two-beat rhythm of the original ('Perché tieni? / Perché burli?'), so the reader hears the eternal argument as a clash and not a translation.

divergences.phrase: ordinò general ministra e duce
divergences.older: Ordained a general ministress and guide (Longfellow); appointed her his general minister and guide (Cary)
divergences.lectio: he set a general minister and guide
divergences.note: Virgil's whole defense of Fortune turns on this word: she is not blind chance but a 'minister' — an angelic intelligence God appointed to govern the shifting of worldly goods, ranked among the other heavenly powers ('the other gods,' as he puts it). We keep 'minister and guide' to preserve that she is an officeholder under God, not a capricious idol; the point of the passage is that mortals curse her wrongly. (See the companion note at VII.91 on 'crucified.')

divergences.phrase: Quest' è colei ch'è tanto posta in croce
divergences.older: And this is she who is so crucified (Longfellow); This is she so reviled (often softened in prose)
divergences.lectio: And this is the one so often nailed to the cross
divergences.note: Dante uses 'posta in croce' — literally put on the cross, crucified — for the abuse people heap on Fortune, a deliberately shocking word that casts her as wrongly condemned, even martyred, by the very people who profit from her. We keep the crucifixion image ('nailed to the cross') rather than flattening it to 'reviled' or 'blamed,' because the violence of the metaphor is the point: those who should praise her instead crucify her with their cursing, and she, blessed, does not even hear it.

divergences.phrase: le sue meschite
divergences.older: Its mosques (Longfellow); the mosques (Cary)
divergences.lectio: its mosques
divergences.note: Dante calls the buildings of the infernal city 'meschite' — mosques — because to a medieval Christian the mosque was the architecture of the enemy faith, so the word marks Dis as utterly hostile ground. The image is strange to a modern reader, but we keep 'mosques' rather than soften it to 'towers' or 'temples,' because the strangeness is the point: this is how Dante's world saw the citadel of the damned.

divergences.phrase: Con piangere e con lutto ... spirito maladetto, ti rimani
divergences.older: With weeping and with wailing, / Thou spirit maledict, do thou remain (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: With your weeping and your wailing, / you cursed spirit, stay right where you are
divergences.note: This is the harsh exchange with Filippo Argenti, and Dante's contempt is meant to be felt, not smoothed. We straighten Longfellow's inverted 'do thou remain' and archaic 'maledict' into plain, cutting modern speech, so the reader hears the cold satisfaction the pilgrim takes in the man's torment — a hardness Dante deliberately stages and Virgil then blesses.

divergences.phrase: le porte ... ne richiusero
divergences.older: They closed the portals, those our adversaries, / On my Lord's breast (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: They slammed the gates, those enemies of ours, / in my lord's face
divergences.note: The fallen angels shut Hell's inner gate against Virgil — the poem's guide, who has never before been refused. Longfellow's 'closed the portals ... on my Lord's breast' is grave but slack. We render the verb hard ('slammed') and put the door 'in his face,' because the humiliation is the dramatic hinge of the canto: even Virgil's authority fails here, and only the coming heavenly messenger will open the way.

divergences.phrase: O voi ch'avete li 'ntelletti sani, / mirate la dottrina che s'asconde / sotto 'l velame de li versi strani
divergences.older: O ye who have undistempered intellects, / Observe the doctrine that conceals itself / Beneath the veil of the mysterious verses! (Longfellow); O ye of sound intellect, mark well the lore / Conceal'd under the veil of strange verse (Cary)
divergences.lectio: O you who have sound and steady minds, / look hard at the teaching that hides itself / beneath the veil of these strange verses.
divergences.note: Dante's most direct address to the reader, breaking the frame to say outright that this scene is an allegory with a hidden meaning. The Italian 'intelletti sani' means healthy, sound minds, not Longfellow's clinical 'undistempered intellects.' We keep the famous metaphor 'veil of strange verses' (velame de li versi strani) intact rather than explaining what lies under it — the whole point of the tercet is that Dante refuses to lift the veil for us, and so do we.

divergences.phrase: passando per lo Stige con le piante asciutte
divergences.older: Was passing o'er the Styx with soles unwet (Longfellow); o'er the Stygian ferry pass'd with unwet feet (Cary)
divergences.lectio: crossing the Styx on foot, his soles never touching the water
divergences.note: The heaven-sent messenger walks dry-shod across the swamp that the damned must wade or be ferried through — a quiet, deliberate miracle that marks him as belonging to a different order entirely. Longfellow's 'soles unwet' is exact but archaic and easy to skim past; we slow the image down ('his soles never touching the water') so the reader registers the wonder of it, since the dry feet are the whole sign of his power.

divergences.phrase: con una verghetta
divergences.older: with a little rod / He opened it (Longfellow); with a wand he touch'd / The gate (Cary)
divergences.lectio: with a little wand he opened it, and nothing held against him
divergences.note: The messenger opens the iron-barred gates of Dis that defeated Virgil with nothing but a 'verghetta' — a slender wand or twig — and meets no resistance ('sanza alcun contasto'). We keep the diminutive ('a little wand') because the contrast is the meaning: the gate that all of Hell's demons held shut against the poets gives way to a touch. We render 'non v'ebbe alcun contasto' as 'nothing held against him,' plainer than Longfellow's 'there was no resistance,' so the effortlessness lands.

divergences.phrase: com'avesse l'inferno a gran dispitto
divergences.older: E'en as if Hell he had in great despite (Longfellow); As if he entertain'd / Great scorn of hell (Cary)
divergences.lectio: as if he held all Hell in great contempt
divergences.note: The defining image of Farinata — the proud Ghibelline leader rising erect from the burning tomb. Dante's 'a gran dispitto' is plain and total: not flinching scorn but settled, towering contempt for the whole place that holds him. Longfellow's archaic 'in great despite' has dropped out of living English, so we render it 'in great contempt' and keep 'all Hell' so the defiance is aimed at the entirety of his damnation, which is the point of the man.

divergences.phrase: dicesti "elli ebbe"? non viv'elli ancora?
divergences.older: Saidst thou,—he had? Is he not still alive? (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: You said held — held? Is he not still alive?
divergences.note: The hinge of Cavalcante's collapse. Dante said his guide led him perhaps to one Guido 'ebbe a disdegno' — used the past tense 'ebbe' (held) — and the grieving father seizes on that one verb, reading his son's death into it. Everything turns on a tense, so the English must put the same word under the same stress; we isolate and repeat 'held' (matching the 'disdain' verb three tercets up) rather than Longfellow's vaguer 'he had,' so a modern reader feels exactly what the father heard.

divergences.phrase: non cinquanta volte fia raccesa / la faccia de la donna che qui regge
divergences.older: But fifty times shall not rekindled be / The countenance of the Lady who reigns here (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the face of the lady who reigns down here / will not be rekindled fifty times
divergences.note: Farinata's prophecy of Dante's exile, given as a riddle of time. 'The lady who reigns here' is the moon — Proserpina/Hecate, queen of the underworld, identified with the moon — so 'fifty kindlings of her face' means fifty new moons, about four years, before Dante himself learns 'how heavy that art is' (the art of returning from exile). We keep the veil exactly as Dante leaves it — a named goddess only by epithet, her 'face' the lunar disk relit each month — rather than flatten it to 'fifty months,' because the prophecy is meant to be decoded, not handed over.

divergences.phrase: frode, ond' ogne coscïenza è morsa ... d'ogne malizia ... ingiuria è 'l fine
divergences.older: But because fraud is man's peculiar vice, / More it displeases God (Longfellow); fraud, / By which the conscience feels itself gnawn (Cary)
divergences.lectio: because fraud is the vice unique to man, / it offends God more
divergences.note: This is the moral hinge of the whole lower Hell: of every malice, the end is injury, and injury comes by force or by fraud — but fraud is 'l'uom proprio male,' the evil proper to humankind, because it abuses reason, the faculty that makes us human. Longfellow's 'man's peculiar vice' has drifted in modern English toward 'odd' or 'quirky'; we render it 'the vice unique to man' so the reader hears the real claim — that fraud is the distinctly human sin, and so the one God hates most.

divergences.phrase: incontenenza, malizia e la matta bestialitade
divergences.older: Incontinence, and Malice, and insane / Bestiality (Longfellow); Incontinence, malice, and mad brutishness (Cary)
divergences.lectio: incontinence, malice, and the mad brutality
divergences.note: Virgil sends Dante back to his 'Etica' — Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics — for the three dispositions Heaven rejects. 'Matta bestialitade' is Dante's Italian for Aristotle's thēriotēs, a savagery below ordinary vice. We keep all three terms as a fixed triad and render 'matta' as 'mad' (not 'insane,' which reads clinical) and 'bestialitade' as 'brutality,' since the point is conduct that has fallen out of the human and into the beast — the load-bearing distinction the canto turns on.

divergences.phrase: sì che vostr' arte a Dio quasi è nepote
divergences.older: So that your art is, as it were, God's grandchild (Longfellow); your art / Is grandchild of the Deity (Cary, paraphrasing)
divergences.lectio: so that your art is, you might say, God's grandchild
divergences.note: The crux of Virgil's argument against usury: Nature follows the divine Intellect, and human art (industry, craft, honest work) follows Nature 'as the student follows the master' — so art stands two generations from God, his 'grandchild' (nepote). The usurer breaks this lineage by making money breed money, scorning both Nature and her follower, art. We keep Dante's startling kinship metaphor exactly ('God's grandchild') rather than abstracting it, because the whole Genesis-and-Aristotle case rests on that genealogy of honest labor.

divergences.phrase: l'infamïa di Creti ... che fu concetta ne la falsa vacca
divergences.older: The infamy of Crete was stretched along, / Who was conceived in the fictitious cow (Longfellow); the Cretans' infamy ... in the false cow conceived (Cary)
divergences.lectio: the shame of Crete, the one conceived inside the counterfeit cow
divergences.note: Dante never names the Minotaur in the line; he names him by his disgrace and his monstrous origin — Pasiphaë's coupling with the bull inside the wooden cow Daedalus built. We keep the veiling epithet ('the shame of Crete') and the strange concrete image of the 'falsa vacca,' rendering it 'counterfeit cow' rather than Longfellow's archaic 'fictitious cow,' so a modern reader feels the contrivance without losing the strangeness. The name Minotaur arrives a few tercets later, exactly where Dante places it.

divergences.phrase: O cieca cupidigia, o ira folle
divergences.older: O blind cupidity, O wrath insane (Longfellow); O blind lust! O foolish wrath! (Cary)
divergences.lectio: O blind greed, O insane wrath
divergences.note: Dante's apostrophe names the two roots of all the violence boiling in this river — cupidigia (greed, grasping appetite) and ira (wrath) — in a single hard line. Longfellow's Latinate 'cupidity' has nearly dropped out of living English; we render it 'greed,' which is what the word means and what the tyrants below are punished for, and keep the paired cry's blunt rhythm rather than smoothing it into a sentence.

divergences.phrase: colui fesse in grembo a Dio / lo cor che 'n su 'l Tamisi ancor si cola
divergences.older: He cleft asunder in God's bosom / The heart that still upon the Thames is honoured (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: That one split open, in the very lap of God, the heart that is still honored on the Thames
divergences.note: The unnamed shade is Guy de Montfort, who murdered Henry of Almain at Mass — 'in grembo a Dio,' in the lap of God, i.e. during the Elevation, on the altar itself — and whose victim's heart was carried back to England and enshrined (legend says on London Bridge over the Thames). Dante leaves the killer unnamed and lets the horror sit in the two images: a murder committed in God's own lap, and a heart still honored on a far river. We keep both intact ('the very lap of God,' 'honored on the Thames') rather than explaining the history, because the withholding and the doubled image are the point.

divergences.phrase: Non fronda verde, ma di color fosco; / non rami schietti, ma nodosi e 'nvolti; / non pomi v'eran, ma stecchi con tòsco
divergences.older: Not foliage green, but of a dusky colour, / Not branches smooth, but gnarled and intertangled, / Not apple-trees were there, but thorns with poison (Longfellow); No branches smooth, but gnarl'd and warp'd (Cary)
divergences.lectio: No green leaves, only the color of soot. / No smooth branches, but gnarled and snarled together. / No fruit, only thorns full of poison.
divergences.note: Dante builds the wood entirely out of negations — three lines each hammering 'non … ma' (not this, but that), so the forest is defined by everything a living wood is not. The drumbeat is the point: nature inverted. We keep all three 'No …' openings rather than smoothing them into ordinary description, and render 'color fosco' as the concrete 'color of soot' instead of Longfellow's faded 'dusky colour,' so the blackness reads as scorched, not merely dim.

divergences.phrase: Io son colui che tenni ambo le chiavi / del cor di Federigo … fede portai al glorïoso offizio
divergences.older: I am the one who both keys had in keeping / Of Frederick's heart, and turned them to and fro (Longfellow); The keys I bore / Of Frederick's heart (Cary)
divergences.lectio: I am the one who held both of the keys / to Frederick's heart, and turned them, locking / and unlocking, so gently … I was so faithful to that glorious office / that I lost my sleep and my strength keeping it.
divergences.note: This is Pier della Vigna — chancellor and most trusted minister of the Emperor Frederick II — destroyed by the envy of the court, who killed himself though innocent of the treason he was accused of. The 'two keys to Frederick's heart' is a deliberate, loaded image: Pier locked and unlocked the emperor's secrets the way Saint Peter holds the keys of Heaven (Matt. 16), and he protests his absolute fidelity even in damnation. We keep the keys-of-the-heart metaphor exactly and literally rather than abstracting it to 'I held his confidence,' because the canto's tragedy is that a man whose whole identity was faithful service was broken by a lie — and because Dante means us to hear the sacred echo of Peter's keys under a suicide's voice. We render 'li sonni e ' polsi' concretely as 'my sleep and my strength' (literally sleep and pulse-beats), the toll the office took on his body.

divergences.phrase: La meretrice che mai da l'ospizio / di Cesare non torse li occhi putti … ingiusto fece me contra me giusto
divergences.older: The courtesan who never from the dwelling / Of Caesar turned aside her strumpet eyes (Longfellow) … Made me unjust against myself, the just (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: The whore who never takes her sluttish eyes / off the house of Caesar … made me unjust against my own just self.
divergences.note: Two cruxes in Pier's speech we refuse to soften. First, 'la meretrice' is Envy personified as a court prostitute who never looks away from the palace — Dante's bluntest possible figure for the jealousy that haunts power, and the older translators' 'courtesan / strumpet' has gone genteel; we keep the hard word 'whore' because the contempt is the meaning. Second, the line 'ingiusto fece me contra me giusto' is a tight, terrible paradox — his despair made him commit an injustice (suicide) against the one person he knew to be just: himself. We keep the paradox intact ('unjust against my own just self') rather than untangle it, because the whole defense of Pier rests on that knot: he was innocent, and the only crime he ever committed was against that innocence.

divergences.phrase: l'anima feroce / dal corpo … come 'l gran di spelta … L'Arpie, pascendo poi de le sue foglie, / fanno dolore, e al dolor fenestra
divergences.older: There like a grain of spelt it germinates … The Harpies, feeding then upon its leaves, / Do pain create, and for the pain an outlet (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: there it sprouts like a grain of spelt … The Harpies, feeding then upon its leaves, / give it pain, and an open wound for the pain.
divergences.note: Pier explains the law of this ring: the suicide's soul, having violently torn itself from its body, is flung by Fortune into the wood and germinates where it lands 'like a grain of spelt' — a coarse wheat, the homely farm image making the horror worse. The Harpies feed on its leaves, and Dante's 'al dolor fenestra' is literally 'a window for the pain' — the wound the soul speaks through. We keep the spelt-grain simile (its strangeness is the point) and render 'fenestra' as 'an open wound' rather than Longfellow's abstract 'outlet,' because the soul can only cry out through a fresh tear in its bark — pain and the means of voicing it are the same gash. The doctrine that the suicides will retrieve their bodies at the Last Judgment but only to hang them on their own thorns — never to wear them again, 'for it isn't right to have what you threw away' — we keep in its full, chilling logic.

divergences.phrase: Qual io fui vivo, tal son morto
divergences.older: Such as I was living, am I, dead (Longfellow); What while I lived I was, the same am I now dead (Cary)
divergences.lectio: What I was living, that am I dead.
divergences.note: Capaneus, one of the Seven against Thebes, who scaled the walls swearing not even Jove could stop him and was struck down by a thunderbolt for it. His one line is the whole man: he is exactly as defiant dead as he was alive, and his refusal to be changed by the fire IS his torment. We keep Dante's stark parallel 'vivo … morto' (living … dead) hinged on one verb, rather than Longfellow's inverted, comma-broken 'am I, dead,' so the defiance lands in a single unbroken breath the way the Italian does.

divergences.phrase: dispettoso e torto
divergences.older: lieth lowering and disdainful (Longfellow); lies / Scornful and writhen (Cary)
divergences.lectio: lying there scornful and twisted
divergences.note: Of every soul on the burning sand, Capaneus alone refuses even to brush off the fire; Dante fixes him with two adjectives — 'dispettoso' (full of scorn) and 'torto' (twisted, contorted). We keep both as plain, hard words ('scornful and twisted') rather than Longfellow's archaic 'lowering,' so the reader sees the body's contempt — a man who will not so much as flinch, lying rigid and bitter under the rain of fire.

divergences.phrase: Dentro dal monte sta dritto un gran veglio ... e Roma guarda come süo speglio
divergences.older: A grand old man stands in the mount erect, / Who holds his shoulders turned tow'rds Damietta, / And looks at Rome as if it were his mirror (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Inside the mountain stands a great old man, / upright, his back turned toward Damietta, / gazing at Rome as if it were his mirror.
divergences.note: The Old Man of Crete — Dante's image of all human history, built like the statue in the Book of Daniel: head of gold, then silver, brass, iron, and one foot of baked clay, the metals declining through the ages of the world. He stands with his back to Damietta (the East, the old fallen empires) and faces Rome as his mirror (the seat of Empire and Church, where history looks to find itself). Every part but the golden head is split by a crack, and the tears that run down through it become the rivers of Hell — Acheron, Styx, Phlegethon, and at the bottom Cocytus. We keep the proper nouns and the strange grandeur intact, only straightening Longfellow's 'holds his shoulders turned' into the plain 'his back turned,' so the figure stands clear: humankind's whole flawed history weeping itself down into Hell.

divergences.phrase: Siete voi qui, ser Brunetto?
divergences.older: Are you here, Ser Brunetto? (Longfellow); And art thou here, Ser Brunetto? (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Are you here, ser Brunetto?
divergences.note: The hinge of the canto: Dante recognizes his old teacher under the rain of fire and addresses him with the formal 'voi' — the respectful plural a pupil uses for a master — while Brunetto answers with the intimate 'tu' ('my son'). The tenderness and the reversal of stations are the whole scene. Longfellow already has the plain modern phrasing here, so we keep it almost untouched; we lowercase 'ser' (a courtesy title, not a proper name) and preserve the proper name Brunetto Latini intact. English can't carry the voi/tu distinction in the pronouns, so the deference is left to live in the bow and the bowed head a few lines on.

divergences.phrase: Ma quello ingrato popolo maligno
divergences.older: But that ungrateful and malignant people (Longfellow); That thankless, malignant race (Cary)
divergences.lectio: But that thankless, malignant people
divergences.note: Brunetto's curse on the Florentines, the bitter heart of his prophecy — the city that will exile Dante for his good deeds. The Italian pairs 'ingrato' (thankless, ungrateful) with 'maligno' (malignant, evil-willed), two hard adjectives Dante means to land like blows. We render 'ingrato' as 'thankless' rather than the longer 'ungrateful,' keeping the line's terse, contemptuous weight, and hold 'malignant' for its full venom rather than softening it; the contempt is the point of the passage.

divergences.phrase: Sieti raccomandato il mio Tesoro
divergences.older: Commended unto thee be my Tesoro, / In which I still live (Longfellow); To thee / My Treasure I commend (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Let my Treasure be commended to you, / the book I still live in
divergences.note: Brunetto's last words point to his own book, the 'Tesoro' (his encyclopedic 'Tresor,' written in French, or its Italian verse companion the 'Tesoretto') — and the pun is deliberate: 'mio Tesoro' is at once 'my Treasure' and the title of the work in which, he says, he still lives on. Longfellow keeps the Italian title 'Tesoro' but leaves a modern reader unsure it is a book; we render it 'my Treasure' so the double sense survives — a man asking to be remembered through the work that outlives him.

divergences.phrase: che corrono a Verona il drappo verde
divergences.older: Who at Verona run for the Green Mantle / Across the plain (Longfellow); the green mantle race at Verona (Cary)
divergences.lectio: who race for the green cloth across the open field at Verona
divergences.note: The canto's startling final image: Brunetto, who must not linger, sprints off after his band like a runner in the famous New Year's footrace at Verona, where the prize was a length of green cloth ('il drappo verde') — and Dante closes by saying he looked like the winner, not the loser. Longfellow's 'Green Mantle' makes it sound like a finished garment or an order of knighthood; the Italian 'drappo verde' is plainly the bolt of green fabric run for as a prize. We keep it 'the green cloth' so the homely, vivid detail lands, and let the last line stand alone — Brunetto, even damned, running like a man who wins.

divergences.phrase: E io, che posto son con loro in croce, / Iacopo Rusticucci fui ... la fiera moglie più ch'altro mi nuoce
divergences.older: And I, who with them on the cross am placed, / Jacopo Rusticucci was; and truly / My savage wife, more than aught else, doth harm me (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: And I, set on the cross here with them, / was Jacopo Rusticucci; and it's true / my fierce wife harmed me more than anything.
divergences.note: Dante writes 'posto son con loro in croce' — literally placed on the cross with them — the same crucifixion image he uses for the abused Fortune at VII.91, here for the torment these three share. We keep 'the cross' rather than soften it to 'punished,' matching this edition's earlier choice to preserve Dante's crucifixion metaphors. And 'la fiera moglie' is a fierce, wild wife, not Longfellow's 'savage'; Rusticucci half-blames his marriage for his sin, and we keep the blunt, bitter aside intact without explaining it.

divergences.phrase: La gente nuova e i sùbiti guadagni / orgoglio e dismisura han generata, / Fiorenza, in te
divergences.older: The new inhabitants and the sudden gains, / Pride and extravagance have in thee engendered, / Florence (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: The newcomers and the quick, easy money / have bred pride and excess in you, / Florence, and already you weep for it!
divergences.note: This is the canto's lament and Dante's diagnosis of Florence's ruin: 'gente nuova' (new people flooding in from the contado) and 'sùbiti guadagni' (sudden, unearned wealth) have bred 'orgoglio e dismisura' — pride and dismisura, the lack of all measure, excess. We render 'gente nuova' as 'the newcomers' and 'sùbiti guadagni' as 'quick, easy money' so the modern reader hears the real social complaint — new money with no restraint — and keep 'pride and excess' as the named twin vices, since this verdict on the city is the moral center of the canto.

divergences.phrase: Io avea una corda intorno cinta, / e con essa pensai alcuna volta / prender la lonza a la pelle dipinta
divergences.older: I had a cord around about me girt, / And therewithal I whilom had designed / To take the panther with the painted skin (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: I had a cord wound around my waist, / and with it I had once thought / to catch the leopard with the painted hide.
divergences.note: The 'lonza a la pelle dipinta' is the spotted beast of Canto I — the leopard with the bright, painted coat — and Dante's mysterious cord, which he once hoped would catch it, is one of the poem's open riddles (a Franciscan girdle? a symbol of self-restraint or fraud?). We render 'lonza' as 'leopard' to match this edition's Canto I, keep 'painted hide' for the deliberate echo of its 'painted skin,' and leave the cord exactly as unexplained as Dante leaves it, since Virgil flings it into the abyss as a signal without ever saying what it means.

divergences.phrase: Ecco la fiera con la coda aguzza ... Ecco colei che tutto 'l mondo appuzza
divergences.older: Behold the monster with the pointed tail ... Behold him who infecteth all the world (Longfellow); Lo! the fell monster with the deadly sting ... Behold the beast that taints the world (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Behold the beast with the pointed tail ... behold the one whose stench fills the whole world!
divergences.note: This is Geryon, the monster of fraud, summoned up from the abyss between the seventh and eighth circles. Dante's verb is crude and physical — 'appuzza,' to stink up, to make foul — not Longfellow's clinical 'infecteth' or Cary's genteel 'taints.' Fraud is filthy, and Dante means us to smell it; we keep the blunt word 'stench' so the disgust lands. We hold the proper name Geryon back exactly where Dante does (it arrives only later, at the mounting), and keep the doubled 'Behold ... behold' that frames the beast like a thing displayed.

divergences.phrase: La faccia sua era faccia d'uom giusto ... e d'un serpente tutto l'altro fusto
divergences.older: The face was as the face of a just man ... And of a serpent all the trunk beside (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Its face was the face of an honest man, so kindly was the look of it outside — and all the rest of its body was a serpent's.
divergences.note: Geryon is the perfect emblem of fraud: an honest, reassuring human face set on the body of a serpent, the paws hairy to the armpits, the back and flanks painted in gaudy heraldic colors, and a scorpion's sting hidden in the tail. The whole portrait is built on that gap between the trustworthy face and the venomous rest, which is exactly what fraud is. We render 'uom giusto' as 'honest man' rather than the abstract 'just man,' because the point is the look of trustworthiness the cheat wears; and we keep the painted hide and the scorpion tail concrete and strange, since the creature's gaudy surface — finer than any Turkish or Tartar cloth, finer than Arachne's web — is the lure that hides the kill.

divergences.phrase: the usurers' pouches — yellow with a blue lion, red with a white goose, white with a blue pregnant sow ... la tasca con tre becchi
divergences.older: Upon a yellow pouch I azure saw / That had the face and posture of a lion ... red as blood, / Display a goose more white than butter ... an azure sow and gravid ... He who shall bring the satchel with three goats (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: a yellow pouch, a blue that had the face and bearing of a lion ... red as blood, display a goose more white than butter ... a blue and pregnant sow stamped on the white field of his little pouch ... the one who'll bring the pouch with the three goats!
divergences.note: The usurers crouch weeping on the burning sand, each with a money-pouch hung at his neck bearing his noble family's coat of arms — and they stare at the pouches the way they once stared at money. Dante names them only by their blazons, and a reader was meant to decode them: the yellow pouch with the blue lion is the Gianfigliazzi (Florentine Black Guelphs), the red with the white goose the Obriachi (Florentine Ghibellines), and the white with the blue pregnant sow the Scrovegni — the family of the Paduan who speaks, Reginaldo degli Scrovegni. He sneers that his neighbor Vitaliano and the 'sovereign cavalier' with the pouch of three goats (Giovanni Buiamonte, the most notorious usurer of the day, named in bitter irony) are still to come. We keep every blazon as a concrete picture rather than naming the families in the line, because the heraldry is the indictment — they dragged their honored family names into this trade — and the decoding is the reader's work. We hold Longfellow's 'three goats' (becchi) as the literal control gives it.

divergences.phrase: Geryon's flight down — 'Or movi, Gerion' ... il misero Icaro ... Fetonte ... si dileguò come da corda cocca
divergences.older: Now, Geryon, bestir thyself ... abandoned Phaeton the reins ... the wretched Icarus ... He sped away as arrow from the string (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Now, Geryon, get moving. Keep the circles wide, the dropping slow ... not when Phaethon let the reins go slack ... nor when poor Icarus felt the feathers peeling from his sides ... he shot away like an arrow off the string.
divergences.note: The terrifying descent: Virgil and Dante mount the monster's back and Geryon spirals slowly down through the dark void to the Eighth Circle, the pilgrim hanging in empty air with nothing visible but the beast beneath him. Dante reaches for the two great myths of catastrophic flight — Phaethon, who lost control of the sun-chariot and scorched the sky, and Icarus, whose wax wings melted — to measure a fear that outdoes both. We keep both proper nouns and the live, physical images (the slack reins, the feathers peeling away as the wax softens, the father's cry) rather than smoothing them to 'the famous falls,' because the strangeness of the comparison is the strangeness of the experience. We render the final 'si dileguò come da corda cocca' — literally 'he vanished as a notch from the bowstring' — as 'he shot away like an arrow off the string,' the plain American image, keeping the speed of the release that ends the canto the instant the two riders dismount.

divergences.phrase: Luogo è in inferno detto Malebolge, / tutto di pietra di color ferrigno
divergences.older: There is a place in Hell called Malebolge, / Wholly of stone and of an iron colour (Longfellow); A place there is within the depths of hell / Call'd Malebolge, all of rock dark-stain'd / With hue ferruginous (Cary)
divergences.lectio: There is a place in Hell called Malebolge, / all of stone the color of iron
divergences.note: Malebolge — Dante's coined name for the whole eighth circle, literally 'evil-pockets' or 'evil-pouches' (mala + bolgia, a sack or ditch). It's a deliberate clash: the Latinate, formal 'Luogo è' set against a brand-new, low-sounding word. We keep the proper noun untouched, as the architecture of the next thirteen cantos, and render 'color ferrigno' as the plain 'color of iron' rather than Cary's archaic 'hue ferruginous,' so the cold gray stone reads as gray stone and not a chemistry term. The name itself we leave unexplained — its strangeness is doing the work.

divergences.phrase: Guarda quel grande che vene, / e per dolor non par lagrime spanda: / quanto aspetto reale ancor ritene!
divergences.older: See that tall one who is coming, / And for his pain seems not to shed a tear; / Still what a royal aspect he retains! (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Look at that tall one coming — / he doesn't seem to shed a tear for his pain. / What a kingly look he still carries!
divergences.note: Jason — leader of the Argonauts, who 'by courage and cunning stripped the Colchians of the Ram' (the Golden Fleece). The whole point of his portrait is that even as a damned seducer driven under the whip, he walks like a king and will not weep — the bearing that let him deceive Hypsipyle and Medea is still on him. We keep 'kingly look' (aspetto reale) plain and let the line land on his unbroken composure, since his refusal to grieve is the man, just as Capaneus's defiance was his at XIV.51.

divergences.phrase: quella sozza e scapigliata fante / che là si graffia con l'unghie merdose
divergences.older: that uncleanly and dishevelled drab, / Who there doth scratch herself with filthy nails (Longfellow); that scurvy wretch / ... who there / Doth rend her with foul nails (Cary)
divergences.lectio: that filthy, disheveled slut down there, / scratching herself with her shit-caked nails
divergences.note: Thaïs — the harlot of the flatterers' ditch, sunk in excrement and clawing at herself. Dante's word for her nails, 'merdose,' is bluntly scatological — caked with shit — and the older translators reach for 'filthy' or 'foul' to keep it decent. We keep the crudeness because it is the punishment: the flatterers, who dressed lies in sweetness, lie now in raw human waste, and Dante means us to smell and see it (the same disgust he loads into 'appuzza' for Geryon at XVII.3). We preserve the proper noun Thaïs and let the harshness of 'slut' and 'shit-caked' carry the contempt the canto is built on.

divergences.phrase: O Simon mago, o miseri seguaci ... per oro e per argento avolterate
divergences.older: O Simon Magus, O forlorn disciples ... For silver and for gold do prostitute (Longfellow); Woe to thee, Simon Magus! woe to you, / His wretched followers! (Cary, paraphrasing)
divergences.lectio: O Simon Magus, O you wretched followers ... whore them out for silver and for gold
divergences.note: The canto opens by naming the sin's patron — Simon Magus, who in Acts 8 tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit from the apostles, and whose name became the word for the sin: simony, the buying and selling of holy office. Dante's verb is 'avolterate' — adulterate, whore out — and his image is sexual and savage: the things of God ought to be the brides of holiness, and these men prostitute them for cash. Longfellow's 'prostitute' is exact but stiff; we keep the hard verb 'whore out' so the violation lands as the outrage Dante means, and hold the proper name Simon Magus, the architecture of the whole apostrophe.

divergences.phrase: se' tu già costì ritto, Bonifazio? ... la bella donna, e poi di farne strazio
divergences.older: Dost thou stand there already, Boniface? ... To take by fraud / The beautiful Lady, and then work her woe (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: are you standing there already, Boniface? ... to seize the beautiful Lady by fraud, and then defile her
divergences.note: The grim comedy at the heart of the canto: Pope Nicholas III, jammed head-down and unable to see, hears footsteps and mistakes Dante for his own successor Boniface VIII — arriving, he thinks, years ahead of the date the record (the book of the future, which the damned can read) had given him. He cannot believe Boniface is tired of his plunder so soon. The 'beautiful Lady' is the Church, whom Boniface 'seized by fraud' (his disputed election, after pressuring Celestine V to abdicate) and then abused. We keep the proper name Boniface and the bitter irony intact — a damned pope scolding the pope who damned Dante — without explaining the politics in the line, since the confusion is the joke and the horror at once.

divergences.phrase: figliuol de l'orsa ... un pastor sanza legge ... Nuovo Iasón sarà
divergences.older: son of the She-bear ... a Pastor without law ... New Jason will he be (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: a son of the She-bear ... a lawless Shepherd ... a new Jason
divergences.note: Nicholas finally names himself, not by name but by his house: he was 'figliuol de l'orsa,' a son of the She-bear — the Orsini, whose name means 'little bears' — so greedy to advance his nephews ('the cubs') that he pocketed wealth in life and is pocketed in the rock in death. He then prophesies the line of simoniac popes stacked beneath him: after Boniface will come 'a lawless Shepherd from the west,' Clement V, the Gascon pope who moved the papacy to Avignon under the thumb of the French king. Dante calls him 'a new Jason,' after the high priest in 2 Maccabees who bought the office from a pliant king. We keep the family riddle (the She-bear, the cubs) and the biblical proper nouns Jason and Maccabees, because the layered prophecy — three popes damned in advance — is the spine of the canto's argument that the Church has been put up for sale.

divergences.phrase: Ahi, Costantin, di quanto mal fu matre, / non la tua conversion, ma quella dote
divergences.older: Ah, Constantine! of how much ill was mother, / Not thy conversion, but that marriage dower / Which the first wealthy Father took from thee (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Ah, Constantine — what a mother of evil, / not your conversion, but that dowry / the first rich Father took from your hands!
divergences.note: The canto's root cause, named at its climax: the Donation of Constantine — the belief that the emperor Constantine, on converting, handed temporal power and wealth over to Pope Sylvester ('the first rich Father'). Dante took the document as genuine (it was exposed as a forgery only a century later, by Lorenzo Valla) and saw in it the original poisoning of the Church: the moment it became rich and worldly, and so corruptible by greed and simony. His cry is precise — it was not Constantine's conversion that was the 'mother of evil' but that 'dote,' the dowry, the endowment of property. We keep the proper name Constantine and the kinship metaphor ('mother of evil,' 'dowry') exactly, because the whole denunciation lands on that single transfer of wealth as the source of everything the canto condemns.

divergences.phrase: tra 'l mento e 'l principio del casso ... 'l pianto de li occhi / le natiche bagnava per lo fesso
divergences.older: For tow'rds the reins the countenance was turned, / And backward it behoved them to advance (Longfellow); the weeping of the eyes / Along the fissure bathed the hinder parts (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the face was twisted back toward the kidneys, / and they had to walk along backward ... the tears the eyes wept / running down the cleft to bathe the buttocks.
divergences.note: The diviners' punishment is a single grotesque image and the whole canto turns on it: those who tried to see too far ahead now have their heads wrenched a half-circle around, so they must walk gazing behind and weep down the length of their own backs. Dante is deliberately crude — 'le natiche bagnava per lo fesso,' the tears bathe the buttocks by way of the cleft — and the older translators flinch into decorum ('the hinder parts'). We keep the body plain and exact ('the cleft,' 'the buttocks') because the indignity is the justice: prophecy turned into a man weeping into his own backside. We straighten Longfellow's inverted 'tow'rds the reins the countenance was turned' but keep 'kidneys' (reni), the concrete spot the face is cranked back toward.

divergences.phrase: Qui vive la pietà quand'è ben morta; / chi è più scellerato che colui / che al giudicio divin passion comporta?
divergences.older: Here pity lives when it is wholly dead; / Who is a greater reprobate than he / Who feels compassion at the doom divine? (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Here pity lives when it is wholly dead. / Who is more of a criminal than the one / who lets his feeling argue against God's judgment?
divergences.note: Virgil's stern rebuke, and one of the poem's hardest sayings: in Hell, to feel pity for the damned is itself a sin, because it sets human feeling against the verdict of God. The first line is a deliberate paradox — pietà is alive in you exactly when it ought to be dead — and we keep it intact rather than untangle it, because the knot is the meaning. For 'al giudicio divin passion comporta' we render 'lets his feeling argue against God's judgment': 'passion' here is emotion overruling reason, not Longfellow's softer 'feels compassion,' and the verb 'comporta' carries the sense of bringing one's passion to bear against the sentence. The doctrine is genuinely cold and we keep it cold.

divergences.phrase: Manto fu, che cercò per terre molte ... fer la città sovra quell' ossa morte; / e per colei che 'l loco prima elesse, / Mantüa l'appellar sanz' altra sorte
divergences.older: Was Manto ... Mantua named it, without other omen (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: was Manto, who searched through many lands ... they built their city over those dead bones, / and for the one who first chose out the spot / they named it Mantua, with no other omen.
divergences.note: Virgil's long digression on Manto — the wandering prophetess, daughter of Tiresias — and the founding of his own city, Mantua, is the structural center of the canto, and Dante gives it real care: the lake Benaco (Garda), the Mincio running down to the Po, the desolate fen where Manto settled to practice her arts and died, the men who later gathered on that defensible swamp and built over her bones. The point of 'sanz' altra sorte' (without other omen / augury) is pointed irony in the diviners' ditch — Mantua, unlike cities founded by reading bird-flight, took its name with no soothsaying at all, just the dead woman who got there first. We keep that phrase ('with no other omen') and hold every proper noun (Manto, Mantua, Benaco, Mincio, Po, Peschiera, Tyrol) so the geography stays a real map. We keep 'over those dead bones' literal rather than abstracting it; the city standing on the witch's corpse is the image Dante wants.

divergences.phrase: tocca l'onda / sotto Sobilia Caino e le spine
divergences.older: under Seville / Touches the ocean-wave, Cain and the thorns (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Cain and his bundle of thorns / already holds the line between both hemispheres / and touches the wave below Seville.
divergences.note: The canto ends on time told by the moon. 'Caino e le spine' is the medieval man-in-the-moon: not our face but Cain, exiled, carrying a bundle of thorns across the lunar disk — so 'Cain and the thorns' simply means the moon. Dante uses it to mark the hour: the moon is now setting on the western horizon, over Seville, so it is past dawn on the morning of Holy Saturday. We keep the strange folk-image whole ('Cain and his bundle of thorns') rather than flatten it to 'the moon,' because the strangeness is information about how Dante's world read the sky — and then let the plain astronomy (the line between the hemispheres, the wave below Seville) carry the time, since that is what Virgil is actually telling Dante: get moving, the night is nearly spent.

divergences.phrase: Quale ne l'arzanà de' Viniziani / bolle l'inverno la tenace pece
divergences.older: As in the Arsenal of the Venetians / Boils in the winter the tenacious pitch / To smear their unsound vessels o'er again (Longfellow); In the Venetians' arsenal as boils / Through wintry months tenacious pitch (Cary)
divergences.lectio: The way, in the Arsenal of the Venetians, / the sticky pitch boils all winter long / for caulking their unsound ships again
divergences.note: Dante's one extended simile in the canto is a working shipyard — the famous Venetian Arsenal, where caulking-tar was boiled all winter to recaulk hulls that couldn't sail. It is the literal picture for the lake of pitch the barrators boil in. We keep every concrete trade detail (caulking, the worn ribs, oars, rope, the mainsail and jib) and render 'tenace pece' as the plain 'sticky pitch' rather than Longfellow's archaic 'tenacious pitch,' because the whole force of the comparison is ordinary, physical labor — the reader should smell the tar, not parse a Latinate adjective.

divergences.phrase: Malebranche ... Scarmiglione ... Malacoda ... Alichino e Calcabrina ... Cagnazzo ... Barbariccia ... Libicocco e Draghignazzo ... Ciriatto ... Graffiacane ... Farfarello ... Rubicante
divergences.older: the Malebranche ... Scarmiglione ... Malacoda ... Alichino and Calcabrina ... Cagnazzo ... Barbariccia ... Libicocco and Draghignazzo ... Ciriatto ... Graffiacane ... Farfarello ... mad Rubicante (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the Malebranche ("Evil-Claws") ... Scarmiglione ... Malacoda ("Evil-Tail") ... Alichino and Calcabrina ... Cagnazzo ... Barbariccia, you take charge of the ten ... Libicocco and Draghignazzo ... tusked Ciriatto and Graffiacane ... Farfarello and crazy Rubicante
divergences.note: Dante invents a whole demon-squad with mock-heroic comic-grotesque names — Malebranche is the troop ('evil-claws'), Malacoda their captain ('evil-tail'), and the detail of ten roll off like a sergeant's muster: Alichino, Calcabrina, Cagnazzo, Barbariccia (the appointed leader of the ten), Libicocco, Draghignazzo, Ciriatto, Graffiacane, Farfarello, Rubicante, with Scarmiglione named and hushed apart. The names are coined for sound and menace and we preserve every one untouched, as proper nouns are the architecture of the work; we keep Longfellow's two live epithets — 'tusked Ciriatto' (the boar-fanged one) and a 'crazy/mad' Rubicante — and render the squad-names exactly so the muster reads as the grim roll-call it is. Where it aids the reader we gloss the two group/captain names inline once (Malebranche = Evil-Claws, Malacoda = Evil-Tail) without disturbing the Italian.

divergences.phrase: Ier, più oltre cinqu' ore che quest' otta, / mille dugento con sessanta sei / anni compié ... ed elli avea del cul fatto trombetta
divergences.older: Yesterday, five hours later than this hour, / One thousand and two hundred sixty-six / Years were complete, that here the way was broken ... And he had made a trumpet of his rump (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Yesterday, five hours past this very hour, / one thousand two hundred sixty-six years / came full since the road here was broken through ... and he had made a trumpet of his rear.
divergences.note: Two cruxes we keep exactly. First, Malacoda's lie: he sends the poets on a path he claims is intact, but his own dating gives him away — the bridge fell '1266 years ago, plus a day and five hours,' i.e. at the moment of the earthquake at Christ's death (Dante dates the descent to Good Friday, 1300), so the broken arch ahead is the literal scar of the Crucifixion and the demon is lying. We keep the precise reckoning rather than flatten it to 'long ago,' because the hidden date is the whole trap. Second, the canto's notorious closing line: 'ed elli avea del cul fatto trombetta' — Barbariccia answers his troops' obscene tongue-signal by making a trumpet of his backside. Dante ends a canto of corruption on a deliberate, crude blast, and we keep the vulgarity ('made a trumpet of his rear') exactly where he puts it, rather than the genteel evasions older versions sometimes reach for, because the bodily insult is the point — the same disgust Dante loads into the lower bolge throughout.

divergences.phrase: in chiesa coi santi, e in taverna coi ghiottoni
divergences.older: in the church / With saints, and in the tavern with the gluttons (Longfellow); in church with saints, with revellers in the tavern (Cary)
divergences.lectio: in church with the saints, in the tavern with the gluttons
divergences.note: Dante drops a homely Italian proverb right after calling the ten demons 'savage company' — the equivalent of 'you keep the company the place calls for.' It is the first beat of a canto Dante deliberately plays as low comedy (the only canto run almost entirely as farce), and the colloquial register is the point. We keep it as a plain proverb in the pilgrim's own mouth rather than elevating it, since the sudden drop into tavern-talk is exactly the tonal shift Dante wants after the high horror of the openings.

divergences.phrase: Tra male gatte era venuto 'l sorco
divergences.older: Among malicious cats the mouse had come (Longfellow); 'Midst evil cats the mouse had stray'd (Cary)
divergences.lectio: The rat had landed among vicious cats
divergences.note: Dante's barnyard metaphor for Ciampolo trapped among the demons — 'sorco' is a rat (a Lombard/Tuscan dialect form), not a mouse. The whole canto is built out of these low animal images (dolphins, frogs, the otter, the boar's tusk, the duck and falcon, the hawk), the burlesque texture that earns this stretch its nickname, the 'comedy of the demons.' We keep the coarse 'rat' rather than the softer 'mouse,' because the squalor of the image matches the squalor of the grafters' pit, and the animal-comedy is the canto's signature.

divergences.phrase: Ciampolo / lo Navarrese — la baratteria
divergences.older: I in the kingdom of Navarre was born ... I set me there to practise barratry (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: I was born in the kingdom of Navarre ... There I set myself to working graft
divergences.note: The unnamed sinner — tradition calls him Ciampolo (Gian Paolo) — is a barrator: a public official who sold his office, took bribes, embezzled. 'Baratteria' is the civic counterpart of the simony of Canto XIX (selling church office); here it is selling secular office. Longfellow's 'barratry' has narrowed in modern English to a nautical/legal term most readers won't know, so we render it plainly as 'graft' and 'working graft,' which is exactly the modern American word for selling public trust for private money — keeping the sin legible while preserving the proper nouns Navarre and King Thibault.

divergences.phrase: Di fuor dorate son, sì ch'elli abbaglia; / ma dentro tutte piombo, e gravi tanto, / che Federigo le mettea di paglia
divergences.older: Without, they gilded are so that it dazzles; / But inwardly all leaden and so heavy / That Frederick used to put them on of straw (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Outside, they're gilded so it dazzles you; / but inside, all lead, and so heavy / that the cloaks Frederick used were straw beside them.
divergences.note: The master image of the canto and its definition of hypocrisy: a cloak blazing gold on the outside, solid lead within. The hood pulled low blinds the wearer; the gilt blinds the onlooker. Dante's comparison is to the lead capes the emperor Frederick II was said to use as a torture — a man wrapped in lead and set near a fire until the metal melted — so by contrast even those were 'di paglia,' straw. Longfellow's 'put them on of straw' is unclear; we render it 'were straw beside them' so the modern reader grasps that the punishment-cloaks here outdo even Frederick's. We keep the proper name Frederick and the literal gold/lead opposition, since the whole circle is built on the gap between bright surface and crushing interior.

divergences.phrase: Quel confitto ... consigliò i Farisei che convenia / porre un uom per lo popolo a' martìri. / Attraversato è, nudo, ne la via ... è mestier ch'el senta / qualunque passa, come pesa, pria
divergences.older: This transfixed one, whom thou seest, / Counselled the Pharisees that it was meet / To put one man to torture for the people. / Crosswise and naked is he on the path ... he needs must feel, / Whoever passes, first how much he weighs (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: This nailed-down man you're looking at / counseled the Pharisees that it was fitting / to put one man to torture for the people. // He lies across the path, naked, / as you can see, and he has to feel / the weight of everyone who passes, first.
divergences.note: This is Caiaphas — the high priest who told the Sanhedrin it was expedient that one man (Christ) should die for the people (John 11:50) — though Dante, true to his method with the worst sinners, never speaks the name. His punishment fits the counsel exactly: he advised laying a burden on one man for all, so now he lies crucified and naked, staked flat across the floor of the ditch, and bears the literal weight of every hypocrite who treads over him forever. Longfellow's archaic 'transfixed,' 'meet,' and inverted 'crosswise and naked is he' obscure a scene that should land as physical horror; we straighten the syntax and keep the brutal concrete image — nailed to the ground, trodden — because the contrapasso (he weighed others, now all weigh on him) is the point. We hold the name Caiaphas back, as Dante does, and let the deed identify him.

divergences.phrase: Mal contava la bisogna colui / ch'i peccator di qua piglia col roco ... ch'elli è bugiardo e padre di menzogna
divergences.older: The business badly he recounted / Who grapples with his hook the sinners yonder ... That he's a liar and the father of lies (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: He gave us a bad account of it, / that one back there who hooks the sinners ... and one was that he lies, and fathers all lies.
divergences.note: The canto's quiet sting: Malacoda, the demon who in Canto XXI sent the poets off with a cheerful lie — that the sixth bridge was merely broken and a nearby one stood whole — turns out to have deceived them; every bridge over this ditch is down. Virgil, who has never been fooled before, stands a moment with his head bowed, then names the lie. The friar twists the knife by quoting the proverb he learned at Bologna — the Devil is 'bugiardo e padre di menzogna,' a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44) — a line that indicts both the demon and, in a circle of hypocrites, the friars themselves. We keep the biblical phrase intact and render Virgil's terse rebuke plainly, since his rare flash of anger, more than any speech, registers how completely Malacoda played them.

divergences.phrase: lo villanello ... la brina / in su la terra assempra l'imagine di sua sorella bianca
divergences.older: What time the hoar-frost copies on the ground / The outward semblance of her sister white ... The husbandman, whose forage faileth him (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: when the hoarfrost copies onto the ground / the likeness of her white sister, the snow ... the farmer, whose feed has run out
divergences.note: The canto's long opening simile: a peasant despairs at the frost-whitened fields, then takes heart when the frost melts and the world's face changes — mirroring Virgil's frown and his quick reassurance a few lines later. Dante's conceit is that the hoarfrost is the snow's short-lived 'sister,' copying her white image onto the ground with a pen whose ink soon fails. We keep that strange family metaphor intact (the hoarfrost as the snow's sister, the failing pen) rather than flatten it to 'frost on the fields,' because the fragile, fast-fading whiteness is exactly the mood the simile sets up — alarm that lifts as fast as it came. We render 'villanello' as the plain 'farmer' and 'forage' as 'feed has run out' so the homely scene reads as a working farm, not a pastoral set-piece.

divergences.phrase: seggendo in piuma / in fama non si vien ... qual fummo in aere e in acqua la schiuma
divergences.older: for sitting upon down, / Or under quilt, one cometh not to fame ... As smoke in air or in the water foam (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: No one wins fame / lying on down, or tucked under a quilt ... as smoke leaves in the air, or foam on water
divergences.note: Virgil's spur to the exhausted pilgrim, and one of the poem's most quoted lines: fame is earned by effort, not by lying soft, and a life without it leaves no more trace than smoke in the air or foam on water. We straighten Longfellow's inverted 'one cometh not to fame' and archaic 'withouten' into plain forward English, and keep the paired images of smoke and foam exactly — the two things that vanish without a mark — since the whole goad depends on that vivid nothingness. The thought (that a life must leave a 'vestigio,' a footprint) is kept hard, not softened into mere encouragement.

divergences.phrase: né O sì tosto mai né I si scrisse ... Così ... che la fenice more e poi rinasce
divergences.older: Nor 'O' so quickly e'er, nor 'I' was written, / As he took fire, and burned ... The phoenix dies, and then is born again (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: No 'O' or 'I' was ever written so fast / as he caught fire and burned ... the Phoenix dies and then is born once more
divergences.note: The thief Vanni Fucci, bitten by a serpent, flares to ash faster than you can write a single letter, then instantly reforms — and Dante reaches for the Phoenix, the bird the 'great sages' say dies and is reborn every five hundred years, feeding on no grain but only on tears of incense and amomum, with nard and myrrh for its shroud. We keep the proper noun Phoenix and the full strange catalog of its spices and winding-sheet rather than trimming it, because the wonder of the myth is the measure of the horror: this is no glorious rebirth but an endless, mechanical resurrection into the same torment. We render Dante's letter-writing image ('né O ... né I') literally — quicker than an 'O' or an 'I' is written — since the speed is the point, and modern readers still know how fast those strokes go.

divergences.phrase: le mani alzò con amendue le fiche ... "Togli, Dio, ch'a te le squadro!"
divergences.older: Lifted his hands aloft with both the figs, / Crying: "Take that, God, for at thee I aim them." (Longfellow); raised / Both hands with fingers clench'd, and cried, "Take that, / God, for at thee I aim them." (Cary)
divergences.lectio: raised both his hands with the fig thrust out, / shouting: "Take that, God — I aim them straight at you."
divergences.note: Vanni Fucci ends his prophecy with the most obscene gesture in the poem: the 'fica' (the fig), the thumb shoved between two fingers, both fists flung up at God. The blasphemy is the whole point of the canto's opening, so we keep the literal gesture rather than soften it to a vague defiance — 'the fig thrust out.' Dante's 'a te le squadro' is street-talk, roughly 'I square these off / aim these at you'; Longfellow's 'at thee I aim them' is right but archaic, so we render it as the snarled taunt it is, 'I aim them straight at you,' and let 'God' land hard at the head of the line where Dante puts it.

divergences.phrase: Taccia Lucano ... Taccia di Cadmo e d'Aretusa Ovidio ... ché due nature mai a fronte a fronte / non trasmutò
divergences.older: Henceforth be silent Lucan ... Be silent Ovid, of Cadmus and Arethusa ... Because two natures never front to front / Has he transmuted (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Now let Lucan fall silent ... Let Ovid be silent on Cadmus and Arethusa ... because two natures, face to face, he never / transmuted so that both their forms / stood ready to trade the matter they were made of.
divergences.note: The canto's astonishing centerpiece — two human thieves and two serpents exchanging forms entirely, smoke meeting smoke, man becoming snake and snake man — and Dante's open boast that he has outdone the great poets of metamorphosis. He silences Lucan (whose soldiers Sabellus and Nasidius merely dissolved from snakebite) and Ovid (whose Cadmus turned into a snake and Arethusa into a spring) because neither ever staged a true two-way transformation, 'a fronte a fronte,' the natures swapping their very matter. We keep the dare exactly — 'I don't begrudge it him' — and the proper nouns Lucan, Ovid, Cadmus, Arethusa, Sabellus, Nasidius, since the literary one-upmanship IS the passage; we only straighten Longfellow's inverted 'never front to front / Has he transmuted' into plain forward English so the claim reads as the proud challenge it is.

divergences.phrase: Questi è Caco ... non va co' suoi fratei per un cammino, / per lo furto che frodolente fece / del grande armento
divergences.older: That one is Cacus, who / Beneath the rock upon Mount Aventine / Created oftentimes a lake of blood ... By reason of the fraudulent theft he made / Of the great herd (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: That one is Cacus, who beneath the rock / of Mount Aventine made a lake of blood / again and again ... because of the fraud and the theft he worked / on the great herd that grazed close by him —
divergences.note: Cacus — in myth a fire-breathing monster, here a Centaur with snakes massed on his back and a dragon at his shoulders — is set apart from the other Centaurs because his crime was theft by fraud (he stole part of Hercules' cattle by dragging them backward to hide the tracks), which puts him among the thieves rather than the violent. We keep the proper noun Cacus and the concrete horror of the 'lake of blood' at Aventine, and make plain what Longfellow's 'fraudulent theft' means — the fraud is exactly why he belongs in this ditch — without naming the backward-dragged cattle, since Dante leaves the trick implied and lets the club of Hercules close the story: 'a hundred blows; he felt not ten.'

divergences.phrase: Godi, Fiorenza, poi che se' sì grande / che per mare e per terra batti l'ali, / e per lo 'nferno tuo nome si spande!
divergences.older: Rejoice, O Florence, since thou art so great, / That over sea and land thou beatest thy wings, / And throughout Hell thy name is spread abroad! (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Rejoice, Florence, since you are so great / that over sea and land you beat your wings, / and your name is spread through Hell itself!
divergences.note: The canto opens with bitter sarcasm — Dante congratulating his own city for the achievement of having so many of her sons damned that her reputation reaches even into Hell. 'Godi' is a mock 'rejoice,' and the irony is the whole point, so we keep the apostrophe direct and the false praise straight-faced ('Rejoice, Florence'), letting the next tercets turn the knife rather than tipping the reader off with editorializing. We straighten Longfellow's inverted 'thou art so great' but keep the soaring 'beat your wings' image, since the mockery rides on the language of glory.

divergences.phrase: Considerate la vostra semenza: / fatti non foste a viver come bruti, / ma per seguir virtute e canoscenza
