divergences.older: Consider ye the seed from which ye sprang; / Ye were not made to live like unto brutes, / But for pursuit of virtue and of knowledge (Longfellow); Call to mind from whence ye sprang: / Ye were not form'd to live the life of brutes, / But virtue to pursue and knowledge high (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Consider where you came from. You were not made / to live like animals, dumb and grazing, / but to follow after virtue and knowledge.
divergences.note: The most famous lines in the canto and among the most famous in the whole poem — Ulysses' exhortation to his old, weary crew to sail past the edge of the known world. The Italian 'semenza' is literally the seed or stock one springs from; 'come bruti' means as brute beasts; 'virtute e canoscenza' is virtue (here closer to human excellence, the full reach of one's powers) and knowledge. We render 'come bruti' as 'like animals, dumb and grazing' to make the contrast physical and immediate — the life Ulysses says they were NOT made for — rather than the abstract 'brutes,' and we keep the climactic pairing 'virtue and knowledge' exactly, since the whole speech, and Dante's tragic judgment of it, balances on those two words. The nobility is the lure: it is a magnificent call to the highest human aspiration, and it sails its speaker straight into a death God forbade — which is precisely why Dante puts it in the mouth of a damned counselor. We keep the grandeur undimmed and let the reader feel both the splendor and the trap.

divergences.phrase: e la prora ire in giù, com'altrui piacque, / infin che 'l mar fu sovra noi richiuso
divergences.older: And the prow downward go, as pleased Another, / Until the sea above us closed again (Longfellow); the bark / Went down, as pleased Another, till the sea / Had closed above us (Cary)
divergences.lectio: and drove the prow down, as Another willed, / until the sea had closed over us again.
divergences.note: The end of the voyage and of the canto: a whirlwind off the dark mountain (Purgatory, glimpsed by living eyes that have no right to see it) spins the ship three times and sinks her. 'Com'altrui piacque' is literally 'as it pleased another' — and Dante, through the pagan Ulysses, will not name that Other. It is God, whose will drowns the man who tried to cross the boundary set for mortals; but the veil is deliberate, the same withholding Dante uses for Christ at the Harrowing (IV.53) and for the unnamed power throughout. We keep it veiled and capitalize it ('as Another willed') so the reader feels the silent, sovereign hand without having the name handed to them — the reticence is the reverence, and it lands harder than any explanation.

divergences.phrase: Come 'l bue cicilian che mugghiò prima / col pianto di colui ...
divergences.older: As the Sicilian bull (that bellowed first / With the lament of him, and that was right, / Who with his file had modulated it) / Bellowed so with the voice of the afflicted (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: As the Sicilian bull — which bellowed first / with the cries of the man who shaped it with his file, / and that was only right — would bellow so with the voice of the one in agony
divergences.note: The opening simile is the bronze bull of Phalaris, the tyrant of Agrigento: its maker Perillus built it so a victim roasted inside would have his screams turned, by the bull's throat, into a bull's bellow — and Phalaris justly tested it first on Perillus himself. Dante uses it to explain how Guido's flame 'speaks': the human words have no opening, so the fire converts them into its own roaring at the tip. We keep the grim justice intact ('and that was only right') and render 'col pianto di colui ... che l'avea temperato con sua lima' as the maker who 'shaped it with his file,' so a reader feels the craftsman killed by his own device, the image that sets up the whole canto's mechanism of suffering forced into a strange voice.

divergences.phrase: lunga promessa con l'attender corto
divergences.older: The promise long with the fulfilment short / Will make thee triumph in thy lofty seat (Longfellow); Large promise with performance scant (Cary, paraphrasing)
divergences.lectio: a long promise kept short on delivery / will make you win your high seat
divergences.note: This is the fraudulent counsel itself — the single line for which Guido da Montefeltro is damned. He tells Pope Boniface VIII how to take the rebel stronghold of Palestrina: promise the defenders generous terms, then break the promise once they yield. Dante's phrasing is a cold proverb of bad faith — 'lunga promessa con l'attender corto,' a long promise with the keeping of it short. We keep that hard symmetry ('a long promise kept short on delivery') rather than Longfellow's flatter 'the promise long with the fulfilment short,' because the line is the crime: counsel built entirely on the gap between what is promised and what is meant.

divergences.phrase: ch'assolver non si può chi non si pente, / né pentere e volere insieme puossi / per la contradizion che nol consente
divergences.older: For who repents not cannot be absolved, / Nor can one both repent and will at once, / Because of the contradiction which consents not (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: You cannot absolve a man who does not repent, / nor can a man repent and will a thing at once — / the contradiction forbids it.
divergences.note: The black cherub's logical trap, and the hinge of the canto: Boniface absolved Guido in advance, before the sin was committed — but absolution requires repentance, and you cannot repent of a sin you are at that very moment willing to commit. The two states cancel each other; the law of non-contradiction does the rest. We keep the syllogism bare and exact rather than soften it, because the horror is precisely that it is airtight — and we let the devil's gleeful 'Forse tu non pensavi ch'io loïco fossi!' land plainly as 'You didn't think, maybe, that I was a logician!', a demon who damns by reasoning better than a pope.

divergences.phrase: Così s'osserva in me lo contrapasso
divergences.older: Thus is observed in me the counterpoise (Longfellow); In me thou hast example fit / Of just retaliation (Cary, paraphrasing)
divergences.lectio: So in me you see the counterpass fulfilled.
divergences.note: The single most important word in the canto, and the only place in the whole Commedia where Dante names his governing principle by name: 'contrapasso' — the punishment shaped to mirror the sin. Bertran de Born, who split a father from his son, walks Hell split from his own head. We render 'contrapasso' as 'counterpass' rather than Longfellow's 'counterpoise' (which suggests mere balance, a scale) because Dante's word is built on the idea of suffering-in-return, the sin turned back on the sinner in kind; the line is the moral key not just to this ditch but to the architecture of Hell, so we keep it as a clean, ringing close and resist explaining it, since Dante lets the severed-head image do the explaining.

divergences.phrase: Or vedi com'io mi dilacco! / ... vedi come storpiato è Mäometto! / Dinanzi a me sen va piangendo Alì, / fesso nel volto dal mento al ciuffetto
divergences.older: See now how I rend me; / How mutilated, see, is Mahomet; / In front of me doth Ali weeping go, / Cleft in the face from forelock unto chin (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: See how I rip myself! ... See how mangled Mohammed is! / In front of me Ali goes weeping, / his face split open from the forelock to the chin.
divergences.note: This is the canto's most charged passage, and we render it exactly as Dante wrote it, plainly and without flinching: Mohammed, placed among the sowers of schism, tears his own ruptured body open to show the pilgrim his wound. It is a canonical literary text and a record of how Dante's fourteenth-century world saw Islam — a view a modern reader should meet as Dante set it down, neither softened nor sharpened. We update the spelling to the standard modern 'Mohammed' and keep 'Ali' as is; we render 'mi dilacco' as the brutal, physical 'I rip myself' (Longfellow's 'rend' has gone archaic) and 'storpiato' as 'mangled.' The wound's exact path — 'dal mento al ciuffetto,' chin to forelock — we keep concrete, because Dante means us to see the precise line of the cleft.

divergences.phrase: Capo ha cosa fatta — "e morte de la tua schiatta"
divergences.older: 'A thing done has an end!' / Which was an ill seed for the Tuscan people. ... 'And death unto thy race' (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: 'A thing done has an end!' / which was the seed of ruin for the Tuscan people. ... 'And death to your own line,' I added.
divergences.note: Mosca dei Lamberti's six fatal words — 'Capo ha cosa fatta,' literally 'a done thing has a head/end' — were the counsel that, in Florentine legend, launched the murder that split the city into Guelphs and Ghibellines and set off generations of feud. The phrase turns on 'capo' meaning both 'head' (a beginning) and 'an end, a conclusion' — get it over with, what's done is done. We keep the proverb's blunt, fatalistic snap ('a thing done has an end') because its very brevity is the horror: a whole civil war set rolling by a throwaway line. We preserve Dante's own cold retort to Mosca — 'and death to your own line' — which caps the exchange, the pilgrim turning the man's seed of ruin back on his family, a small contrapasso of speech that foreshadows the canto's last word.

divergences.phrase: spirto del mio sangue ... Geri del Bello
divergences.older: I think a spirit of my blood laments / The sin which down below there costs so much ... and heard him called Geri del Bello (Longfellow); a spirit of mine own blood (Cary)
divergences.lectio: a spirit of my own blood mourns / the sin that costs so much down in that place ... and heard him called Geri del Bello
divergences.note: Geri del Bello was Dante's own kinsman (a first cousin of his father), murdered in a feud, and at the time of the poem still unavenged — which, by the blood-vengeance code Dante's Florence took for granted, left a stain on the whole family. That is why the shade points at Dante and threatens 'hard with his finger' (minacciava forte): the gesture is an accusation, not a greeting, and Dante's pity is shot through with guilt. We keep the proper name Geri del Bello and render 'spirto del mio sangue' as the plain, literal 'a spirit of my own blood' rather than abstracting it to 'a kinsman,' because the kinship-by-blood is exactly what the unavenged death indicts. We also keep the periphrasis for Bertran de Born — 'the one who once held Hautefort' (colui che già tenne Altaforte) — unexplained, the way Dante leaves it.

divergences.phrase: non vidi già mai menare stregghia / da ragazzo ... sì traevan giù l'unghie la scabbia, / come coltel di scardova le scaglie
divergences.older: And never saw I plied a currycomb / By stable-boy for whom his master waits ... And the nails downward with them dragged the scab, / In fashion as a knife the scales of bream (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: I never saw a stable-boy work a currycomb / so fast, with his master standing there waiting ... And the nails dragged the scabs down off them / the way a knife scrapes the scales from a bream
divergences.note: The signature image of the alchemists' ditch — the falsifiers of metals lie in stinking heaps, raked by a leprous, scabbing plague, and claw at themselves so furiously that Dante reaches for the homeliest possible comparison: a stable-boy currying a horse in a hurry because his master (or his bed) is waiting. The deliberate drop in register — high horror rendered through a barnyard chore — is the point, so we keep the currycomb and the impatient stable-boy concrete rather than smoothing them into 'scratching.' For the second simile we keep Dante's exact fish, the scardova (bream), and his exact verb-image: nails scraping scabs off skin the way a knife scrapes scales off a fish. The crudeness is the punishment, and we let it stay crude.

divergences.phrase: com'io fui di natura buona scimia
divergences.older: How I a skilful ape of nature was (Longfellow); how I of nature was / A skilful ape (Cary)
divergences.lectio: what a good ape of nature I was
divergences.note: Capocchio's last line — and the canto's last line — is a grim joke. An alchemist counterfeits metals by imitating what nature makes, so he calls himself 'di natura buona scimia,' a good ape of nature: the word for his crime (mimicry, falsification) is the same word he uses to boast of his skill. We keep the literal 'ape of nature' rather than flattening it to 'imitator,' because the pun is the man — even damned and clawing at his own scabs, Capocchio is still proud of how well he forged. We preserve the proper nouns Capocchio and Griffolino (the unnamed Aretine 'burned by Albert of Siena,' identified by tradition as Griffolino of Arezzo) intact.

divergences.phrase: fatto a guisa di lëuto
divergences.older: made in fashion of a lute (Longfellow); fashioned like a lute (Cary)
divergences.lectio: shaped like a lute
divergences.note: Master Adam, swollen with dropsy, is the canto's master image — a body bloated into the round belly and thin neck of a lute. Dante's simile is grotesquely exact (a man would only need his legs cut away at the fork to complete the instrument). We keep it plain and visual rather than letting 'in fashion of'/'fashioned like' soften the shock; the comparison should land as a physical fact, not a decoration.

divergences.phrase: Quel folletto è Gianni Schicchi
divergences.older: That mad sprite is Gianni Schicchi (Longfellow); That sprite of air is Gianni Schicchi (Cary)
divergences.lectio: That mad imp is Gianni Schicchi
divergences.note: Schicchi is a falsifier of persons: he impersonated the dead Buoso Donati and dictated a fraudulent will to steal the prize mare of the herd. 'Folletto' is a goblin-imp, a malicious darting spirit — we keep the proper noun fixed and choose 'mad imp' over the airy, almost gentle 'sprite,' since the soul here is rabid, running and biting like a loosed hog.

divergences.phrase: leccar lo specchio di Narcisso
divergences.older: to lick up the mirror of Narcissus (Longfellow); to lick the glass of Narcissus (Cary)
divergences.lectio: to lap up the mirror of Narcissus
divergences.note: Sinon jeers that Master Adam, parched with dropsy, would gladly drink the pool Narcissus stared into — 'the mirror of Narcissus' is Dante's elegant kenning for any sheet of water. We keep the strangeness of the image rather than flattening it to 'a pool,' since the insult turns on its cruel courtliness, but use 'lap up' so the verb reads as the animal craving of a man dying of thirst.

divergences.phrase: Raphèl maì amècche zabì almi
divergences.older: Raphael mai amech izabi almi (Longfellow); Raphel may amech zabi almi (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Raphèl maì amècche zabì almi
divergences.note: Nimrod's single line is deliberate nonsense — speech with no meaning, the fitting punishment for the man whose Tower of Babel scattered the world's one language. Generations of editors have tried to 'fix' the spelling; Petrocchi's accented text (which we follow) keeps the babble strange and unparsable rather than nudging it toward a guessable phrase. We render it exactly, untranslated, because the whole point is that it cannot be translated — to Nimrod every tongue is now noise, and his is noise to everyone. Virgil's reply confirms it: no one will ever read sense into these words.

divergences.phrase: O tu che ne la fortunata valle ... mettine giù, e non ten vegna schifo
divergences.older: O thou, who in the valley fortunate ... Place us below, nor be disdainful of it (Longfellow); O thou! who in the fortunate vale ... set us down, nor scorn / To do the bidding (Cary)
divergences.lectio: O you who once, in that fortunate valley ... set us down below, and don't think it beneath you
divergences.note: Virgil's whole speech to Antaeus is flattery with a hook: he praises the giant's old glory (the lions he hunted in the Scipio–Hannibal valley, the war on the gods his brothers nearly won) precisely to coax him into lifting the travelers down — and seals it with the one thing a damned soul still wants, fame back in the living world. We keep the coaxing, courtly turn of 'non ten vegna schifo' as 'don't think it beneath you' and 'do not curl thy lip' as 'don't curl your lip at us,' so the reader hears Virgil working the giant's pride rather than commanding him. The bribe is the living poet himself: 'this man can give you what is hungered for here.'

divergences.phrase: Qual pare a riguardar la Carisenda / sotto 'l chinato, quando un nuvol vada / sovr'essa sì, ched ella incontro penda
divergences.older: As seems the Carisenda, to behold / Beneath the leaning side, when goes a cloud / Above it so that opposite it hangs (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: The way the Garisenda looks, seen from below / on the side it leans, when a cloud goes over / so that the tower seems to topple the other way
divergences.note: The Garisenda is a real leaning tower in Bologna; standing under its overhanging side while a cloud drifts across the sky makes the tower itself seem to fall toward you. Dante uses this everyday optical illusion to convey the terror of watching the giant Antaeus bend down over him. We keep the proper noun and the precise mechanism of the illusion — the cloud moving makes the leaning stone appear to come down — rather than smoothing it into a vague comparison, because the exactness is what makes the dread physical.

divergences.phrase: Vexilla regis prodeunt inferni
divergences.older: 'Vexilla Regis prodeunt Inferni' Towards us (Longfellow, leaves the Latin untranslated); THE banners of Hell's Monarch do come forth (Cary)
divergences.lectio: "Vexilla regis prodeunt inferni — the banners of the king of Hell advance"
divergences.note: This is the only line of Latin in the whole Inferno, and it lands as a blasphemous joke: Virgil twists the opening of Venantius Fortunatus's great Good Friday hymn to the Cross ('The banners of the king advance') by adding a single word — inferni, 'of Hell.' The hymn celebrates Christ's victory; here it heralds Satan. We keep the Latin so the reader sees the sacred phrase intact, then give it plainly in English so the parody is legible. Longfellow leaves it untranslated and trusts the reader's Latin; we don't.

divergences.phrase: Lo 'mperador del doloroso regno
divergences.older: The Emperor of the kingdom dolorous (Longfellow); That emperor, who sways the realm of sorrow (Cary); The emperor of the woeful realm (Norton)
divergences.lectio: The emperor of the kingdom of all grief
divergences.note: Dante never names Lucifer in the climactic vision — he is titled, the way a sovereign is: 'the emperor of the dolorous kingdom.' The grandeur of the title against the obscenity of the body (buried to the chest, drooling, weeping from six eyes) is the whole point. Longfellow's 'dolorous' is exactly the period word that now reads as costume; we keep the imperial register but trade the Latinate adjective for plain English ('the kingdom of all grief') so the title still rings without sounding archaic. The proper noun Lucifer is preserved where Dante does use it (line 89).

divergences.phrase: E quindi uscimmo a riveder le stelle
divergences.older: Thence we came forth to rebehold the stars (Longfellow); Thus issuing we again beheld the stars (Cary); and thence we came forth to see again the stars (Norton)
divergences.lectio: And from there we came out, to see again the stars
divergences.note: The most famous closing line in the poem, and the first of the three — each cantica ends on 'stelle.' After the suffocation of the ice and the climb through the body of evil, the line has to open and lift. We keep it as a single hanging line, as the original does, and choose 'see again the stars' over Longfellow's 'rebehold' — the force is in the simple verb returning, not in an elevated one. The plainness is the relief.

divergences.phrase: quattro stelle / non viste mai fuor ch'a la prima gente
divergences.older: four stars / Ne'er seen before save by the primal people (Longfellow); four stars... ne'er seen but by the ken / of our first parents (Cary)
divergences.lectio: four stars / seen by no one since the first people
divergences.note: The four stars are read both as the Southern Cross — unseen from Dante's hemisphere — and as the four cardinal virtues (prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance) that light Cato's face. 'La prima gente' is Adam and Eve, who alone, in Eden before the Fall, could see them. We keep the line as Dante leaves it — a plain, astonishing fact — without unpacking the allegory, so the reader meets the wonder before the gloss.

divergences.phrase: un veglio solo / degno di tanta reverenza in vista
divergences.older: an old man alone, / Worthy of so much reverence in his look (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: an old man, alone, / so worthy in his look of reverence / that no son owes his father more
divergences.note: The 'veglio' is Cato of Utica — the pagan suicide whom Dante, against every theological expectation, makes the stern guardian of the shore of Purgatory, because he died for liberty. We keep his name out of the verse (Dante withholds it too) and let the reverence land first; the proper noun arrives only later, through Virgil's appeal to Cato's love of freedom and his wife Marcia.

divergences.phrase: un giunco schietto ... l'umile pianta ... si rinacque
divergences.older: a smooth rush ... the humble plant, such it sprang up again (Longfellow); a slender reed ... the lowly plant (Cary)
divergences.lectio: a smooth rush ... the humble plant, another sprang up at once, / the very same
divergences.note: Cato orders Virgil to gird Dante not with the proud cord of Hell but with a 'giunco' — a humble rush, the emblem of the bending humility Purgatory requires; the reed that 'will not bend to the blows' would die, only the yielding one lives. That it renews itself the instant it is plucked makes humility inexhaustible, a grace that cannot be used up. We hold the plain horticultural miracle and let the meaning rise from it rather than naming the virtue.

divergences.phrase: Poscia, più che 'l dolor, poté 'l digiuno
divergences.older: Then hunger did what sorrow could not do (Longfellow); Famine of grief can get the mastery (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Then fasting did what grief had failed to do.
divergences.note: The most debated line in the poem. Literally 'then, more than grief, hunger had the power' — and Dante leaves it open whether hunger simply finished off a starving man, or whether Ugolino, blind and three days past his sons' deaths, ate them. Longfellow's 'hunger' and Cary's gloss both lean toward plain starvation; we keep 'fasting' (the word's root sense, digiuno) and the bare 'did what grief had failed to do,' so the horror stays a possibility the reader must hold open, exactly as the original refuses to resolve it.

divergences.phrase: Padre, assai ci fia men doglia / se tu mangi di noi
divergences.older: Father, much less pain 'twill give us / If thou do eat of us (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Father, it would grieve us less / if you would eat of us.
divergences.note: The children's offer is the canto's unbearable pivot, and it must land as something a child would actually say to a parent. We strip Longfellow's inverted 'twill give us / If thou do eat' down to plain, direct speech — 'it would grieve us less if you would eat of us' — and keep the tender follow-on ('you dressed us once in this poor flesh — now take it off') intact, since the body Ugolino gave them is exactly what they are offering back.

divergences.phrase: Ahi Pisa, vituperio de le genti / del bel paese là dove 'l sì suona
divergences.older: Ah! Pisa, thou opprobrium of the people / Of the fair land there where the 'Si' doth sound (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Ah, Pisa — shame of all the peoples / of that fair country where the word for yes is sì
divergences.note: Dante's curse on Pisa turns on naming Italy by its word for yes — sì — the same device he uses to name the whole 'land of sì' elsewhere. 'Opprobrium' is a word no modern reader carries; we render vituperio as the plain, heavier 'shame,' and we keep sì itself rather than translating it away, since the line's force is that Pisa disgraces the very tongue it speaks.

divergences.phrase: uccel divino / sì che l'occhio da presso nol sostenne
divergences.older: The Bird Divine, more radiant he appeared (Longfellow); the bird of God (Cary)
divergences.lectio: the Bird of God came nearer ... up close my eyes could not hold him
divergences.note: The swift Angel Boatman is the canto's first great image: an angel who needs no oar and no sail but his own deathless wings, ferrying the saved across from the Tiber's mouth. We keep Dante's strange and tender phrase 'uccel divino' as 'Bird of God' rather than smoothing it to 'angel' — the bird-likeness is the whole point of the wings-for-sails picture — and we keep the detail that the brightness grows past what the eye can bear, so the reader feels the holiness as Dante does, by having to look away.

divergences.phrase: Ohi ombre vane, fuor che ne l'aspetto! / tre volte dietro a lei le mani avvinsi, / e tante mi tornai con esse al petto
divergences.older: O empty shadows, save in aspect only! / Three times behind it did I clasp my hands (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: O empty shadows — solid only to the eye! / Three times I clasped my hands behind him, / and three times brought them back against my chest
divergences.note: Dante's three failed attempts to embrace Casella deliberately echo Aeneas reaching for the shades of Creusa and Anchises in the Aeneid — the arms close on nothing and come back empty. We keep the threefold gesture exact and concrete rather than abstracting it into 'I could not hold him,' because the bodily reaching-and-failing is the grief; and we render 'fuor che ne l'aspetto' as 'solid only to the eye,' which is the literal paradox: a shade looks whole and is air.

divergences.phrase: Amor che ne la mente mi ragiona
divergences.older: Love, that within my mind discourses with me (Longfellow); Love that discourses in my thoughts (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Love that discourses in my mind
divergences.note: Casella sings the opening line of one of Dante's own canzoni (from the Convivio), and the moment is the heart of the canto — a poet hearing his words sung back to him by a dead friend, the whole shore held rapt until Cato breaks the spell. We keep the line as a quoted song-title, near-literal, and keep the word 'discourses': Dante means love that reasons and argues inside him, not merely speaks — the canzone is a philosophical love poem, and softening 'ragiona' to 'speaks' would lose that the song is also a piece of thinking.

divergences.phrase: State contenti, umana gente, al quia
divergences.older: Mortals, remain contented at the 'Quia' (Longfellow); Rest, mortals, in the WHEREFORE (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Be content with the because, humankind
divergences.note: Dante's 'al quia' is a Scholastic technical phrase — the quia is the fact that a thing is so, as opposed to the propter quid, the reason why it is so. Longfellow leaves the Latin 'Quia' on the page and Cary reaches for 'wherefore,' both of which stop a modern reader cold. We render it as 'the because': the plain truth that things are as they are, with the understanding that the why is sealed off from us. The strangeness of resting in a bare 'because' is the thought itself, so we keep it rather than smooth it into 'accept your limits.'

divergences.phrase: Io dico d'Aristotile e di Plato / e di molt' altri
divergences.older: I speak of Aristotle and of Plato, / And many others (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: I mean Aristotle, and Plato, / and many more
divergences.note: This is the canto's quiet wound: Virgil names the great pagan minds — himself among the unnamed 'many more' — whose longing for God can never be satisfied, and then bows his head and goes silent. We keep the bluntness of the naming and the breaking-off; the grief is in what he stops saying, not in any added adjective. 'I mean' (Io dico) is Virgil pointing at his own circle in Limbo without quite saying so.

divergences.phrase: biondo era e bello e di gentile aspetto / … Io son Manfredi
divergences.older: Blond was he, beautiful, and of noble aspect (Longfellow); I am Manfredi (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: He was blond, and beautiful, and noble to look at … I am Manfred
divergences.note: Manfred — the excommunicate Hohenstaufen king, beautiful and fair-haired with a split eyebrow and a chest wound — is the human heart of the canto, and his name and his daughter Constance's are load-bearing, so both are kept exactly. His teaching that the Church's curse delays but cannot bar salvation ('as long as hope keeps anything green,' mentre che la speranza ha fior del verde) and that the prayers of the living shorten the wait is the canto's argument; we render 'fior del verde' as hope keeping 'anything green' to hold Dante's living plant-image rather than flattening it to mere 'hope.'

divergences.phrase: the higher a man climbs, the less it hurts
divergences.older: ever / At the beginning down below 'tis tiresome, / And aye the more one climbs, the less it hurts (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the start of it, down low, is always hard, / and the higher a man climbs, the less it hurts
divergences.note: The signature consolation of the whole cantica — Mount Purgatory inverts an ordinary climb: brutal at the base, easier with every step up, until ascending feels like drifting downstream. Longfellow's 'tiresome' undersells Dante's grave (heavy, grievous); we keep the contrast hard/hurts so the relief lands as the soul's, not just the legs'.

divergences.phrase: Belacqua: "Brother, what's the use of climbing?"
divergences.older: And he: 'O brother, what's the use of climbing? / Since to my torment would not let me go / The Angel of God, who sitteth at the gate' (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: And he: "Brother, what's the use of climbing? / The angel of God who sits up at the gate / wouldn't let me go on to the torments.
divergences.note: Belacqua — the Florentine lute-maker famous for sloth — keeps his name and his dry, deadpan resignation. The Italian 'O frate, andar in sù che porta?' is a shrug, not a lament; we render it as plain, wry refusal. The late-repentant must idle outside as long as they delayed in life — the same waiting-outside law Manfred described in Canto III, kept consistent here.

divergences.phrase: the chariot of the light, entering between us and the north wind
divergences.older: the chariot of the light, / Where 'twixt us and the Aquilon it entered (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the chariot of the light, / entering between us and the north wind
divergences.note: Virgil's astronomy lesson: in the southern hemisphere the sun crosses to the north, not the south as Dante knew it. We unpack Longfellow's Latinate 'Aquilon' into 'the north wind' so the geography reads on the first pass — the strangeness of a flipped sky is the point, and shouldn't be buried under an archaic name.

divergences.phrase: sta come torre ferma, che non crolla / già mai la cima per soffiar di venti
divergences.older: Stand like a steadfast tower, that never wags / its top for all the blowing of the winds (Longfellow); be as a tower, that, firmly set, / shakes not its top for any blast that blows (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Stand like a firm tower that never bends / its top, no matter how the winds may blow
divergences.note: Virgil's rebuke is the canto's moral hinge: do not let other people's chatter — or your own runaway thoughts — pull you off course. We keep the plain, hard image of the tower and drop Longfellow's archaic 'wags,' which now reads as comic rather than steadfast. The register is firm but unfussy, the gentler Purgatorio voice rather than Inferno's heat.

divergences.phrase: io fui di Montefeltro, io son Bonconte … per una lagrimetta
divergences.older: I was of Montefeltro, and am Buonconte (Longfellow); for one poor little tear, that takes him from me (Longfellow); for a single tear (Cary)
divergences.lectio: I was of Montefeltro; I am Buonconte … for one small tear, that takes him from me
divergences.note: Buonconte da Montefeltro fell at Campaldino (1289); his body was never found. The whole episode turns on the contrast between the soul, saved at the last instant by Mary's name and a single tear of repentance, and the corpse, which the cheated devil claims by raising a storm to wash it down the Archiano into the Arno. We preserve the proper nouns (Buonconte, Campaldino, Archiano, Arno, Casentino, Pratomagno) and keep the diminutive 'lagrimetta' as 'one small tear' — the smallness is the theological point: salvation hung on almost nothing.

divergences.phrase: ricorditi di me, che son la Pia; / Siena mi fé, disfecemi Maremma
divergences.older: Do thou remember me who am the Pia; / Siena made me, unmade me Maremma (Longfellow); call thou to mind / La Pia. Sienna gave me life, Maremma took it from me (Cary)
divergences.lectio: remember me. I am La Pia. / Siena made me, Maremma unmade me
divergences.note: The most famous lines in the canto, and among the most quoted in the whole poem: a complete life in two place-names. We keep the made/unmade pairing intact — it is the line's whole engine, the verb turned against itself — and keep the proper nouns Pia, Siena, and Maremma. She asks for nothing but to be remembered, and her courtesy (she lets Dante rest first before she speaks) is the gentlest moment in a canto full of violent deaths. We resist over-explaining the husband's identity, which Dante deliberately leaves veiled — 'he knows it.'

divergences.phrase: Ahi serva Italia, di dolore ostello, / nave sanza nocchiere in gran tempesta, / non donna di province, ma bordello!
divergences.older: Ah! servile Italy, grief's hostelry! / A ship without a pilot in great tempest! / No Lady thou of Provinces, but brothel! (Longfellow); Ah slavish Italy! thou inn of grief, / Vessel without a pilot in loud storm, / Lady no longer of fair provinces, / But brothel-house impure! (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Slave Italy, hostel of grief, / ship without a pilot in a great storm, / no lady of provinces — a brothel!
divergences.note: The most famous apostrophe in the Commedia, and the hinge of this canto: the sight of Sordello embracing a fellow Mantuan throws into relief an Italy whose own cities tear at each other. 'Serva' is literally 'enslaved' — we keep the hard word 'slave' rather than soften to 'servile.' 'Di dolore ostello' is an inn/lodging-house of grief: we keep the concrete 'hostel' over Longfellow's archaic 'hostelry.' The third line's contempt — once the mistress (donna) of provinces, now a bordello — we keep blunt and undecorated; Cary's 'brothel-house impure' pads it, and the Italian gives no adjective. The line is meant to land like a slap.

divergences.phrase: "O Mantoano, io son Sordello / de la tua terra!"; e l'un l'altro abbracciava.
divergences.older: "O Mantuan, I am Sordello / Of thine own land!" and one embraced the other. (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: "O Mantuan, I am Sordello, / from your own land!" — and the two embraced.
divergences.note: Sordello (the thirteenth-century Mantuan troubadour) does not even ask who Virgil is — only the sound of the shared city, 'Mantua,' moves him to rise and embrace a stranger. We keep the proper nouns Sordello and Mantua intact, since the whole invective that follows detonates from this one word of belonging. We render the patriot's leap plainly ('the two embraced') rather than Longfellow's inverted 'one embraced the other,' so the human gesture, not the grammar, carries the moment.

divergences.phrase: Quando si parte il gioco de la zara
divergences.older: Whene'er is broken up the game of Zara (Longfellow); Soon as the game of dice breaks up (Cary)
divergences.lectio: When the game of hazard breaks up
divergences.note: Zara is the medieval dice game whose name gave English the word 'hazard.' Longfellow keeps the foreign name 'Zara,' which strands a modern reader; Cary flattens it to 'dice.' We use 'the game of hazard,' which is true to the etymology and instantly legible as gambling — the simile needs the reader to picture the winner mobbed at the table, since that is exactly the crowd of prayer-hungry souls pressing Dante in the next tercet.

divergences.phrase: Io son Virgilio; e per null'altro rio / lo ciel perdei che per non aver fé
divergences.older: I am Virgilius; and for no crime else / Did I lose heaven, than for not having faith (Longfellow); I am Virgil; and for no other crime / Lost Heaven, than for unbelief (Cary)
divergences.lectio: I am Virgil; and I lost heaven / for no other fault than this — that I had no faith.
divergences.note: Virgil names the exact terms of his damnation: not sin, but the absence of faith — he lived before Christ and could not believe. Longfellow's 'rio' as 'crime' overstates it; the Italian is closer to 'fault' or 'wrong,' and the point is precisely that there was no crime, only a lack. We keep that distinction, since it is the theological hinge of the whole encounter — the noblest pagan, blameless yet barred.

divergences.phrase: Loco è là giù non tristo di martìri, / ma di tenebre solo
divergences.older: A place there is below not sad with torments, / But darkness only (Longfellow); There is a place beneath, not made by pain / Of torment sad, but darkness sole (Cary)
divergences.lectio: There is a place down there — not grieved by torments, / but by darkness only, where the laments / are not the sound of wailing but of sighs.
divergences.note: This is Limbo as Virgil describes it from inside — the gentlest region of Hell, where there is no torture, only a grief that has no fire in it. Dante's contrast is exact and quiet: not 'guai' (cries of pain) but 'sospiri' (sighs). We keep that downshift from wailing to sighing intact, because the whole sorrow of Limbo is that it is sorrow without violence — the ache of being shut out, nothing more.

divergences.phrase: la valletta / 'Salve, Regina' in sul verde e 'n su' fiori
divergences.older: By herbage and by flowers within that hollow ... 'Salve Regina,' on the green and flowers / There seated, singing, spirits I beheld (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: set against the grass and flowers in that hollow ... "Salve, Regina" — there on the green and the flowers / I saw souls seated, singing.
divergences.note: The Valley of the Negligent Princes is Dante's first burst of color and scent in the poem — a flowering hollow whose grass and blossoms would outshine gold, emerald, and scarlet, where rulers who put worldly cares before their souls now sing the 'Salve Regina,' the evening hymn to Mary, the prayer of those still in exile longing for home. We keep the Latin hymn-title untranslated, as Dante does, and keep the lavish catalogue of colors plain and concrete rather than smoothing it, because the sensory overflow is the point — the negligent are not punished here but suspended in a beautiful waiting, gazing up at the climb they delayed in life.

divergences.phrase: Era già l'ora che volge il disio … che paia il giorno pianger che si more
divergences.older: ’Twas now the hour that turneth back desire / In those who sail the sea, and melts the heart … / That seemeth to deplore the dying day (Longfellow); It was the hour that wakens fond desire (Cary)
divergences.lectio: It was now the hour that turns the longing back / in those who sail the sea, and melts the heart … / a bell that seems to mourn the dying of the day
divergences.note: The most famous evening in the poem, and the most often over-sweetened. Cary's 'wakens fond desire' gets the feeling backward — Dante's hour does not wake longing, it volge il disio, turns it homeward, the seaman's heart bending back toward the friends he left that very morning. We keep that homeward turn, and we keep the line's plain ache: a far bell that seems to mourn (pianger) the day as it dies. No 'deplore,' no 'twas — just the sound carrying across water at dusk.

divergences.phrase: una biscia, / forse qual diede ad Eva il cibo amaro … li angeli … ali verdi
divergences.older: a serpent was; perchance / The same which gave to Eve the bitter food … the celestial falcons (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: a serpent — perhaps / the very one that gave Eve the bitter food … the heavenly hawks
divergences.note: Dante does not name Satan; he lets the serpent be the serpent — 'perhaps the very one' that tempted Eve, the ancient enemy returning each evening to the valley of the rulers. We keep the doubt ('perhaps') the original holds open rather than resolving it into a theological label. And the routing is fast and wordless on purpose: the green-winged angels move before the eye can catch how they started ('I did not see, so I cannot say'), and the serpent simply flees. We keep that speed — the menace and the rescue both pass in an instant.

divergences.phrase: quelle tre facelle … Le quattro chiare stelle che vedevi staman
divergences.older: those three torches / With which this hither pole is all on fire … The four resplendent stars / Thou sawest this morning (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: those three torches / that set this whole near pole on fire … The four bright stars / you saw this morning have sunk low
divergences.note: The four stars of the dawn (Canto I) are the cardinal virtues — prudence, justice, courage, temperance; the three that have now climbed into the night sky are the theological virtues — faith, hope, love, the ones a soul needs after dark. Dante never spells the allegory out, so neither do we: he simply notes that the four have set and the three have risen where they were. We keep 'facelle' as torches, small living flames, not abstract 'lights,' and let the reader who looks feel the swap.

divergences.phrase: tre gradi / bianco marmo … tinta più che perso … porfido
divergences.older: marble white, so polished and so smooth (Longfellow); The second, tinct of deeper hue than perse … Cracked all asunder lengthwise and across; The third … Porphyry seemed to me, as flaming red / As blood (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the first step, white marble, so polished I saw myself mirrored in it as I am; the second, darker than the deepest blue, a rough, scorched, brittle stone, cracked through its whole length and across; the third, porphyry, flaming red as blood that spurts up from a vein
divergences.note: The three steps are the canto's allegorical core — the soul's path into Purgatory: the bright mirror-marble is self-examination, the confession that shows you yourself; the cracked dark stone is contrition, the heart split open; the blood-red porphyry is satisfaction, the work of love that pays the debt. We keep all three images literal and concrete rather than glossing them, so the reader meets the allegory the way Dante built it — as physical stone — and feels the steps before reading them. 'Perso' (Longfellow's archaic 'perse') is a dark blue-black; we render it 'darker than the deepest blue' so the color lands without a footnote.

divergences.phrase: Sette P ne la fronte mi descrisse / col punton de la spada
divergences.older: Seven P's upon my forehead he described / With the sword's point (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Seven P's he cut into my forehead with the point of his sword
divergences.note: The seven P's stand for the seven peccata, the deadly sins — one for each terrace of the mountain, to be erased one by one as Dante climbs. Longfellow's 'described' is the old sense of 'inscribed,' but to a modern ear it reads as 'spoke about,' which loses the cut. We use 'cut into,' since the angel marks them with a sword-point and they are explicitly wounds — 'wash these wounds once you're inside' — wounds the climb itself will heal. We keep the bare letters 'P' rather than spelling out 'sins,' because the riddle of the marks is part of how Dante teaches the scheme.

divergences.phrase: di fuor torna chi 'n dietro si guata
divergences.older: I give you warning / That forth returns whoever looks behind (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: I warn you, whoever looks back goes back out
divergences.note: The angel's warning at the gate echoes Orpheus and Lot's wife: the one who turns to look behind loses the ground gained. Longfellow's 'forth returns' inverts the syntax in a way that muddies a plain, hard rule. We make it flat and absolute — 'looks back goes back out' — because the line is a law of the place, not a flourish, and Dante means it to ring as one.

divergences.phrase: visibile parlare
divergences.older: this visible language (Longfellow); this speech, made visible to sight (Cary)
divergences.lectio: this speech you could see
divergences.note: Dante's famous oxymoron for the carvings God made on the marble: parlare (speech) that is visibile (seeable). It is the canto's central marvel — relief sculpture so alive it seems to speak. Longfellow's 'visible language' is exact but stiff; we keep the paradox plain and immediate, 'speech you could see,' so the strangeness of carved stone that talks lands on a modern ear without a gloss.

divergences.phrase: noi siam vermi / nati a formar l'angelica farfalla
divergences.older: we are worms, / Born to bring forth the angelic butterfly (Longfellow); we are worms, / Yet made at last to form the winged insect / That soars to judgment (Cary)
divergences.lectio: we are worms, / born to become the angelic butterfly / that flies toward justice with nothing to shield it
divergences.note: Dante's rebuke to the proud rests on the caterpillar-to-butterfly image: the human soul is a grub whose whole purpose is to be transformed into something that can rise to God's judgment unprotected (sanza schermi, 'without screen'). We render 'formar' as 'become' rather than the older 'bring forth,' which misleads — the worm does not give birth to the butterfly, it turns into it; that is the whole point about pride. We keep 'sanza schermi' as 'with nothing to shield it,' preserving the nakedness before judgment that the proud refuse to face.

divergences.phrase: O superbi cristian, miseri lassi
divergences.older: O ye proud Christians! wretched, weary ones! (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: O you proud Christians — worn out, miserable —
divergences.note: The direct apostrophe to proud Christians is the moral hinge of the canto, and its force depends on sounding spoken, not declaimed. Longfellow's exclamatory 'O ye... wretched, weary ones!' is period pulpit-cadence; we keep the address but let it fall the way a serious voice would actually press it, the adjectives 'miseri lassi' landing as the plain, tired truth they name rather than a flourish.

divergences.phrase: O Padre nostro, che ne' cieli stai … 'l pan cotidiano … Non per noi, che non è di bisogno, / ma per color che dietro a noi restaro
divergences.older: "Our Father, thou who dwellest in the heavens, / Not circumscribed, but from the greater love / Thou bearest to the first effects on high … Give unto us this day our daily manna … This last petition verily, dear Lord, / Not for ourselves is made, who need it not, / But for their sake who have remained behind us." (Longfellow); "O thou Almighty Father, who dost make / The heavens thy dwelling" (Cary)
divergences.lectio: "Our Father, you who dwell in the heavens — / not bound there, but because you love / your first creation in the heights most of all … Give us this day our daily bread … This last request, dear Lord, we do not make / for ourselves, who no longer need it, / but for the sake of those we left behind."
divergences.note: Dante takes the Lord's Prayer the souls of the proud all know by heart and lets them widen it line by line — a humility exercise built out of the one prayer pride cannot say without bending. We keep it plainly recognizable as the Our Father (no thee/thou, no 'manna' — Dante writes pan cotidiano, daily bread) while keeping the expansions Dante adds: God 'not bound' to heaven but loving the highest creation most; strength 'so easily broken' set against the 'old Enemy.' The turn that makes the whole canto is the last tercet, and we keep its quiet shock intact: the dead, who are past all danger, pray this not for themselves but for the living they left behind. The prayer ends looking back over its shoulder, downward, at us.

divergences.phrase: Credette Cimabue ne la pittura / tener lo campo, e ora ha Giotto il grido … così ha tolto l'uno a l'altro Guido / la gloria de la lingua … Non è il mondan romore altro ch'un fiato / di vento, ch'or vien quinci e or vien quindi, / e muta nome perché muta lato
divergences.older: "In painting Cimabue thought that he / Should hold the field, now Giotto has the cry … So has one Guido from the other taken / The glory of our tongue … Naught is this mundane rumour but a breath / Of wind, that comes now this way and now that, / And changes name, because it changes side" (Longfellow); "the mundane noise / Of fame is but a blast of wind" (Cary)
divergences.lectio: "Cimabue thought he held the field / in painting; now it's Giotto people cry up, / and the older man's fame has gone dim. // And so one Guido has taken from the other / the glory of our tongue … // Worldly fame is nothing but a breath / of wind, that blows now from here, now from there, / and changes its name as it changes its quarter."
divergences.note: This is the canto's great meditation, and Oderisi — a miniaturist already eclipsed by Franco of Bologna — is the perfect mouth for it. We keep every proper name as architecture, since the point is precisely that names rise and fall: Cimabue overtaken by Giotto in painting; one Guido (Guinizelli) overtaken by another (Cavalcanti) in poetry; and — Dante's sly, half-hidden third term — 'one is born, perhaps, who'll chase them both out of the nest,' which is Dante himself, the proud man writing the canto against pride. We do not gloss who the Guidos are inside the line (the riddle is Dante's), but we keep the nest image he uses. The famous line we render flat and physical: fama is un fiato di vento, a breath of wind that 'changes its name as it changes its quarter' — like a wind named for the direction it blows from. Cary's 'blast' is too loud; Dante's word is a fiato, a single quiet exhalation, and that smallness is the whole argument.

divergences.phrase: Quel è Provenzan Salvani … Liberamente nel Campo di Siena, / ogne vergogna diposta, s'affisse … per trar l'amico suo di pena … condusse a tremar per ogne vena
divergences.older: "That," he replied, "is Provenzan Salvani … Freely upon the Campo of Siena, / All shame being laid aside, he placed himself … And there to draw his friend from the duress / Which in the prison-house of Charles he suffered, / He brought himself to tremble in each vein." (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: "That is Provenzano Salvani … he set himself, of his own will, / in the Campo of Siena, all shame put aside … and there, to free his friend from the suffering / he bore in Charles's prison, he brought himself / to beg — to tremble in every vein."
divergences.note: Provenzano Salvani ruled Siena and was proud enough to want 'all Siena in his hands' — yet he is climbing the mountain early, ahead of the rule that makes late-repentant souls wait outside as long as they once lived. The reason is one concrete act of self-abasement: he stood in the Campo, Siena's great public square, the very stage of his power, and begged for the ransom to free a friend held in King Charles of Anjou's prison. We keep liberamente as 'of his own will' (the humbling was chosen, not forced) and keep Dante's plainest, most physical line — condusse a tremar per ogne vena, 'he brought himself to tremble in every vein' — because the trembling is the body's record of a proud man making himself beg. We render s'affisse not as the abstract 'placed himself' but with the act it names: he set himself there to beg. Oderisi's closing hint that 'your neighbors' will soon make Dante understand this is the poet's own coming exile, left dark on purpose; we keep the darkness.

divergences.phrase: the carved pavement of Pride
divergences.older: the buried dead their tombs in earth / Bear sculptured on them what they were before (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: carved figures cut into the floor of the terrace, like the effigies carved on tomb-slabs you walk across in a church
divergences.note: The whole second terrace is a single image: thirteen scenes of pride struck down, cut into the pavement so the climbers must walk bowed and read them underfoot — the way medieval church floors hold the carved likenesses of the dead. We keep the comparison concrete (tomb-floor effigies) rather than Longfellow's abstract 'tombs in earth,' because the point is the posture it forces on Dante: the proud must look down.

divergences.phrase: Vedea ... O ... Mostrava (the UOMO acrostic)
divergences.older: I saw / O / Displayed (Longfellow, who preserves the anaphora but not the hidden word)
divergences.lectio: four tercets opening "I saw," four opening "O," four opening "It showed," then a closing tercet whose lines reopen all three in turn
divergences.note: In the Italian, the twelve example-tercets fall into three blocks of four: the first four begin Vedea, the next four with the cry O, the next four Mostrava — V, O, M — and the thirteenth tercet (lines 61-63) reopens each line with V, O, M again, so the first letters spell VOMO / UOMO, 'man.' The whole catalogue of fallen pride is signed, vertically, with the word for the creature it indicts. The acrostic can't be carried letter-for-letter into English, but we keep what makes it audible: the three hammering anaphoras ('I saw' / 'O' / 'It showed'), so a reader still feels the threefold drumbeat even where the hidden word is lost.

divergences.phrase: smote upon my forehead with his wings ... I found but six the letters
divergences.older: There smote upon my forehead with his wings (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the Angel of Humility brushes the first P from Dante's brow, and he learns it is gone only because the climb has turned light — he reaches up and finds six letters where there were seven
divergences.note: Each of the seven terraces erases one P (peccatum, 'sin') the gate-angel carved on Dante's forehead. Here the first falls. Dante doesn't see it happen; he infers it from his own lightened body, then confirms it by touch — six letters left, not seven. We render 'smote' as 'brushed,' since the gesture is a blessing, not a blow, and the whole point of the Beatitude sung at the turn — Blessed are the poor in spirit — is that humility is what lifts the weight.

divergences.phrase: col livido color de la petraia
divergences.older: With but the livid colour of the stone (Longfellow); a livid hue (Cary)
divergences.lectio: nothing but the livid, bruise-dark stone
divergences.note: Italian 'livido' is the gray-blue of a bruise, the chosen color of the terrace of envy — the body's own mark of a grudge. Longfellow keeps the Latinate 'livid'; we let the bruise show through, since that is exactly the association Dante wants and a modern reader no longer hears in 'livid' alone.

divergences.phrase: a tutti un fil di ferro i cigli fóra / e cusce sì, come a sparvier selvaggio
divergences.older: For all their lids an iron wire transpierces, / And sews them up, as to a sparhawk wild (Longfellow); an iron thread their eyelids... pierced and sewed (Cary)
divergences.lectio: for an iron wire runs through the lids of all of them / and sews them shut — the way it's done / to a wild hawk that will not hold still
divergences.note: The image is falconry: a wild hawk was 'seeled,' its eyelids stitched shut to tame it. We drop the now-obsolete 'sparhawk' and 'seel' for a plain 'wild hawk... sewed shut,' but keep the literal iron wire and the stitching — softening either would blunt the contrapasso, the envious who could not bear to see another's good blinded until they learn to.

divergences.phrase: Savia non fui, avvegna che Sapìa / fossi chiamata
divergences.older: Sapient I was not, although I Sapia / Was called (Longfellow); Wise I was not, though Sapia named (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Wise I was not, though Sapìa was the name / they called me
divergences.note: Dante puns her name against the word for wise — 'savia' (wise) beside 'Sapìa.' We keep the proper noun Sapìa intact and let the irony stand plainly in 'Wise I was not, though Sapìa they called me,' rather than reaching for an English coinage; the accent is preserved so the name reads as Dante's, and the wordplay survives in the juxtaposition.

divergences.phrase: Tra brutti porci... Botoli... can farsi lupi... le volpi sì piene di froda
divergences.older: 'Mid ugly swine... Curs findeth it... the dogs becoming wolves... the foxes so replete with fraud (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Among filthy hogs... it finds curs... those dogs turning to wolves... foxes so stuffed full of fraud
divergences.note: Guido's survey down the Arno is a sustained bestiary of insult — each people along the river degraded into an animal: the hogs of the Casentino, the curs (botoli, small snapping mongrels) of Arezzo, the wolves of Florence, the foxes of Pisa. The point is that the river itself debases what it touches, as if Circe were keeping the whole valley in her sty. We keep every animal concrete and the contempt audible, rather than softening the slur into general 'corruption.' 'Botoli' are specifically yapping curs whose noise outruns their strength — Dante's jab at Arezzo's bark-without-bite — so we render them 'curs' and keep the snarling.

divergences.phrase: «Anciderammi qualunque m'apprende» ... «Io sono Aglauro che divenni sasso»
divergences.older: "Shall slay me whosoever findeth me!" ... "I am Aglaurus, who became a stone!" (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: "Whoever finds me will kill me!" ... "I am Aglauros, who was turned to stone!"
divergences.note: The two examples of envy punished come not as carved images but as disembodied voices cracking past like thunder. The first is Cain after the murder of Abel (Genesis 4:14), unnamed, his terror its own confession; the second is Aglauros, who out of envy of her sister was turned to stone by Mercury. We keep both cries blunt and first-person — the lash of the example is that you hear the sin speaking, not a narrator describing it. Longfellow's inverted 'Shall slay me whosoever findeth me' is exactly the period word-order that buries the panic; we let Cain's line land plainly.

divergences.phrase: Ma voi prendete l'esca, sì che l'amo / de l'antico avversaro a sé vi tira
divergences.older: But you take in the bait so that the hook / Of the old Adversary draws you to him (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: But you all swallow the bait, so the hook / of the old Adversary draws you in
divergences.note: Virgil's closing image of the human predicament: the world's lures (l'esca, the bait) are a hook the 'old adversary' — Satan, the ancient enemy — uses to drag the eye downward, even while heaven turns overhead displaying its eternal beauties and calls. We keep the fishing metaphor live and the 'old Adversary' capitalized as the title it is, rather than flattening it to 'the enemy.' The 'voi'/'vi' is plural — Virgil indicts the whole human race, not Dante alone — so we render it 'you all' to carry the sweep the singular English 'you' would lose.

divergences.phrase: ché per quant' io di lui parlar ti odo, / là dove per compagnia parte si scema, / invidia move il mantaco a' sospiri
divergences.older: Because are thither pointed your desires / Where by companionship each share is lessened, / Envy doth ply the bellows to your sighs (Longfellow); Because ye point your wishes at a mark, / Where, by communion of possessors, part / Is lessen'd, envy bloweth up men's sighs (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Because your longing fastens on those goods / where having a partner means each share is less, / envy works the bellows under your sighs.
divergences.note: This is the diagnostic half of the canto's great teaching, and it has to land plainly for the cure to make sense. Dante's image is mechanical and exact — invidia move il mantaco, envy pumps the blacksmith's bellows that fan the fire of the sighs. Longfellow's 'ply the bellows' and Cary's 'bloweth up' both keep the image but in syntax a modern reader has to untangle. We keep the bellows — it is too good and too physical to lose — but set the cause first in plain order: earthly goods are the kind where a sharer subtracts from you, so the heart that wants them must envy. That sets up the reversal in the next tercets.

divergences.phrase: ché, per quanti si dice più lì 'nostro', / tanto possiede più di ben ciascuno, / e più di caritate arde in quel chiostro … e quanta gente più là sù s'intende, / più v'è da bene amare, e più vi s'ama, / e come specchio l'uno a l'altro rende
divergences.older: For there, as much the more as one says 'Our,' / So much the more of good each one possesses … And the more people thitherward aspire, / More are there to love well, and more they love there, / And, as a mirror, one reflects the other (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: For there, the more there are who say 'our own,' / the more of good each single soul possesses, / and the more love burns bright in that cloister. … And the more souls who aspire toward that height, / the more there are to love, and the more they love, / and each, like a mirror, gives the others back.
divergences.note: The hinge of Canto XV, and of Dante's whole answer to envy: heavenly goods are the opposite of earthly ones. The more a thing of heaven is shared, the more each sharer has of it, because the good in question is love, and love is multiplied by reflection — like a hall of mirrors where every added light brightens all the others. We keep Dante's homely 'ours' (nostro) as 'our own,' keep the monastic 'cloister' (chiostro) where charity burns, and keep the literal mirror image (come specchio l'uno a l'altro rende) rather than abstracting it, because the mirror IS the proof — light that grows by being reflected, not divided. The argument is left deliberately incomplete: Virgil defers its fullness to Beatrice, and we keep that deferral intact rather than over-explaining.

divergences.phrase: the three ecstatic visions of meekness: Mary in the temple, Pisistratus's mild reply, and the stoning of the young man who prays for his killers
divergences.older: rendered by Longfellow and Cary as three discrete vision-tableaux, with Pisistratus and (by tradition) Stephen named only in the commentary, not the text
divergences.lectio: Mary's gentle 'Son, / why have you treated the two of us like this?'; Pisistratus's 'What shall we do to those who wish us harm, / if we condemn the one who loves us?'; and the young man stoned to death who 'made his eyes forever gates to heaven,' praying that the high Lord 'would pardon those who hunted him.'
divergences.note: These are the 'whips of meekness' — the examples of gentleness that goad the souls of the wrathful, set against the smoke to come. Dante never names two of the three: the boy in the temple is Jesus and the mother Mary (the only one half-named, by 'father and I'); the stoned young man is Saint Stephen, the first martyr, praying for his killers as in Acts. We keep Dante's reticence — he leaves them unnamed for the reader to recognize, and naming them outright in the verse would break the dreamlike, half-seen quality of the trance. Only Pisistratus, the Athenian tyrant whose temperate reply is the pagan example between the two Christian ones, is named in the text, and we keep his name. The phrase 'gates to heaven' (fenestra del cielo / made gates of his eyes) is kept literal: even dying, Stephen turns his eyes into openings toward heaven — the strange, concrete image is the point and we don't smooth it into 'looked up to heaven.'

divergences.phrase: in voi è la cagione
divergences.older: In you the cause is, be it sought in you (Longfellow); in yourselves / The fault is, if not heav'n's (Cary)
divergences.lectio: the cause is in yourselves; look there for it
divergences.note: This is the hinge of the whole canto, and of Dante's whole moral physics: the world's corruption is not written in the stars. We render Marco's line as a flat, direct charge a modern reader can't slide past — 'the cause is in yourselves' — because the Italian places the blame squarely on the second person plural and refuses the comfort of fate. Free will, he has just argued, survives the heavens' pull and 'conquers all if well nourished'; the responsibility lands on us.

divergences.phrase: due soli
divergences.older: Two suns to have, which one road and the other ... made manifest (Longfellow); two suns, that vision gave / Of either road (Cary)
divergences.lectio: two suns, and they lit up the one road and the other — the road of the world, and the road of God
divergences.note: Dante's famously contested image: not the conventional 'sun and moon' (papacy greater, empire lesser, drawing its light from Rome) but TWO SUNS — empire and Church as coequal lights, each sovereign in its own road, the worldly and the divine. We keep 'two suns' literal and unsoftened because the doctrine is the point: when one sun (the Church) snuffs out the other and seizes the temporal sword, both go dark. The sword 'welded to the crook' (la spada / col pasturale) is the same charge made concrete.

divergences.phrase: l'anima semplicetta che sa nulla
divergences.older: Issues the simple soul, that nothing knows (Longfellow); from his plastic hand ... the simple soul (Cary)
divergences.lectio: comes the simple soul, that knows nothing at all
divergences.note: The soul leaves God's hand 'like a little girl who cries and laughs in her childish play' — a tender, deliberately small simile that Dante uses to ground a hard claim: the soul is born innocent and untaught, drawn by instinct to small pleasures, and so it NEEDS law and a guide. We keep the diminutive warmth ('little girl,' 'small childish play') rather than abstracting it, because the gentleness is the argument: a creature this newborn cannot be blamed for going wrong if its guides have failed it.

divergences.phrase: amore, o naturale o d'animo … malo obietto / o per troppo o per poco di vigore
divergences.older: love / Natural or spiritual (Longfellow); love / Or natural, or rational (Cary)
divergences.lectio: love — either love of nature or love of the mind … by fixing on a wrong object, or by too much, or too little force
divergences.note: This is the hinge of Virgil's discourse — and of the whole poem, which sits at its structural center. Dante splits love in two: amore naturale, the built-in pull toward one's proper good, which 'never goes astray,' and amore d'animo, the love of the deliberate mind, which can. Longfellow's 'spiritual' and Cary's 'rational' both narrow it; the Italian d'animo is the love that chooses, the soul's own motion. We render it 'love of the mind' and keep all three of its possible errors intact — wrong object, too much force, too little — because the entire moral architecture of Purgatory hangs on those three failures.

divergences.phrase: amor sementa in voi d'ogne virtute / e d'ogne operazion che merta pene
divergences.older: love must be / The seed within yourselves of every virtue, / And every act that merits punishment (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: love must be the seed in you of every virtue, and of every act that earns a punishment
divergences.note: The line the whole Comedy turns on: love (amore) is the single root — sementa, 'seed' — of every good deed and every sin alike. Not two forces, one good and one evil, but one force aimed well or badly. We keep 'seed' literal rather than softening it to 'source,' because the agricultural image is the point: virtue and sin grow from the same planting. This is Dante's reply to the question of where evil comes from — not from some dark opposite of love, but from love itself, misdirected.

divergences.phrase: in tre modi … questo triforme amor … in tre cerchi … perch'io te stesso cerchi
divergences.older: born in three modes in your clay … This threefold love is wept for down below … lamented in three circles … that thou seek it for thyself (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: born three ways in your clay … This threefold love is wept for down below … wept for in three circles up above us … so that you seek it out yourself
divergences.note: Virgil lays out the map of the mountain. Love gone wrong toward a neighbor's harm — pride, envy, wrath — is purged on the three terraces 'down below,' already climbed. Defective love, slack toward the true good, is sloth, purged here on this fourth terrace. Excessive love of lesser goods — avarice, gluttony, lust — is wept for in 'three circles up above us.' We keep Dante's deliberate withholding at the end: Virgil names the scheme but refuses to spell out the top three, telling the pilgrim to 'seek it out yourself' — a teacher closing the lesson so the student will finish it (which Statius will, in the next canto). We don't resolve the riddle the poet chose to leave open.

divergences.phrase: innata v'è la virtù che consiglia, / e de l'assenso de' tener la soglia
divergences.older: Innate within you is the power that counsels, / And it should keep the threshold of assent. (Longfellow); In you there is a faculty that counsels, / And it behoves it well to guard the threshold / Of assent (Cary)
divergences.lectio: there is born in you the power that counsels, / whose task is to keep the threshold of consent.
divergences.note: This is the hinge of Dante's defense of free will. Desire may rise in us by nature, but Dante locates moral responsibility in a separate faculty — la virtù che consiglia, the power that deliberates — whose office is to stand at the soglia, the doorway, and grant or withhold assent. We keep the literal image of a guarded threshold rather than abstract it into 'judgment,' because the whole moral argument rests on consent being a door we ourselves hold.

divergences.phrase: Color che ragionando andaro al fondo, / s'accorser d'esta innata libertate; / però moralità lasciaro al mondo
divergences.older: Those who, in reasoning, to the bottom went, / Were of this innate liberty aware, / Therefore bequeathed they Ethics to the world. (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Those who reasoned their way to the bottom of it / saw this freedom, born in us, / and so they left the world its book of Ethics.
divergences.note: Dante credits the moral philosophers — Aristotle above all, whose Ethics he treats as the human reasoning that stops exactly where faith must take over — with discovering that this liberty is innata, native to us, not granted from outside. We render moralità as 'the book of Ethics' to make plain that Dante means a body of moral teaching (Aristotle's), not 'morality' in the loose modern sense, and we straighten Longfellow's inverted 'bequeathed they.'

divergences.phrase: ratto, ratto, che 'l tempo non si perda / per poco amor ... ché studio di ben far grazia rinverde
divergences.older: Quick! quick! so that the time may not be lost / By little love! ... For ardour in well-doing freshens grace! (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Faster, faster! Don't let the time be lost / for want of love! ... for eagerness in doing good revives grace!
divergences.note: On the fourth terrace the slothful purge their old lukewarmness by running without pause, and their own cries enact the cure — the doubled 'ratto, ratto' is the running made audible. We keep the breathless repetition and render studio di ben far ... rinverde as 'eagerness in doing good revives grace,' the green of rinverde (re-greens) carried as renewal, so the contrast with their former coldness lands. They shout examples of zeal (Mary hurrying to the hill country, Caesar racing to Ilerda) against examples of sloth punished (the Hebrews who died short of the Jordan, the Trojans who stayed behind and lost glory).

divergences.phrase: the sweet Siren
divergences.older: I am the Siren sweet / Who mariners amid the main unman (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: I am the sweet Siren, / the one who strands the sailors out at sea
divergences.note: Dante's 'dolce serena' is the figure of the false good: ugly and crippled until the dreamer's own gaze beautifies her, then she sings she is the Siren who lured even Ulysses. We keep the proper noun 'Siren' and let her seduction read plainly, so a modern reader feels the trick — that the allure is projected by the looker — rather than admiring period-pretty diction. Longfellow's 'unman' is archaic; 'strands the sailors' carries the wreck without the antique verb.

divergences.phrase: my soul has clung to the dust
divergences.older: “Adhaesit pavimento anima mea” (Longfellow, Latin retained)
divergences.lectio: "My soul has clung to the dust"
divergences.note: The avaricious lie face-down in the dust, chanting Psalm 118:25. Older editions leave the Latin tag untranslated, which stops a modern reader cold. We render it in English so the punishment is legible — the soul that clung to earthly things is now pressed flat against the earth — while keeping the Psalm's plain, liturgical weight.

divergences.phrase: I was once the successor of Peter / fellow-servant under one Power
divergences.older: Scias quod ego fui successor Petri ... conservo sono teco (Longfellow, Latin/literal)
divergences.lectio: know this: that I was once the successor of Peter ... I am a fellow-servant / with you and with the rest, under one Power
divergences.note: Adrian V tells how only on gaining the papacy did he see the heart finds no rest in worldly things. When Dante kneels, he refuses it: in death he is no longer Peter's successor but a fellow-servant — all equal under God. We English the Latin 'successor Petri' and keep 'fellow-servant under one Power' (conservo... ad una podestate) so the leveling lands, and preserve the names Adrian and his niece Alagia, whose prayers are all he asks.

divergences.phrase: Ugo Ciappetta / Hugh Capet
divergences.older: Hugh Capet was I called upon the earth (Longfellow); Hugh Capet was I named (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Over there I was called Hugh Capet
divergences.note: Dante's spirit names himself flatly, then immediately disowns his own line — "the root of that evil plant" that shadows all Christendom. We keep the name unaltered (it is the architecture of the indictment that follows) but render the surrounding boast-then-self-condemnation in plain forward English, so a modern reader feels the founder of the French royal house cursing his own descendants rather than reciting a genealogy. Longfellow's "upon the earth" is replaced by "over there," Dante's idiom for the living world seen from the afterlife.

divergences.phrase: veggio in Alagna intrar lo fiordaliso ... il novo Pilato
divergences.older: I see the flower-de-luce Alagna enter, / And Christ in his own Vicar captive made ... I see the modern Pilate so relentless (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: I see the fleur-de-lis enter Anagni, / and Christ made captive in his own Vicar ... I see the new Pilate, so pitiless
divergences.note: Alagna is Dante's spelling of Anagni; we restore the town's standard modern name so the reference lands — the Outrage of Anagni (1303), where agents of Philip the Fair of France (the "new Pilate") seized Pope Boniface. The fiordaliso is the French royal arms, the fleur-de-lis, which we keep in French rather than Longfellow's archaic "flower-de-luce." Dante stages the attack on the Pope as the Passion repeated — Christ mocked, given vinegar and gall, and killed anew in the person of his Vicar — and we keep that blasphemy-charge fully visible rather than softening it.

divergences.phrase: tremar lo monte ... 'Gloria in excelsis Deo'
divergences.older: the mountain tremble, whence a chill seized on me (Longfellow); 'Gloria in excelsis Deo,' all / Were saying
divergences.lectio: I felt the mountain shake, like something / about to fall — and a chill took hold of me ... "Glory to God in the highest" — that was what / they were all saying
divergences.note: The canto's turn from invective to awe. We render the earthquake as a felt, physical jolt ("like something about to fall") and keep Dante's death-chill image intact. For the hymn we translate the Latin into English in the line itself — "Glory to God in the highest" — because the Vernacular's job is to let the cry land for a reader with no Latin, while the simile of the shepherds (Luke's nativity) makes its source plain; we leave Dante's fear and bafflement unexplained, as he does, since the canto ends on an open question he cannot yet answer.

divergences.phrase: de l'Eneïda dico, la qual mamma / fummi, e fummi nutrice, poetando
divergences.older: Of the Aeneid speak I, which to me / A mother was, and was my nurse in song (Longfellow); the Aeneid; mother and nurse to me in poetry (Cary)
divergences.lectio: I mean the Aeneid; it was a mother to me, and a nurse to me in poetry
divergences.note: Statius's two words for Virgil's poem — 'mamma' and 'nutrice' — are the heart of the canto, and they are deliberately humble, almost childlike: not 'mother' the abstraction but the mother who bears, and the nurse who feeds. We keep both, plainly, and resist Longfellow's inverted 'a mother was'; the warmth is in the simplicity. Statius's last line measures the debt against money — 'sanz' essa non fermai peso di dramma,' I would not have weighed a single drachma — which we render with a modern unit of weight so the metaphor still lands.

divergences.phrase: né figlia di Taumante
divergences.older: Nor the daughter of Thaumas (Longfellow); nor Thaumas' daughter (Cary)
divergences.lectio: and no daughter of Thaumas — the rainbow, that keeps shifting her place below
divergences.note: Dante names the rainbow by the old mythological periphrasis: Iris, daughter of Thaumas. A modern reader has no way to decode 'daughter of Thaumas' on the page, and a footnote would break the line. We keep the strangeness Dante wanted — the personified rainbow that 'changes her region' — but fold the plain identification ('the rainbow') into the line itself, so the image survives without a gloss.

divergences.phrase: ben vedrai che coi buon convien ch'e' regni
divergences.older: Well shalt thou see he with the good must reign (Longfellow); thou wilt see he must reign with the good (Cary)
divergences.lectio: you will see plainly he belongs among the saved
divergences.note: Virgil's point is that the Angel's marks on Dante's brow prove he is destined for heaven — 'must reign with the good.' The literal 'reign with the good' reads, to a modern ear, like political rule rather than salvation. We render the sense Dante intends — that Dante belongs among the saved — while keeping Virgil's quiet confidence; the theology is preserved, only the dead idiom is cleared away.

divergences.phrase: che porta il lume dietro e sé non giova, / ma dopo sé fa le persone dotte
divergences.older: Who bears his light behind, which helps him not, / But wary makes the persons after him (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: and carries the lamp behind him — no help to himself, / but he makes the ones who follow wise
divergences.note: Dante's image for Virgil: he prophesied Christianity in his Fourth Eclogue without believing it himself, like a man walking at night who holds his lantern behind his back — it lights the road for those who come after but never for him. We keep the literal picture (light carried behind) rather than smoothing it to 'guided' or 'led,' because the strangeness of the simile is the point: the pagan who saved others he could not save himself.

divergences.phrase: Per te poeta fui, per te cristiano
