divergences.older: Through thee I Poet was, through thee a Christian (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Through you I became a poet; through you, a Christian.
divergences.note: The hinge of the canto and one of the most startling claims in the poem: Statius says Virgil's pagan verse converted him. We render 'fui' as 'became' rather than the archaic 'I was,' and keep the parallel bare, so the shock lands the way the Italian lands it — Virgil made him both, and made him the second without ever knowing it.

divergences.phrase: o sacra fame / de l'oro, l'appetito de' mortali
divergences.older: O cursed hunger / Of gold, the appetite of mortal men (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: O cursed hunger for gold, / do you not drive the appetites of men?
divergences.note: Dante is quoting Virgil back to Virgil — the Aeneid's 'auri sacra fames.' 'Sacra' is the old Latin double sense (sacred / accursed); here it means accursed, and we follow the tradition in saying 'cursed.' The joke beneath it is real: the very line that damns greed is the line that, by warning Statius off it, helped purge him of the opposite excess.

divergences.phrase: chi nel viso de li uomini legge 'omo' / ben avria quivi conosciuta l'emme
divergences.older: Whoever in the face of men reads 'omo' / Might well in these have recognised the 'm' (Longfellow); who reads OMO / In man's face, here the M had clearly mark'd (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Anyone who reads the word OMO in a human face would easily have made out the M right here
divergences.note: A medieval commonplace: the human face was said to spell out 'OMO' (Latin homo, 'man') — the two eyes are the O's, and the brows, cheekbones, and nose form a gothic M between them. In these starved penitents the flesh has fallen away until the bone-structure M stands out stark and legible. We keep the literal OMO and M rather than paraphrasing the conceit away, because the image only works if the reader sees the letters in the face the way Dante did; the glance is grotesque and tender at once.

divergences.phrase: io dico pena, e dovria dir sollazzo
divergences.older: I say our pain, and ought to say our solace (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: I say our pain, and ought to say our solace
divergences.note: Forese corrects himself mid-sentence — the hunger that draws the gluttons toward the unreachable tree is not torment but the very thing healing them, so the right word is not 'pain' but 'solace.' We keep the self-correction intact rather than smoothing it into a single calm statement; the stumble is the theology. The same logic governs 'sweet wormwood' (dolce assenzo) a few tercets later — a deliberate paradox we preserve rather than resolve.

divergences.phrase: la Nella mia con suo pianger dirotto
divergences.older: My Nella with her overflowing tears (Longfellow); My Nella with her floods of tears (Cary)
divergences.lectio: It is my Nella who has led me so soon to drink the sweet wormwood of these torments — with her flooding tears
divergences.note: Forese's swift climb is credited to the prayers and tears of his widow Nella, and Dante sets her devotion against his bitter aside on the 'brazen women of Florence' who go about with the breast bared. Both proper anchors — Nella, Florence, and the Barbagia of Sardinia (a wild Sardinian region named as a byword for immodesty) — are kept. We render 'mostrando con le poppe il petto' plainly as showing the breast with nipples bare rather than softening it; the bluntness is Dante's, and the moral contrast with Nella depends on it landing.

divergences.phrase: I' mi son un che, quando / Amor mi spira, noto, e a quel modo / ch'e' ditta dentro vo significando
divergences.older: One am I, who, whenever Love doth inspire me, note, and in that measure which he within me dictates, singing go (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: I am one who, when Love breathes in me, takes note, and in the way he dictates within, I set it down
divergences.note: Dante's own definition of the dolce stil novo, the hinge of the canto. The verbs are exact and deliberate: 'noto' (I take note, I attend) and 'vo significando' (I go on putting it into signs, into words) — an act of faithful transcription, not performance. Longfellow's 'singing go' imports song that the Italian does not state and softens the claim. We keep the plain, almost clerical verbs ('takes note,' 'set it down'), because the whole boast is that the new style merely follows what Love dictates within, exactly, where the old poets (the Notary, Guittone) fell short.

divergences.phrase: O frate, issa vegg'io ... il nodo
divergences.older: O brother, now I see ... the knot (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: O brother, now I see ... the knot
divergences.note: Bonagiunta's recognition. 'Issa' is a homely, regional 'now' (Lucchese in flavor), and 'nodo' is the knot that 'held' the old poets back — the same image of a tie being slipped that runs through Purgatorio. We keep 'knot' literal rather than abstracting it to 'difficulty,' since the canto turns it physical: their pens could not 'follow close behind the one who dictates,' so they stayed tangled, 'short of' the new style.

divergences.phrase: Beati cui alluma / tanto di grazia ... / esuriendo sempre quanto è giusto
divergences.older: Blessed are they whom grace so much illumines ... Hungering at all times so far as is just (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Blessed are they whom grace so lights from within ... hungering always only as much as is just
divergences.note: The sixth beatitude, recasting 'blessed are they who hunger and thirst after righteousness' for the terrace of gluttony. The Latin 'esuriendo' (hungering) deliberately echoes the Vulgate beatitude; we keep the verb 'hungering' rather than smoothing it, and render 'quanto è giusto' as 'only as much as is just' to catch the measure the whole terrace teaches — appetite kept to its true size, not killed.

divergences.phrase: lo motor primo... spira / spirito novo, di vertù repleto
divergences.older: The primal Motor turns to it well pleased... and inspires / A spirit new with virtue all replete (Longfellow); the Primal Motor... breathes a spirit new (Cary)
divergences.lectio: the First Mover turns to it, glad... and breathes into it a new spirit, full of power
divergences.note: This is the doctrinal hinge of the canto: the vegetative and sensitive soul grow up from matter, but the rational soul is breathed in directly by God — "spira spirito novo." Older versions reach for "inspires," which a modern reader hears as encouragement rather than literal in-breathing. We keep the plain physical verb "breathes," so the reader feels the act for what Dante means it to be: God exhaling a soul into the formed body. "First Mover" carries the Aristotelian weight without the dead Latinism of "primal Motor."

divergences.phrase: move e sente, / come spungo marino
divergences.older: now it moves and feels / Like a sea-fungus (Longfellow); moving and feeling, as a sea-shell (Cary)
divergences.lectio: it stirs and feels, like a sea-sponge
divergences.note: Dante reaches for the simplest living thing that already moves and feels — "spungo marino," the sea-sponge, the threshold of the sensitive soul. Longfellow's "sea-fungus" and Cary's "sea-shell" both blur the creature; the Italian is the sponge, and the strangeness of it — an animal barely an animal — is exactly the point at the moment the embryo crosses from plant-life into feeling. We keep the creature exact.

divergences.phrase: l'aere vicin quivi si mette / e in quella forma... è chiamata ombra
divergences.older: the neighbouring air doth shape itself / Into that form... It is called shade (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the neighboring air takes on / the very form the soul stamps upon it... it is called a shade
divergences.note: Dante's answer to Dante's own riddle — how a bodiless soul can grow thin from hunger, weep, and speak. After death the soul keeps its formative power and presses the surrounding air into an "aerial body" that mirrors every faculty and feeling, down to sight; this stamped air is the "ombra," the shade. We render "stamps" rather than the limp "shapes itself," because the soul is the active agent imprinting the air like a seal in wax — which is why the shade can suffer real hunger and shed real tears.

divergences.phrase: miglior fabbro del parlar materno
divergences.older: a better smith of the mother tongue (Longfellow); of the mother tongue / A fabricator more renown'd (Cary)
divergences.lectio: a better craftsman of the mother tongue
divergences.note: Guinizelli's verdict on Arnaut Daniel — and one of the most famous lines in the poem (Pound and Eliot later borrowed 'il miglior fabbro' for each other). 'Fabbro' is literally a smith, a worker at the forge; the metaphor is of poetry hammered out like metal. 'Smith' alone now reads as a surname to a modern ear, so we keep the forge-sense with 'craftsman' while preserving that this is praise for sheer workmanship — Guinizelli, whom Dante has just called his own poetic father, humbly names a still better maker.

divergences.phrase: Tan m'abellis vostre cortes deman … sovenha vos a temps de ma dolor
divergences.older: Longfellow and Cary print Arnaut's reply in Provençal and footnote a prose English version below the canto.
divergences.lectio: Arnaut's eight lines kept in the original Occitan, with a plain English rendering set beside them in brackets
divergences.note: Dante does the unthinkable: he hands the climax of his meditation on love-poetry to another language. Arnaut Daniel — the great troubadour of the trobar ric — answers not in Italian but in Provençal (Occitan), the only character in the whole Comedy to speak a vernacular other than Dante's own. To translate the lines away would erase the point, so we keep the Occitan exactly and gloss it. We follow the standard critical text (Petrocchi) rather than Longfellow's older spelling — e.g. 'Ieu sui Arnaut' and 'al som de l'escalina' — and render 'a temps' as 'in good time' (he asks to be remembered while it can still help), the sense most editors prefer.

divergences.phrase: Sodom and Gomorrah / Pasiphaë and the bull
divergences.older: "Sodom and Gomorrah!" … "Into the cow Pasiphae enters, / So that the bull unto her lust may run!" (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the two cries kept blunt and unsoftened — "Sodom and Gomorrah!" against "Into the cow climbs Pasiphaë, / so the bull will come running to her lust"
divergences.note: On the seventh terrace the lustful run in two bands and shout, at parting, the example that names their sin. Dante does not soften either, so neither do we. Pasiphaë, queen of Crete, had Daedalus build a hollow wooden cow so she could couple with a bull — hence Guinizelli's own band, the 'beasts' who broke human law, cry her name; the other band cries the cities of Genesis. The earthiness ('climbs,' 'the wooden beast') is the poet's, kept rather than tidied into abstraction.

divergences.phrase: 'Tra Beatrice e te è questo muro' ... 'Sì com'fui dentro, in un bogliente vetro / gittato mi sarei per rinfrescarmi, / tant'era ivi lo 'ncendio sanza metro'
divergences.older: 'Twixt Beatrice and thee there is this wall ... When I was in it, into molten glass / I would have cast me to refresh myself, / So without measure was the burning there! (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: between Beatrice and you stands only this wall ... Once I was in it, I would have flung myself / into boiling glass to cool down, / the burning there was so far past all measure.
divergences.note: The hinge of the canto. The Angel of Chastity sings the sixth beatitude — 'Beati mundo corde,' blessed are the pure in heart — and the last cleansing is the wall of fire: no soul climbs to the Earthly Paradise until the flame has bitten. Dante, who has walked through Hell, is paralyzed with a bodily terror older translations keep, and rightly — he stiffens 'against his own conscience,' remembering human bodies he watched burn. What finally moves him is not courage but a name: Virgil says only that Beatrice waits on the far side, and the name 'that wells up in me and never stops' carries him in. We keep the violence of the heat exact — 'bogliente vetro,' boiling/molten glass he would have hurled himself into to cool, the fire 'sanza metro,' without measure — because the cost of the passage is the measure of the love that drives him through it. We render the load-bearing 'muro' plainly as 'wall' and let Beatrice's name do, in English, what it does in the Italian: break the will free.

divergences.phrase: ch'i' mi son Lia, e vo movendo intorno / le belle mani a farmi una ghirlanda ... Rachel ... lo veder mi appaga / come 'l fare lei
divergences.older: That I am Leah, and go moving round / My beauteous hands to make myself a garland ... never does my sister Rachel leave / Her looking-glass ... Her, seeing, and me, doing satisfies (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: that I am Leah, and I move my lovely hands / all round, to make myself a garland ... my sister Rachel never leaves / her mirror ... Looking fills her; doing fills me.
divergences.note: Dante's third and last Purgatorial dream, set just before dawn at the summit: two sisters, Leah gathering flowers and weaving a garland with her own hands, and Rachel sitting all day before her mirror, never tiring of her own eyes. They are the medieval emblem of the two lives — Leah the active life of good works, Rachel the contemplative life of vision — and the dream readies Dante for the two women he is about to meet in Eden, Matilda (active) and Beatrice (contemplative). We keep both proper names exactly (Leah for Lia, Rachel for Rachele) and render the closing antithesis as a plain, balanced pair — 'Looking fills her; doing fills me' — rather than Longfellow's inverted 'Her, seeing, and me, doing satisfies,' so the symmetry that is the whole point of the dream lands cleanly in English. We leave the allegory unspoken on the page, as Dante does, and let the two satisfied women stand for it.

divergences.phrase: Non aspettar mio dir più né mio cenno; / libero, dritto e sano è tuo arbitrio, / e fallo fora non fare a suo senno: / per ch'io te sovra te corono e mitrio.
divergences.older: Expect no more or word or sign from me; / Free and upright and sound is thy free-will, / And error were it not to do its bidding; / Thee o'er thyself I therefore crown and mitre! (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Expect no more word, no more sign from me. / Your will is free, upright, and whole, / and it would be wrong not to do as it bids — // so over yourself I crown and mitre you.
divergences.note: Virgil's last words in the whole poem — he never speaks again, ceding to Beatrice in the next canto. Having guided Dante 'by intellect and craft' as far as reason can reach, he declares the work of purgation done: the will that Hell deformed is now 'libero, dritto e sano' — free, upright, and whole — so trustworthy that to disobey it would itself be sin. The final line is the canto's crown: 'te sovra te corono e mitrio,' I crown and mitre you over yourself — investing Dante with both regalia, the king's crown (temporal self-rule) and the bishop's mitre (spiritual self-rule), making him sovereign of himself, answerable now to no guide but his own restored conscience. We keep the doubled image exact — both crown and mitre — because the two emblems together are the point: full self-mastery, the end of the long ascent. We hold the line as the last thing Virgil ever says, plain and weighted, and let the silence that follows be his farewell.

divergences.phrase: una donna soletta che si gia / cantando e scegliendo fior da fiore
divergences.older: A lady all alone, who went along / Singing and culling floweret after floweret (Longfellow); A lady all alone... cropping flower from flower (Cary)
divergences.lectio: a lady, all alone, who walked along / singing, picking flower after flower
divergences.note: This is Matelda — though Dante does not name her until Purgatorio XXXIII. Longfellow's "culling floweret after floweret" doubles down on the diminutive and the archaic verb; the Italian is simpler and more direct, "scegliendo fior da fiore," choosing flower from flower. We keep her solitary, singing, and unhurried — the first soul of the Earthly Paradise — without the Victorian prettiness.

divergences.phrase: Quinci Letè; così da l'altra parte / Eunoè si chiama
divergences.older: Here Lethe, as upon the other side / Eunoe, it is called (Longfellow); Lethe on this side, on the other Eunoe (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Here it is called Lethe; over there, / Eunoë
divergences.note: Matelda's key teaching: the two streams do not come from rain or vein but from a single unfailing fountain by the will of God — Lethe washes away the memory of sin, Eunoë restores the memory of good. The proper nouns Lethe and Eunoë are preserved exactly; "Eunoë" (Dante's own coinage, from Greek for "good mind") keeps its diaeresis. We make the divine, not earthly, cause of the water and wind plain, which is the whole point she is correcting in the pilgrim.

divergences.phrase: Quelli ch'anticamente poetaro / l'età de l'oro... forse in Parnaso esto loco sognaro
divergences.older: Those who in ancient times have feigned in song / The Age of Gold... / Dreamed of this place perhaps upon Parnassus (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Those who long ago set the Age of Gold to song... / were perhaps dreaming, on Parnassus, of this place
divergences.note: Matelda's famous turn: the pagan poets who imagined a lost Golden Age and the inspiration of Parnassus were, perhaps, dreaming of this very garden — Eden. Longfellow's "feigned in song" carries a faint charge of falsehood the Italian "poetaro" (simply, made poetry) does not; we render it as "set to song," keeping the generosity of Dante's "forse," perhaps. Parnassus and the Age of Gold are kept as the named architecture of the classical imagination she is gently claiming for Christian truth.

divergences.phrase: un carro, in su due rote, trïunfale, / ch'al collo d'un grifon tirato venne
divergences.older: A chariot triumphal on two wheels, / Which by a Griffin's neck came drawn along (Longfellow); a car / Triumphal, on two wheels, came drawn along / By a yoked Gryphon's neck (Cary)
divergences.lectio: a triumphal chariot on two wheels, / drawn at the neck of a Griffin
divergences.note: The chariot is the Church and the Griffin is Christ — eagle above, lion below, his two natures (divine and human) in one body. We keep both the chariot and the Griffin as plain, concrete things rather than glossing the allegory in the line; the pageant is meant to be read as a vision first and decoded second. 'Griffin' is preserved as a proper noun, as the brief asks.

divergences.phrase: onde fa l'arco il Sole e Delia il cinto
divergences.older: Whence the sun's bow is made, and Delia's girdle (Longfellow); Wherewith sun fashioneth his bow, and moon / Her zone (Cary)
divergences.lectio: the colors / the sun makes in its bow, and Delia in her ring
divergences.note: The seven streaming bands take the colors of two heavenly halos: the rainbow (the sun's 'bow') and the lunar halo. 'Delia' is Diana, the moon — her 'cinto' (girdle/belt) is the ring of light around her. We keep the name Delia rather than flattening it to 'the moon,' and render the girdle as a 'ring' so the lunar-halo image reads cleanly to a modern eye without a footnote.

divergences.phrase: di quel sommo Ipocràte che natura / a li animali fé ch'ell' ha più cari
divergences.older: Of that supreme Hippocrates, whom nature / Made for the animals she holds most dear (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: of great Hippocrates, whom nature made / for the creatures she holds dearest
divergences.note: The first of the two final elders is Luke, named not by name but by his trade — a physician, and so a 'follower of Hippocrates.' (The second, with the bright sword, is Paul.) Dante's 'animali' here means living creatures, mankind among them, the beings medicine serves; we render it 'creatures' rather than the false-friend 'animals,' which to a modern reader narrows the sense wrongly.

divergences.phrase: conosco i segni de l'antica fiamma
divergences.older: I know the traces of the ancient flame (Longfellow); the ancient flame I know its tokens well (Cary)
divergences.lectio: I know the signs of the ancient flame
divergences.note: This is the canto's hidden detonation. Dante turns to speak to Virgil and quotes Virgil's own line — Dido's words in Aeneid IV.23, 'agnosco veteris vestigia flammae,' 'I recognize the marks of the old flame.' He gives the master his own verse back, the love of his life, in the very instant he speaks — and at that instant Virgil is already gone. We keep 'signs of the ancient flame' literal and unsoftened so the Aeneid quotation survives intact; to paraphrase it (e.g. 'I feel my old love stir') would erase the one allusion the whole moment is built on.

divergences.phrase: Ma Virgilio n'avea lasciati scemi / di sé, Virgilio dolcissimo patre, / Virgilio a cui per mia salute die' mi
divergences.older: But us Virgilius of himself deprived / Had left, Virgilius, sweetest of all fathers, / Virgilius, to whom I for safety gave me (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: But Virgil had left us empty of himself, / Virgil, the gentlest of all fathers, / Virgil, to whom I gave myself to be saved.
divergences.note: Three lines, three times the name 'Virgilio,' tolling like a bell — the most devastating anaphora in the poem, the sound of a loss being said over and over because it cannot be believed. We hold the threefold 'Virgil' exactly where Dante puts it and let the repetition do its own work, refusing Longfellow's inverted 'of himself deprived,' which buries the blow under nineteenth-century word order. 'Empty of himself' keeps the strange literal force of 'scemi di sé' — they are left lessened, hollowed, by his absence.

divergences.phrase: Dante, perché Virgilio se ne vada
divergences.older: Dante, because Virgilius has departed (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Dante, though Virgil is leaving you
divergences.note: The only time the name 'Dante' appears in the entire Commedia — and Beatrice is the one who speaks it, as a reproof, the instant he is weeping for Virgil. Dante flags it himself ('which I set down here only because I must'). We leave the name bare and first, with no cushioning, so it lands with the force the poet intended: the self, named for the only time, at the moment of being judged. We render 'perché... se ne vada' as 'though Virgil is leaving you' rather than 'because Virgil has departed' — the tenderness is real, but the next words refuse it: do not weep yet, there is a worse grief coming.

divergences.phrase: the river that erases sin
divergences.older: Longfellow names it only as "the sacred river," and the explicit Lethe stays implicit in the canto's drama.
divergences.lectio: We keep Beatrice's opening "sacred river" but let the gloss surface the name where she warns the waters have not yet washed the memory clean ("The waters have not yet / washed the bitter memory out of you").
divergences.note: The river is Lethe (Italian Lete), which in Dante erases the memory of sin once crossed. The whole canto turns on it: Beatrice must extract the confession BEFORE Matelda draws him through, because afterward the guilt is gone. Preserving the proper noun Lethe in the gloss keeps that machinery legible.

divergences.phrase: the Griffin reflected in Beatrice's eyes — "or con altri, or con altri reggimenti"
divergences.older: Longfellow: "Within them was the twofold monster shining, / Now with the one, now with the other nature" — accurate but abstract ("twofold monster").
divergences.lectio: "the twofold creature shone inside her eyes, / now with the one nature, now with the other" — we keep "twofold creature" plain and let the divergence carry the doctrine, rather than freighting the line itself.
divergences.note: The Griffin (eagle above, lion below) is Christ: the eagle is the divine nature, the lion the human. In Beatrice's eyes — the eyes of revelation — Dante sees not the Griffin directly but its reflection alternating between its two forms: the mystery of the two natures in one person, glimpsed only as the soul can bear it. "Reggimenti" (bearings/aspects) is rendered "nature" to make the theology audible.

divergences.phrase: "the second beauty which thou dost conceal" — unveiling the mouth/smile
divergences.older: Longfellow: "unveil / Thy face to him... / The second beauty which thou dost conceal."
divergences.lectio: "unveil your mouth to him, so that he may see / the second beauty that you still keep hidden."
divergences.note: Dante distinguishes Beatrice's two beauties: her eyes (the first, already revealed) and her mouth/smile (the second, still veiled). The Italian "bocca" — mouth, and so smile — is the precise object; "face" blurs it. The eyes lead to wisdom; the smile, unveiled, is beyond the poet's power to tell, which is where the canto breaks off.

divergences.phrase: una pianta dispogliata / di foglie e d'altra fronda in ciascun ramo ... men che di rose e più che di vïole / colore aprendo, s'innovò la pianta
divergences.older: a tree despoiled / Of blooms and other leafage on each bough ... Less than of rose and more than violet / A hue disclosing, was renewed the tree (Longfellow); a tree, despoil'd / Of blossoms and each other leaf ... was changed, / And took a tint of colour, more than rose, / But less than violet (Cary)
divergences.lectio: a tree stripped bare, / not a leaf, not a flower on any branch ... opening a color less than rose / and more than violet, the tree made itself new / that had stood with its boughs so bare before
divergences.note: The barren tree is the canto's central image — read as the tree of Eden, of knowledge, of justice, and of Empire all at once, the one law Adam broke. It blooms again only when the Griffin binds the chariot's pole to it, which is why we make the bare-then-blooming arc plain and physical rather than ornamental: the wood goes from stripped to new in a single visible motion, the whole allegory of Empire restored to its root. We keep the strange, exact half-shade 'less than rose and more than violet' literal — Dante is naming a real color between, not reaching for a stock 'crimson,' and the precision is the point.

divergences.phrase: seder sovresso una puttana sciolta / m'apparve con le ciglia intorno pronte
divergences.older: there appeared to me / A shameless whore, with eyes swift glancing round (Longfellow); A shameless whore I saw, with eyes / Quick glancing round (Cary); an ungirt harlot (Norton)
divergences.lectio: there appeared to me, seated on the thing, / a brazen harlot, her eyes darting everywhere
divergences.note: The harlot enthroned on the seven-headed monster is the corrupt papacy, an inversion of the bride of Christ — Dante is rewriting Revelation's whore of Babylon and pointing it at Rome. We keep the blunt word: 'puttana' is coarse, deliberately so, and softening it to 'wanton' or 'courtesan' (as the genteel tradition does) blunts the rage that is the whole point. 'Sciolta' means loosed, unbound, unrestrained — we carry that into 'brazen' and the restless, darting eyes ('le ciglia intorno pronte'), the look of someone selling herself to whoever passes.

divergences.phrase: vidi di costa a lei dritto un gigante ... disciolse il mostro, e trassel per la selva
divergences.older: Upright beside her I beheld a giant ... He loosed the monster, and across the forest / Dragged it so far (Longfellow); a giant ... Loos'd / The monster, and dragg'd on, so far across / The forest (Cary)
divergences.lectio: I saw a giant standing at her side ... he loosed the monster and dragged it off / through the forest, so far that the trees alone / made a shield
divergences.note: The giant is the French monarchy — Philip the Fair — and the kiss-then-beating is Dante's verdict on the papacy's alliance with France: the Church prostitutes itself to a worldly power that first courts it, then jealously abuses it, and finally drags it bodily off (the move of the papal seat to Avignon — the 'Babylonian captivity'). We keep the brutal sequence intact and in order — kiss, scourge, drag away — because the allegory lives in that exact arc of corruption: seduction, possession, captivity. The canto ends with the chariot-turned-monster vanishing into the wood, the bleakest image of the Church in the whole poem, and we let it end abruptly, unresolved, as Dante does.

divergences.phrase: nel quale un cinquecento diece e cinque, / messo di Dio, anciderà la fuia / con quel gigante che con lei delinque
divergences.older: Within which a Five-hundred, Ten, and Five, / One sent from God, shall slay the thievish woman / And that same giant who is sinning with her (Longfellow); a five hundred, five, and ten, / One sent from God (Cary)
divergences.lectio: in which a Five hundred, Ten, and Five, / sent down from God, will kill the thieving harlot / and the giant who sins there at her side
divergences.note: The most famous riddle in the poem. "Cinquecento diece e cinque" is a deliberate cipher — the Roman numerals D, X, V, which rearranged spell DVX, "leader," the coming deliverer Beatrice will not name. We keep the numeral hidden, exactly as Dante hides it: "Five hundred, Ten, and Five," never "515" and never decoded to "DUX." To solve it on the reader's behalf would erase the prophecy's whole point — that it is given veiled, to be understood later. "La fuia," the thieving woman, is the harlot of the corrupted chariot (Canto XXXII); "the giant" is the French crown that drags her off. We hold both concrete rather than flattening them into "the corrupt Church" — the allegory is meant to be read, not pre-chewed.

divergences.phrase: ma tosto fier li fatti le Naiade, / che solveranno questo enigma forte / sanza danno di pecore o di biade
divergences.older: But soon the facts shall be the Naiades / Who shall this difficult enigma solve, / Without destruction of the flocks and harvests (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: but soon the facts themselves will be the Naiads / that solve this hard enigma for you — / with no destruction of the flocks and grain
divergences.note: Beatrice warns that her "dark telling" (narrazion buia) may baffle Dante the way the riddles of Themis and the Sphinx baffled their hearers — but events themselves will solve it. The reference to the Naiads comes from a textual corruption Dante inherited (Ovid's "Laiades," son of Laius, i.e. Oedipus who solved the Sphinx, misread in his manuscript as "Naiades"). We keep "Naiads" rather than silently correcting to Oedipus, because the line as Dante wrote it is what the tradition received and what the Italian says; modernizing the error would rewrite the poet. The Sphinx's plague on Thebes — destroying flocks and crops — is why the solving comes "with no destruction of the flocks and grain": this time the riddle's answer brings no ruin.

divergences.phrase: Io ritornai da la santissima onda / rifatto sì come piante novelle / rinovellate di novella fronda, / puro e disposto a salire a le stelle
divergences.older: From the most holy water I returned / Regenerate, in the manner of new trees / That are renewed with a new foliage, / Pure and disposed to mount unto the stars (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: From those most holy waters I came back / remade — the way new plants are renewed / with new leaves — / pure and ready to rise to the stars
divergences.note: The end of the entire Purgatorio, and one of three lines in the poem that close each cantica on the word "stelle," stars. Dante has drunk of Eunoë, the river that restores the memory of every good deed, and is made new like a plant in spring — "rifatto... rinovellate di novella fronda," a triple chime of renewal (re-made, re-newed, new) that we keep audible with "remade... renewed... new leaves." We render "disposto a salire" as "ready to rise" rather than Longfellow's "disposed to mount": disposto carries readiness and right-ordering at once — he is not merely able to ascend but now rightly inclined to. The line is left to land bare on "the stars," with no added image, so the cantica ends exactly where Dante leaves it: pointed upward, toward Paradise.

divergences.phrase: Trasumanar significar per verba
divergences.older: To represent transhumanise in words (Longfellow); Words may not tell of that transhuman change (Cary); Transhumanizing cannot be signified in words (Norton)
divergences.lectio: To say in words what it is to pass beyond the human
divergences.note: Trasumanar is Dante's own coinage — a verb he invents on the spot because no word exists for what he means: a human nature exceeding itself into the divine. The paradox is that by minting the word he proves language can graze the unsayable. The older 'transhumanise / transhumanizing' is a dead Latinate calque a modern reader bounces off; we keep the strangeness of the act by stating it plainly ('to pass beyond the human') rather than resolving it into a smoother abstraction.

divergences.phrase: Le cose tutte quante / hanno ordine tra loro, e questo è forma / che l'universo a Dio fa simigliante
divergences.older: All things whate'er they be / Have order among themselves, and this is form, / That makes the universe resemble God (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: All things whatever they are / have order among themselves, and this is the form / that makes the universe resemble God
divergences.note: This opens Beatrice's great discourse on the order of the universe — that every nature carries an inborn bent drawing it toward God as its final harbor, the way a freed soul rises as naturally as a river falls. 'Forma' here is the scholastic term for the shaping principle, not mere shape; we keep 'the form' rather than flatten it to 'pattern' or 'design,' since the whole argument turns on order being what makes the cosmos God-like.

divergences.phrase: per lo gran mar de l'essere
divergences.older: O'er the great sea of being (Longfellow); Through the vast sea of being (Cary)
divergences.lectio: over the great sea of being
divergences.note: The image is exact and we hold it whole: all created things, each carried by an instinct given it, sail toward their different harbors across one 'great sea of being.' It is the line that makes the metaphysics concrete — a seascape — and a modern reader needs no help with it, so we change nothing but the archaic 'O'er.'

divergences.phrase: piccioletta barca
divergences.older: some pretty little boat (Longfellow); little bark (Cary)
divergences.lectio: a little boat
divergences.note: Longfellow's "pretty" mistakes the Italian: piccioletta is simply the diminutive of piccola, small, with no prettiness about it. The point is the boat's smallness against an uncrossed sea — the reader who is not ready will be lost. We keep it plainly small.

divergences.phrase: pan de li angeli
divergences.older: the bread of Angels (Longfellow); the bread of Angels (Cary)
divergences.lectio: the bread of the angels
divergences.note: The metaphor is the food of the intellect that feeds on God — wisdom one can taste in this life but never finish. We keep the image literal rather than glossing it; lowercase "angels" reads as Dante's plain Italian (li angeli) and lets the figure carry its own weight.

divergences.phrase: li segni bui ... di Cain favoleggiare
divergences.older: the dusky spots ... that fabulous tale of Cain (Longfellow); the dusky spots ... the fabled tale of Cain (Cary)
divergences.lectio: the dark markings ... that old fable about Cain
divergences.note: The "man in the moon" — the dark patches medieval folklore read as Cain banished there with his bundle of thorns. Dante asks the literal question (what causes the spots) and gets a lesson in cosmology back. We name the legend plainly as a fable rather than dressing it in "fabulous," which now reads as praise instead of "made-up."

divergences.phrase: essa è formal principio
divergences.older: This is the formal principle that produces (Longfellow); 'tis the form / Productive (Cary)
divergences.lectio: This is the formative principle that makes
divergences.note: Beatrice's conclusion overturns Dante's guess: the differences across the heavens come not from matter being dense or thin but from differing formative virtues — the influence the angelic Intelligences shed down through the spheres, as joy shines through a living eye. We render principio formal as "formative principle" rather than the scholastic "formal principle," so a modern reader hears what it does — it forms, it shapes — instead of stalling on a term of art.

divergences.phrase: ch'accese amor tra l'omo e 'l fonte
divergences.older: to that which kindled love 'twixt man and fountain (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the error opposite to the one that lit love between the boy and the spring
divergences.note: Dante never names Narcissus, but the whole image turns on him: Narcissus mistook a real reflection for a real person; Dante does the reverse, mistaking real souls for mere reflections. Longfellow's bare 'man and fountain' leaves a modern reader stranded. We keep Dante's allusive method — no footnote name — but render 'fonte' as 'spring' (the pool Narcissus bent over) and 'omo' as 'the boy,' so the myth surfaces on its own. The strangeness of the inverted error is the point and is kept intact.

divergences.phrase: frate, la nostra volontà quïeta / virtù di carità
divergences.older: Brother, our will is quieted by virtue / Of charity (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Brother, the power of charity quiets our will / and makes us wish only for what we have
divergences.note: This is the canto's doctrine and its emotional core: Piccarda, placed in the lowest sphere, feels no lack. The older 'quieted by virtue / Of charity' reads as abstraction; the Italian is active — charity does the quieting. We make charity the agent and 'will' the thing acted on, and keep Dante's plain follow-through ('nor gives us thirst for more') rather than smoothing it into philosophy. The thought is hard and is left hard; only the grammar is modernized.

divergences.phrase: E 'n la sua volontade è nostra pace
divergences.older: And his will is our peace (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: And in his will is our peace. It is the sea toward which all things are moving
divergences.note: The most quoted line of the canto, and arguably of the Paradiso. We keep it almost exactly as the tradition has fixed it — 'in his will is our peace' — because the cadence is load-bearing and any cleverness here would be vandalism. The one decision is to let the following image stand as its own sentence: the will is 'quel mare,' the sea toward which everything created moves. Longfellow's enjambment ('this is the sea / To which is moving') is faithful but tangled; we give the metaphor a clean breath of its own so the line lands and then opens out, the way the Italian does.

divergences.phrase: D'i Serafin colui che più s'india ... non hanno in altro cielo i loro scanni ... ma per far segno
divergences.older: He of the Seraphim most absorbed in God ... Have not in any other heaven their seats ... but to give sign (Longfellow); The Seraph that in God / Deepest is plunged ... have not in other heaven their seats ... but to make sign (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Not the Seraph most in-Godded of them all ... has his seat in any other heaven than these ... but to give a sign of the heaven that stands the lowest of them all
divergences.note: The doctrinal heart of the canto: every blessed soul truly dwells with God in the Empyrean, and the souls Dante meets in the spheres appear there only as a SIGN — a gradation staged for human eyes, the way Scripture gives God hands and feet and the Church paints angels with faces. We keep Dante's coined verb s'india ("in-Gods itself") as "in-Godded" rather than smoothing it to "absorbed in God," because the strangeness is the theology: the soul does not approach God, it is taken into Him. The accommodation itself we render plainly — the spirits appear "to give a sign" — so a modern reader meets Beatrice's whole teaching, that what is divided across the heavens is the appearance, not the souls.

divergences.phrase: nasce 'l dubbio a piè del vero; ed è natura / ch'al sommo pinge noi di collo in collo
divergences.older: Therefore springs up, in fashion of a shoot, / Doubt at the foot of truth; and this is nature, / Which to the top from height to height impels us (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: And so, at the foot of truth, doubt springs up / like a green shoot; and this is nature's doing, / urging us upward, peak to peak, to the height
divergences.note: Beatrice's word on the life of the mind: truth is where the intellect rests "like a wild beast in its den," but at the foot of each truth a new doubt sprouts, and this is no defect — it is nature itself driving us up the mountain of knowing, di collo in collo, ridge to ridge. We keep the live botanical and mountaineering images Longfellow preserves (the shoot, the climb) but unstiffen the grammar, letting doubt be the spur that lifts us rather than an abstraction "in fashion of a shoot." The thought is left as hard as Dante leaves it; only the period syntax is cleared away.

divergences.phrase: se fu volontà perfetta / qual tenne Lorenzo in su la grada, / e Muzio a la sua man
divergences.older: If their will had been perfect, like to that / Which Lawrence fast upon his gridiron held, / And Mutius made severe to his own hand (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Had their will held whole and unbroken, the will / that kept Lawrence steady on the burning grill, / that made Mucius hard against his own scorched hand
divergences.note: The second doubt turns on the difference between absolute will, which never consents to wrong, and the "mixed" will that yields under fear. Beatrice's proof is two bodies that did not yield: Saint Lawrence, who joked on the gridiron, and Mucius Scaevola, who thrust his own hand into the fire to punish it for missing its mark. We keep both proper names and render the will as "whole and unbroken" rather than the abstract "perfect," so the reader feels what perfection means here — a will that the body's agony cannot bend — which is exactly the standard the broken-vow souls failed to meet.

divergences.phrase: lo maggior don che Dio per sua larghezza / fesse creando … è de la volontà la libertate
divergences.older: the freedom of the will (Longfellow); the freedom of the will (Cary)
divergences.lectio: the freedom of the will — the greatest gift that God, in His largeness, made in creating
divergences.note: This is the doctrinal hinge of the canto, so we keep it unmistakable rather than letting it sit buried mid-sentence as in the older verse. Dante's claim is precise: free will is the gift God prizes most because it is the one most like His own goodness — which is exactly why a vow, which gives that very freedom back to God, cannot be lightly undone.

divergences.phrase: due cose si convegnono … l'una è quella di che si fa, l'altr' è la convenenza
divergences.older: two things convene together; and the one is that / of which 'tis made, the other is the agreement (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Two things go into the substance of this sacrifice: the one is the matter of which it is made, the other is the compact, the agreement itself.
divergences.note: Longfellow's 'convene together' is dead Latinate clutter. The thought underneath is the whole argument: a vow has two parts — the compact (the binding agreement to give) and the matter (the thing offered). The compact can never be cancelled; the matter may sometimes be exchanged, never for less. We name both parts plainly so the distinction the canto turns on is legible at a glance.

divergences.phrase: ogne permutanza credi stolta, / se la cosa dimessa in la sorpresa / come 'l quattro nel sei non è raccolta
divergences.older: every permutation deem as foolish, / if in the substitute the thing relinquished, / as the four is in six, be not contained (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: count every exchange as foolish unless the thing laid down is held inside the thing put in its place, as four is in six
divergences.note: The math image is load-bearing and we keep it intact rather than smoothing it to abstraction: a swap is valid only if the new offering exceeds and contains the old, the way six contains four. We render 'permutanza' as the everyday 'exchange' and untangle Longfellow's inverted clause so the proportion lands cleanly. The 'white key and the gold' two lines above are the Church's keys of dispensation — kept literal.

divergences.phrase: Cesare fui e son Iustinïano
divergences.older: Caesar I was, and am Justinian (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Caesar I was, and am Justinian
divergences.note: The whole canto is spoken by one soul, the emperor Justinian, and this is the line where he names himself — the only single-voice canto in the Comedy. The tense shift is the point and is kept exactly: 'I was Caesar' (the earthly office, finished) and 'I am Justinian' (the man, the codifier of Roman law, still himself in Heaven). The tradition has fixed this line; we leave it almost untouched because the contrast between the dead title and the living name is load-bearing. We keep the Italian spelling 'Justinian' and resist any gloss — he goes on to explain himself, that he stripped the laws of 'il troppo e 'l vano' (the excess and the idle), and that Pope Agapetus led him from the heresy of Christ's single nature to the true faith before grace moved him to his great work.

divergences.phrase: l'uccel di Dio — lo benedetto segno
divergences.older: the bird of God / the standard sacrosanct (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the bird of God / the sacred standard
divergences.note: The center of the canto is the long flight of the Roman eagle through history — the 'sacrosanto segno,' the sacred standard carried from Aeneas (the ancient who took Lavinia) and Pallas, through the Roman kings and the Horatii ('three against three'), against Brennus and Pyrrhus, through the Scipios and Caesar leaping the Rubicon, to Augustus shutting the temple of Janus, and at last to the eagle in the 'third Caesar's' hand — Tiberius — under whom the Crucifixion accomplished God's just vengeance for Adam's sin, a vengeance later avenged on Jerusalem under Titus. We keep every proper noun and let the flight build at speed, as the Italian does, rather than slowing it with explanation. The doubled 'vendetta' — vengeance taken on the vengeance — is Dante's hardest knot and is kept hard: the eagle first bore the punishment of Adam's sin in Christ's death, then punished those who carried it out. Justinian's point is moral, not antiquarian — the rebuke that frames it: both the Ghibellines who oppose the sacred standard and the Guelfs who oppose it with their party-emblem, the yellow lilies, are wrong to part it from justice.

divergences.phrase: e se 'l mondo sapesse 'l cor ch'elli ebbe … assai lo loda, e più lo loderebbe
divergences.older: and if the world could know the heart he had … Though much it laud him, it would laud him more (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: and if the world could know the heart he carried … much as it praises him, it would praise him more
divergences.note: The canto closes on Romeo de Villeneuve, the just steward of Raymond Berenger who married off four daughters as queens and then, slandered, was driven to wander poor and unthanked — 'rendering twelve for ten,' giving back more than he was given. The final couplet is the emotional landing of the whole canto and we render it plainly, keeping Dante's own movement: the world already praises Romeo, and would praise him more if it knew the heart with which he begged his bread. We change Longfellow's 'laud' to 'praise' (the archaism trips a modern ear) but keep the exact logic of the comparison — 'assai … e più' — because the quiet, unfinished generosity of 'and would praise him more' is the line's whole power. Romeo, like Justinian, belongs to Mercury's small sphere of spirits whose love of fame dimmed their zeal — good souls, content in just proportion.

divergences.phrase: quell'uom che non nacque
divergences.older: that man who ne'er was born (Longfellow); he, who ne'er had birth (Cary)
divergences.lectio: that man who never was born
divergences.note: This is Adam, and the phrase is doing precise theological work: he is the one human who was never born of a mother but made directly by God. Older versions keep the riddle but in inverted syntax ('who ne'er was born') that reads as a puzzle rather than a fact. We keep the strange, exact claim — that Adam was unborn — because the whole argument about inherited guilt turns on it: when the unborn first man bound human nature, he bound everyone made from him.

divergences.phrase: Più liberal fu Dio a dar sé stesso
divergences.older: For God more bounteous was himself to give (Longfellow); More liberal God was, His own self to give (Cary)
divergences.lectio: for God, in giving his own self, was more openhanded
divergences.note: The hinge of the canto, and of Beatrice's whole case for the Incarnation: redemption by God's self-gift was a greater good than redemption by simple pardon, because the highest goodness gives of itself. Longfellow's 'bounteous' and Cary's 'liberal' have both drifted in modern English toward generosity-with-money. We render 'liberal' as 'openhanded' to recover the root sense — free, ungrudging self-giving — and keep 'his own self' front and center, since the entire point is that God gave not a thing but himself.

divergences.phrase: ciò che da lei sanza mezzo distilla / non ha poi fine
divergences.older: Whate'er from this immediately distils / Has afterwards no end (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Whatever rains straight down from it, with nothing between, has no end after
divergences.note: Here Beatrice proves the immortality of the soul and the certainty of resurrection: what God creates directly — 'sanza mezzo,' with no intermediary — is incorruptible, because God's seal, once set, can never be removed. The load-bearing word is 'sanza mezzo,' which Longfellow flattens into the adverb 'immediately' — a word a modern reader hears only as 'right away,' losing the real meaning, which is 'with nothing in between.' We restore the spatial sense ('straight down... with nothing between') so the argument lands: the rational soul, breathed in directly by God, has no cause of decay, and therefore the body it belongs to is sure to rise again.

divergences.phrase: la bella Ciprigna ... il folle amore raggiasse, volta nel terzo epiciclo
divergences.older: the fair Cypria delirious love / Rayed out, in the third epicycle turning (Longfellow); the fair Cyprian fancied to rain down / mad love (Cary)
divergences.lectio: lovely Venus, wheeling in the third / epicycle, rayed down mad love on men
divergences.note: Dante opens on the ancients' mistake: that the goddess of the sphere literally beamed erotic madness into the world. We keep Venus by name (the planet the canto stands in) rather than Longfellow's learned 'Cypria,' which sends a modern reader to a footnote; 'folle amore' is the canto's pointed phrase — not 'love' but mad love, the error the ancients worshipped — so we keep its bite. The astronomy ('terzo epiciclo') is load-bearing strangeness, an old picture of the heavens, and we keep it rather than smoothing it away.

divergences.phrase: com' esser può, di dolce seme, amaro
divergences.older: How from sweet seed can bitter issue forth (Longfellow); how bitter springs / from sweet seed (Cary)
divergences.lectio: how can a sweet seed bring forth bitter fruit?
divergences.note: This is the hinge of the canto — Dante's question to Charles Martel about why good fathers beget unworthy sons. The Italian is stark and proverbial; 'amaro' is simply 'the bitter.' We supply 'fruit' to complete the figure the seed already opens (and to let it land cleanly aloud), keeping the line plain and weighty rather than inverted. The whole second half of the canto is Charles's answer.

divergences.phrase: Ma voi torcete a la religïone tal / che fia nato a cignersi la spada, / e fate re di tal ch'è da sermone; / onde la traccia vostra è fuor di strada
divergences.older: But you unto religion wrench aside / Him who was born to gird him with the sword, / And make a king of him who is for sermons; / Therefore your footsteps wander from the road (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: you wrench toward the cloister / one born to buckle on the sword, and crown / a man fit only for the pulpit king; / and so the track you walk runs off the road
divergences.note: Charles's teaching, made concrete: Providence gives each person a native bent through the influence of the stars, regardless of bloodline, so a society needs diverse natures — and forcing a man against his inborn bent breaks everything. 'Torcete' is physical, to twist or wrench, and we keep that violence; 'da sermone' we render 'fit for the pulpit' for immediacy. The closing image — 'la traccia vostra è fuor di strada,' your track is off the road — is the canto's verdict on misrule, and we let it close hard and plain.

divergences.phrase: Cunizza fui chiamata
divergences.older: Cunizza was I called (Longfellow); Cunizza was I named (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Cunizza I was called
divergences.note: Cunizza da Romano — sister of the tyrant Ezzelino, the "burning brand" born of the same hill — was notorious in life for her loves, yet Dante sets her shining in the heaven of Venus. The whole force of the passage is that she neither hides nor regrets her name: she says it plainly and forgives herself "gladly" (lietamente ... indulgo). We keep the proper noun front and center and drop Longfellow's inverted "was I called," which buries the one word that matters.

divergences.phrase: qui non si pente, ma si ride
divergences.older: Yet here is no repenting, but we smile (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Yet here we do not repent — we smile, / not at the sin, which never comes back to mind, / but at the Power that ordered and foresaw
divergences.note: This is the theological hinge of the canto, and it is genuinely strange: Folco, once a love-poet who burned hotter than Dido, does not repent in Heaven. Dante is precise — the souls smile non al fallo (not at the fault, which is wiped from memory) but at the Providence (la virtù ch'ordinò e provide) that turned even their disordered love to good. We keep the paradox sharp rather than softening it into pious regret; the difficulty here is load-bearing and must stay.

divergences.phrase: si tranquilla Raab ... nel sommo grado si sigilla
divergences.older: Rahab, and being to our order joined, / With her in its supremest grade 'tis sealed (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: is Rahab — joined now to our order, and stamped / into its very highest rank, its crown
divergences.note: Rahab — the harlot of Jericho who hid Joshua's spies — is, Dante claims, the first soul Christ drew up from Limbo at the Harrowing, and she shines at the very top of the Venus sphere. Longfellow's "'tis sealed" is opaque; the Italian si sigilla is the image of a seal pressed home, fixing her in the supreme grade. We render it as "stamped... its crown" to keep the concrete metaphor and the shock of the placement: a foreign prostitute set highest, named in the same breath as the Pope who has forgotten the Holy Land she helped win.

divergences.phrase: Lift up then, Reader, to the lofty wheels / with me thy vision (Longfellow); leva dunque, lettore, a l'alte rote / meco la vista
divergences.older: Lift up then, Reader, to the lofty wheels / With me thy vision straight unto that part (Longfellow); Look, reader, upward to the lofty wheels / With me (Norton, prose)
divergences.lectio: Lift up your eyes with me, then, Reader — lift them / to the high wheeling spheres
divergences.note: The canto's signature move is the direct address: Dante reaches out and pulls the reader's gaze upward with his own. Longfellow's 'thy vision' and inverted clause put a pane of glass between reader and sky. We keep the gesture immediate and physical — 'lift up your eyes with me' — and let the repetition ('lift them') do the urging Dante's imperative does, so the invitation lands as a hand on the shoulder rather than an instruction.

divergences.phrase: Lights many saw I... make us a centre and themselves a circle (Longfellow); io vidi più folgór vivi e vincenti / far di noi centro e di sé far corona
divergences.older: Lights many saw I, vivid and triumphant, / Make us a centre and themselves a circle (Longfellow); I saw many living and conquering splendours make of us a centre and of themselves a crown (Norton)
divergences.lectio: I saw lights, many of them, vivid, triumphant, / make us their center and themselves a ring ... When those burning suns ... had whirled three times in a circle around us
divergences.note: This is the crown of the wise — twelve blazing souls (Aquinas, Albert, Gratian, Peter Lombard, Solomon, and the rest) wheeling three times around Dante and Beatrice like a halo, 'sweeter in voice than they were bright to see.' We render 'corona' as a ring/crown of light rather than a flat 'circle,' and keep Dante's startling claim that in this heaven the souls are known by radiance, not color ('apparent not by colour but by light') — the strangeness is the theology, so we hold onto it instead of smoothing it into ordinary brightness.

divergences.phrase: come orologio che ne chiami ... tin tin sonando con sì dolce nota
divergences.older: Then, as a horologe that calleth us / What time the Bride of God is rising up ... Ting! ting! resounding with so sweet a note (Longfellow); like a clock which calls us at the hour ... tin-tin sounding with note so sweet (Norton)
divergences.lectio: Then, like a clock that calls us up to wake / at the hour the Bride of God is rising ... ting, ting, ringing out a note so sweet / the well-tuned spirit swells with love at it
divergences.note: The canto ends on Dante's most modern, most domestic image: the geared mechanical clock — then a new invention — whose wheels turn one another and chime the faithful to matins, here become the figure for the wheeling, singing ring of the blessed. 'Horologe' is exactly the dead Victorian word that breaks the spell, so we use 'clock.' We keep Dante's onomatopoeic 'tin tin' as 'ting, ting' rather than abstracting it to 'chiming' — the small homely sound is the point, the everyday made eternal.

divergences.phrase: non dica Ascesi, ché direbbe corto, ma Orïente
divergences.older: Say not Ascesi, for he would say little, / But Orient (Longfellow); let him not say Ascesi, which were to say too little, but Orient (Cary)
divergences.lectio: not say Assisi — that would say too little — but Orient, if he means to name it right
divergences.note: Dante is making a deliberate pun a modern reader can't see: the town's medieval Tuscan name was 'Ascesi,' which to his ear sounds like 'ascesi/ascendere' (risen, ascended) — too small a word for the man born there. The true name, he says, is 'Oriente' — the East, the sunrise — because Francis rose on the world like a sun. We keep the modern 'Assisi' so the place is recognizable, but preserve 'Orient' untranslated and let the sun imagery of the surrounding tercets carry the wordplay rather than flattening it into 'the East.'

divergences.phrase: la sua donna ... Povertà
divergences.older: for certain Dame, to whom, as unto death, / The gate of pleasure no one doth unlock (Longfellow); his Lady ... Poverty (Cary)
divergences.lectio: a certain Lady to whom, as to death itself, no one unbars the door of joy ... Francis and Poverty ... the two lovers
divergences.note: The whole heart of the canto is a sustained allegory: Francis 'marries' Lady Poverty, the bride left widowed since Christ died on the cross — 'reft of her first husband ... eleven hundred years and more' with no suitor until Francis came. The Vernacular keeps the conceit fully literal and erotic-romantic as Dante built it (bride, bridegroom, the door of joy, the marriage 'et coram patre') rather than glossing it into the abstraction 'a life of poverty.' Poverty stays capitalized as a person, because in this canto she is one. The Latin tag 'et coram patre' (before the father — Francis's literal renunciation before his bishop and earthly father) is preserved as Dante left it untranslated.

divergences.phrase: da Cristo prese l'ultimo sigillo
divergences.older: From Christ did he receive the final seal, / Which during two whole years his members bore (Longfellow); from Christ took the last signet (Cary)
divergences.lectio: he took from Christ the final seal, which his body wore for two whole years
divergences.note: This is the stigmata — the wounds of the crucified Christ appearing on Francis's own body at La Verna ('the bare rock between the Tiber and the Arno'). Dante never says the word; he calls it 'l'ultimo sigillo,' the last seal, as if Christ were stamping His own image onto Francis to certify the imitation as complete. We keep the metaphor of the seal exactly — not 'wounds' or 'stigmata' — because the seal is the point: a signature, a final confirmation pressed into flesh.

divergences.phrase: siede la fortunata Calaroga ... il santo atleta
divergences.older: Is situate the fortunate Calahorra ... the athlete consecrate (Longfellow); the blest Calaroga (Cary)
divergences.lectio: sits fortunate Calaruega ... the holy athlete
divergences.note: Dante's 'Calaroga' is Caleruega in Old Castile, Saint Dominic's birthplace — Longfellow's 'Calahorra' is a nineteenth-century misidentification (a different Spanish town). We restore the place Dante means. We keep 'athlete' for 'atleta': Dominic is literally Christ's wrestler/contender for the Faith, the militant counterweight to Francis's bridegroom-of-Poverty in the canto before — softening it to 'champion' would lose the bodily, agonistic charge.

divergences.phrase: come si dipigne ... d'iri ... la vaga / di ch'amor lui consunse come sol vapore
divergences.older: Two rainbows parallel ... Like to the speaking of that vagrant one / Whom love consumed as doth the sun the vapours (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: two rainbows, parallel and matched in color ... that wandering nymph's voice answered, she / whom love burned off as the sun burns mist
divergences.note: The two crowns of wise souls wheel as a double rainbow — the outer arc 'born of' the inner, like an echo of an echo. Dante's 'la vaga' is the nymph Echo, who wasted away for love of Narcissus until only her voice remained; the outer rainbow answers the inner the way Echo answers a speaker. Longfellow's flat 'that vagrant one' loses the myth entirely. We name what she is (a wandering nymph whose voice answers) so the image of one bow echoing another lands, and keep the Noah's-covenant pledge the doubled bow signifies.

divergences.phrase: l'una rota de la biga ... il calavrese abate Giovacchino
divergences.older: If such the one wheel of the Biga was ... the Calabrian Abbot Joachim (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: If this was one wheel of the chariot ... the Calabrian abbot Joachim
divergences.note: The 'biga' is the ancient two-wheeled war-chariot; Dominic and Francis are its two wheels, the Church's war-cart that won the field. We render it plainly as 'chariot' rather than transliterate a Latin word a modern reader would stumble on, but keep the single-image logic (one wheel implies the other) intact. The garland's last and most pointed name is Joachim of Flora — the apocalyptic prophet whose followers Bonaventure had officially opposed; that a Franciscan in bliss places him among the wise, right after lamenting his own order's split, is the canto's deliberate, unresolved sting. We keep the name and the placement and don't editorialize it away.

divergences.phrase: regal prudenza
divergences.older: A regal prudence is that peerless seeing (Longfellow); kingly prudence is that wisdom unrivalled (Cary)
divergences.lectio: that peerless seeing is a king's own prudence
divergences.note: This is Aquinas resolving Dante's doubt, and the whole answer turns on a single qualifier. Solomon was not the wisest mind that ever lived — Adam and Christ were made perfect. He was a king who, when offered anything, asked only for the wisdom to rule well, and in THAT kind he has no equal. We make 'kingly' load-bearing rather than ornamental: 'peerless' is true only of a king's practical prudence, not of knowledge in general. The closing image of the 'rose' (the Italian 'rege,' kings) is the same point — 'unmatched' means unmatched among rulers, of whom good ones are rare.

divergences.phrase: la cera di costoro e chi la duce / non sta d'un modo
divergences.older: Neither their wax, nor that which tempers it, / Remains immutable (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: Neither their wax nor the hand that stamps it / stays the same
divergences.note: Dante's account of creation: every created thing is the divine Idea shining through the nine heavens like a seal pressed into wax. But the wax (matter) and the stamping (the secondary causes — nature, the wheeling heavens) are never constant, so the imprint comes out 'more or less' — creatures fall short of the Idea. We keep the wax-and-seal metaphor fully concrete, where 'that which tempers it' goes abstract, because the trembling-handed artist a few lines later is the same image and must rhyme with it. Only Adam and Christ, stamped directly by Love and Vision, were ever made perfect.

divergences.phrase: esser dee piombo a' piedi
divergences.older: And lead shall this be always to thy feet (Longfellow); Let this be ever as lead to weigh thy feet (Cary)
divergences.lectio: And let this always be lead at your feet, / to make you, like a tired man, move slowly / toward the Yes and the No you cannot see
divergences.note: The canto closes on Aquinas's warning against hasty judgment, and the figure is physical: a weight on the feet that forces a tired man to walk slowly to 'yes' and 'no.' We keep the bluntness of the named fools — Parmenides, Melissus, Bryson, Sabellius, Arius — and the two homely proofs Dante gives against verdicts rushed before the evidence is in: the thornbush that looks dead all winter and then crowns itself with a rose, and the ship that sails its whole course only to sink at the harbor's mouth. The lesson is not skepticism but patience — judge no harvest before it ripens.

divergences.phrase: Ma sì come carbon che fiamma rende, / e per vivo candor quella soverchia
divergences.lectio: But like a coal that throws a living flame / and by its own white core outshines the flame, / so that the coal stays plainly what it is
divergences.older: But even as a coal that sends forth flame, / And by its vivid whiteness overpowers it / So that its own appearance it maintains (Longfellow); as burning coal, / That sends the flame forth, with its vivid white / Outglowing it (Cary)
divergences.note: Solomon's answer to Dante's unspoken question about the resurrection body: after the Last Judgment, when soul rejoins flesh, the saints' radiance will grow brighter, not be dimmed by the body. The image is exact and counter-intuitive — the live coal is so incandescent it outshines the very flame it produces, yet remains visibly itself. We keep all three of its moving parts (the coal, the flame it gives off, and the coal's white core overpowering that flame) rather than smoothing it into a single glow, because the whole point is that the restored flesh will not veil the soul's light but blaze past it — while the glorified eyes, strengthened, will bear the greater brightness without being wearied.

divergences.phrase: ne la profonda e chiara sussistenza / ... quella croce lampeggiava Cristo
divergences.lectio: so, constellated deep within the body of Mars, / those rays traced out the venerable Sign ... / for on that cross flashed Christ, like lightning gone
divergences.older: Thus constellated in the depths of Mars ... / For on that cross as levin gleamed forth Christ (Longfellow); So in the depth of Mars the rays / Described the venerable sign ... lightened Christ (Cary)
divergences.note: The sudden rise to the fifth heaven, the red planet Mars, where the souls of the holy warriors are arrayed in a vast glowing cross of light. We render 'lampeggiava Cristo' as 'flashed Christ, like lightning gone' — Dante uses Christ's name as the verb's lightning-flash, a Christ-figure that comes and is gone faster than the eye, and that he openly confesses lies beyond his words to tell ('here my memory outruns my skill'). We keep Mars named and concrete and preserve Dante's admission of failure rather than supplying the simile he says he cannot find; the strangeness — a planet's red light woven into a cross on which Christ himself breaks like lightning — is the vision, not an ornament to be tidied.

divergences.phrase: che i vivi suggelli / d'ogne bellezza più fanno più suso
divergences.lectio: putting off the delight of those fair eyes ... / but whoever considers that the living seals / of every beauty gain in power the higher they rise
divergences.older: Postponing the delight of those fair eyes ... / But who bethinks him that the living seals / Of every beauty grow in power ascending (Longfellow)
divergences.note: After the hymn ('Rise' and 'Conquer') sweeps the cross and ravishes him though he cannot make out the words, Dante stops to confess that this once he has not mentioned Beatrice's eyes — and excuses himself by it: the higher one rises in Paradise, the more powerful those 'living seals of beauty' become, so that not yet turning to them was no slight but a measure of how far he had climbed. We keep 'living seals' (vivi suggelli) literally rather than glossing it to 'living mirrors' or 'lamps,' because the seal is what stamps and confirms — her eyes remain the living seal of his joy even in the one canto that leaves them unnamed, and the paradox (the joy is not absent, only grown too pure to disclose) is the note he ends on.

divergences.phrase: paventava la figlia al nascer / che 'l tempo e la dote non fuggien quinci e quindi la misura
divergences.older: Not yet the daughter at her birth struck fear / Into the father, for the time and dower / Did not o'errun this side or that the measure (Longfellow); No daughter's birth brought fear unto the sire, / For nor the age nor dower past compass swell'd (Cary)
divergences.lectio: A daughter's birth did not yet frighten her father: / the age of marriage and the size of the dowry / had not run past all measure on either side.
divergences.note: Dante's compressed civic complaint is that in old Florence a baby girl was not yet a financial dread — marriages had not crept too early and dowries had not ballooned too high. Longfellow's 'time and dower' leaves a modern reader guessing; we spell out 'age of marriage' and 'size of the dowry' so the social grievance lands, without adding anything the Italian does not already mean.

divergences.phrase: Fiorenza dentro da la cerchia antica ... si stava in pace, sobria e pudica
divergences.older: Florence, within the ancient boundary / From which she taketh still her tierce and nones, / Abode in quiet, temperate and chaste (Longfellow); Florence, within her ancient limit-mark ... abode in quiet, temperate and chaste (Cary)
divergences.lectio: Florence, inside the ring of her old walls — / from which she still takes the bells of terce and nones — / lived in peace, sober and chaste.
divergences.note: The whole portrait of old Florence turns on 'sobria e pudica' — sober and chaste. Longfellow's 'temperate and chaste' softens the first word; Dante's 'sobria' is plainer and harder, the moral keynote of Cacciaguida's nostalgia, so we keep 'sober.' 'Cerchia antica' is literally the ancient circle of walls, and we keep the concrete image of the wall rather than abstracting it to 'boundary,' since the contrast of the small old city against the sprawling new one is the point.

divergences.phrase: in la vostra Pagan San Giovanni / fui battezzato ... e venni dal martiro a questa pace
divergences.older: And in your ancient Baptistery at once / Christian and Cacciaguida I became ... And came from martyrdom unto this peace (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: and in your ancient Baptistery I became, / in one stroke, a Christian and Cacciaguida ... and I came from martyrdom into this peace.
divergences.note: Cacciaguida frames his whole life as an arc from the baptismal font of San Giovanni to the peace of this heaven, with crusade-death as the hinge — 'martiro' he names flatly, claiming martyrdom for himself. We preserve the bluntness ('martyrdom,' not 'a martyr's death') and the single-stroke pairing of sacrament and name ('a Christian and Cacciaguida'), which the Italian sets side by side; the line is the emotional clasp of the canto and we let it close as plainly as Dante does.

divergences.phrase: O our poor little nobility of blood
divergences.older: O thou our poor nobility of blood (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: O our poor little nobility of blood
divergences.note: Dante's "O poca nostra nobiltà di sangue" addresses noble birth itself as a small, paltry thing. We keep "poor" but restore "little" (poca) so the diminishment lands, and drop the archaic "thou" — the whole canto's argument is that bloodline is worthless unless renewed by virtue, the cloak Time trims back daily.

divergences.phrase: the fall of the great families
divergences.older: illustrious even in their fall / undone by their own pride (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the Ughi... the Catellini... illustrious citizens even as they fell... those now undone by their own pride
divergences.note: Dante's long roll of Florentine houses (Ughi, Catellini, Ravignani, Cerchi, Buondelmonti) is an elegy: names spoken in their rise and their ruin. We keep every proper noun and the bare cadence of the list, letting the names carry the weight rather than glossing each lineage — the point is the sound of a city's vanished aristocracy, not a genealogy.

divergences.phrase: the lily never reversed, never turned red
divergences.older: the lily / Never upon the spear was placed reversed, / Nor by division was vermilion made (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the lily / was never set reversed upon the staff, / nor turned to red by faction
divergences.note: Two images of disgrace Florence had not yet suffered: a banner carried upside-down meant military defeat, and Dante recalls the old white lily on red, before faction inverted the colors to a red lily on white. We render "per division" as "by faction" so a modern reader feels the civil-war stain in the heraldry without a footnote.

divergences.phrase: come sa di sale / lo pane altrui, e come è duro calle / lo scendere e 'l salir per l'altrui scale
divergences.older: Thou shalt have proof how savoureth of salt / The bread of others, and how hard a road / The going down and up another's stairs (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: You shall learn how salt is the taste / of another man's bread, and how hard the path / going down and climbing up another man's stairs.
divergences.note: The most famous lines in the canto, and Dante's own taste of exile. The Italian is plain and physical — salt bread (Tuscan bread is unsalted, so a stranger's salted loaf literally tastes wrong in the mouth), and the bodily labor of climbing a patron's stairs. We keep both concrete images and straighten Longfellow's inverted 'how savoureth of salt' into living speech, so the bitterness lands as sensation, not as poetry about sensation.

divergences.phrase: Con lui vedrai colui che 'mpresso fue, / nascendo, sì da questa stella forte, / che notabili fier l'opere sue
divergences.older: With him shalt thou see one who at his birth / Has by this star of strength been so impressed, / That notable shall his achievements be (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: With him you shall see one so stamped at birth / by this strong star that his deeds / will be worth remembering.
divergences.note: This is Can Grande della Scala — the young lord (only nine at the dramatic date) whom Cacciaguida foretells as Dante's future patron and the age's great hope; Dante never names him, only points. We preserve the deliberate mystery — Dante withholds the name on purpose ('written in your mind... but not repeat it') — and render 'stella forte' as the strong star (Mars) that marked him at birth, keeping the astrological frame rather than flattening it to 'born great.'

divergences.phrase: rimossa ogne menzogna, / tutta tua vision fa manifesta; / e lascia pur grattar dov'è la rogna
divergences.older: all falsehood laid aside, / Make manifest thy vision utterly, / And let them scratch wherever is the itch (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: let every lie fall away, / make your whole vision plain, / and let them scratch wherever it may itch.
divergences.note: Cacciaguida's charge to Dante — and the poem's defense of itself. The image is deliberately coarse ('rogna' is scabies, the mange): if the truth makes people itch, let them scratch. We keep the bluntness rather than soften it to a polite metaphor, because the whole point is that the vision must be told without flinching even when it stings — bitter at first taste, vital nourishment once digested.

divergences.phrase: DILIGITE IUSTITIAM QUI IUDICATIS TERRAM
divergences.older: 'Diligite justitiam,' these were / First verb and noun ... 'Qui judicatis terram' were the last (Longfellow); leaves the Latin untranslated (Cary, Norton)
divergences.lectio: DILIGITE IUSTITIAM — Love justice — were the first verb and noun ... QUI IUDICATIS TERRAM — you who judge the earth — were the last.
divergences.note: The opening words of the Book of Wisdom, which the just souls spell out across the sky in living letters. Older versions keep the Latin and trust the reader to know it; we keep the Latin (the souls literally form these letters — to translate it away would erase the image) but fold a plain English gloss right into the line so a modern reader gets the meaning without a footnote. The Latin stays as the thing seen; the English carries the sense.

divergences.phrase: la testa e 'l collo d'un'aguglia
divergences.older: The head and neck beheld I of an eagle / Delineated by that inlaid fire (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: I saw the head and the neck of an eagle / drawn out in that inlaid fire.
divergences.note: The final M of TERRAM does not stay a letter: sparks rise from it like a flock of birds and shape first a heraldic lily, then the head and neck of an eagle — Dante's sign of just empire, the Roman eagle reborn as the emblem of righteous rule. We keep the strangeness of the transformation literal (letter to lily to eagle) rather than smoothing it into a generic 'symbol of justice,' because the slow morphing is the vision.

divergences.phrase: lo pan che 'l pïo Padre a nessun serra / Ma tu che sol per cancellare scrivi
divergences.older: the bread the pitying Father shuts from none ... Yet thou, who writest but to cancel (Longfellow)
divergences.lectio: the bread the merciful Father shuts from no one ... But you, who write only to cancel it out —
divergences.note: Dante's bitter close against the corrupt papacy (aimed at John XXII): the Church now wages war not with swords but by withholding the Eucharist — excommunication and interdict — for money, denying the bread God denies to no one. 'Who write only to cancel' is precise and venomous: the pope issues decrees only to revoke benefices so the Curia can pocket the proceeds. We keep the sting rather than soften it to administrative language, and end on the threat that the Peter and Paul he trades on 'are still alive.'

divergences.phrase: Un uom nasce a la riva / de l'Indo... ov' è questa giustizia che 'l condanna?
